The Committee has also power to recommend name of all persons of the scheduled castes and Scheduled Tribes. (x) The Committee is empowered to recommend names for inclusion of all persons included in the list prepared by the Committee. (x). The Committee shall be constituted by a body called the State Legislative Assembly. (x), The State Government shall after consultation with the Committee, after considering the report of the Committee, make such further reference to it on the basis of the report of any Committee.

7131: The respondent assessee filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the levy of additional tax on the ground that unpaid "not disputed" tax was not payable. The Division Bench dismissed the same. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that no part of the evad tax levied under section 5(1) of the Act had remained unpaid and the matter should be remitted back for determination by the appellate authority. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder including those relating to refund or exemption from tax shall apply in relation to the levy and collection of the additional tax before the appeal is entertained. [890B] 2. Section 20 (1) of which provides for the payment of the additional Tax is a levy distinct from the impost under section 6B of the Act. It does not say that the tax is not levied under any other law. The power to make a provision for the payment is subject to the provisions of the relevant provisions of the statute. The fact that the quantum of the additional duty levied under section 613 is the subject matter of the appeal. [891E F] 3. The word "tax" has been defined to mean a tax leviable under the provisions of a particular Act. The definition of "tax" includes the addition to the words "anything done or intended to be done in a particular manner". The expression "anything actually done or intended" means something done or intended by a person who is not a dealer in goods but is an agent of the dealer. Therefore, the legislature has used the term "that what may be done or intended in a particular case" in the context of the expression "any thing done or intended with reference to the taxable income. [892D E] 4. The word 'income ' in the definition of " tax" in section 2(g) of the Karnataka Sales Tax Act, 1957 must be construed as meaning the amount of tax payable by the dealer. [895C D]
2907: The respondent, a member of a scheduled tribe, was granted a lease to the respondent for a period of 20 years. The respondent then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the amount claimed was not recoverable under the Assam Forest Regulation, VII of 1891, and passed an order quashing the proceeding for recovery. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The rule is applicable only to recovery of money in execution of a contract. It does not apply to recovery of the amount alleged to be due for failure to carry out the obligations of the tender by proceedings under the Assam Forests Regulation, 7 of 1891. [769 E] (ii) The rule does not apply when there are two alternative remedies available to the party claiming the same. The rule does no more than what is provided for in the rule. The rule is intended to give rise to any liability to pay a sum of money. The rule cannot be construed as retrospective operation. [770 C D] (iii) The rule has been made with reference to the rules of the Assam Forest Regulations, 769 and 770 of 1918. The Rules do not provide for payment of arrears of land revenue or other dues payable to Government. The rule provides for payment of interest on delayed payment of the amount which may be due from the principal debtor. The rule makes provision for payment of penal rent or penalty. The rule gives rise to any obligation to pay a certain amount. The rule requires payment of interest at the rate of 15% per annum. The rule also requires payment of simple interest at the rates specified in the rule and the rule provides for the payment of penal interest at the maximum rate of 12% per annum on the ground that the amount was due under Rule 10 promulgated in exercise of power under the Regulation and on that account it was recoverable as an arrear of land revenue. 2986: The appellant was tried and convicted for the offence of criminal conspiracy. On the basis of the evidence led before the Magistrate, he filed a charge sheet before the Magistrate. The appellant contended that the prosecution had failed to examine witnesses during the committal proceedings but on a perusal of the charge sheet and the documents filed before him under section 173 Cr. P.C., he did not examine any witnesses during the time when the investigation commenced; that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to take cognizance of the offence of abetment of an offence of forgery and impersonation so far as the appellant was concerned and not of the offence under section 120B of the Indian Penal Code. Held, that the Magistrate took cognizance of the offences alleged in the charge sheet because it was in respect of those offences that the police had applied to him to initiate proceedings against Bakshi Singh and the appellant was given no opportunity to examine witnesses at all. The question whether the Magistrate could have taken cognizance of the crime of conspiracy is one of fact which must be determined by the trial court. In such a case the question whether there has been a violation of the provisions of section 195A(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure or otherwise should be decided by the trial Court.

If the assessing authority fails to do so, the Assessing Authority would issue a notice to the assessee to appear and give his reasons for the same. The failure to comply with the said provision will result in denial of its right to appeal. [75E F] 3. The requirement must be satisfied before issuing the notice under sub section(4) can be dispensed with. The requirement cannot be dispensed with except when the assessing authority has recorded reasons for refusing to issue the notice. The requirement has to be satisfied before the assessing authori ty is to issue the notices. The requirement does not confer discretion on the assessing authorities to refuse to issue the notification. [75F
886: The appellant, who was a displaced person from Pakistan, entered into an agreement with the owners of certain lands in village Mohammadpur to purchase them at Rs. 5 per sq. A. 80 per sq. The terms of the agreement were that the land would be given to the appellant and that the said land would be allotted to him by the Government. The appellant made a representation to the State Government that he should be asked to make a report on the First Information Report lodged by him and that the case started by him was still pending with the police. The State Government rejected this request and directed the appellant to submit his return. Thereupon the appellant moved the High Court under section 561 A Cr. P.C., for quashing the proceedings initiated by the first information Report. The High Court held that no case had been made out for quashing the proceeding under s.561 A. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Held: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 17(3) of the Act. The allegations made against the appellant did not constitute an offence alleged but there was either no legal evidence adduced in support of the allegation or evidence adduced clearly or manifestly fail to prove the charge. The High Courts have erred in holding that there was no legal evidence to establish the charge. In the present case the allegations made against him were not proved. (ii) The High Courts are wrong in assuming that they could have taken the view that the appellant has come to this Court under article 136 of the Constitution. The High courts have failed to take into consideration the material before it. The High court has failed to take note of the fact that the appellant had come to this court by special leave, and the High Court has failed to do so. [501 H] (iii) The High court is bound to act according to law. It cannot go beyond what the High Court can interfere with the order passed by the trial court. The High 'Court does not function as appellate court. The power of the High Court to interfere with such orders are subject to the limitations imposed by the Supreme Court. The High. Court has also committed error in coming down the limits of the scope of the powers conferred by the Supreme court under
2023: The assessee was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1950 51 and 1952 52. In respect of income tax, it claimed that he had been exempted from taxation under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, in respect of income which accrued or arose to him or was received by him up to 26th January 1950. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the assessee enjoyed immunity from taxation under a law made by him during the relevant accounting year. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the appeals of the assessee. The High Court held that under the International Law, the assessee being a sovereign up to January 25, 1950, his income upto that date was exempt from taxation under an Indian Income tax. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The assessee was not liable to tax under the Covenant entered into by him with the Government of India at the time of merger. He was therefore a sovereign in India. He could not claim exemption under the Covenants. [316 C] (ii) The assessee 's income was exempt from tax under the Constitution. It was not a trading receipt. The income was exempt under the Constitution as it stood before its amendment. The exemption did not apply to the assessee. [317 D E] (iii) The exemption granted by the Ruler of the State was not intended to be extended to the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The exemption was granted by the President only after the amendment of the Constitution. The exemption granted was not intended by the President to extend the Indian IncomeTax Act, 1922 and the income derived therefrom was exempt from income tax. [318 B C] (iv) The exemption was not intended for the purpose of income tax. The exemption could not be said to be given retrospective in operation. The exemption would have come into effect only if the income was treated as income. [319 H; 321 A] (v) The exemption could be withdrawn only when there is no income in the previous year. The exemption cannot be withdrawn except in certain cases where the income has already been treated as income and the income must be deemed to be income. [420 G H] (vi) The exemption will not apply to income tax even though the income may be regarded as income.
5771: % The appellant was declared elected to the State Legislative Assembly. He filed an election petition challenging the election of the respondent, who was an elector in the Jodhpur City Constituency No. 183. His nomination paper was rejected on the ground that he had failed to file a certified copy of the relevant entry in the electoral roll of Sardarpura constituency alongwith her nomination, and that the date of scrutiny was 9.2.1985. The High Court set aside the election of respondent holding that the rejection of nomination papers of three candidates was not justified by the Returning Officer as both the candidates had attained the qualifying age of 25 years on the date of their nomination and that the rejection was improper. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the rejection order passed by the Returning officer was without jurisdiction because the rejection of the nomination papers of 3 candidates were invalid and that the result of the election was materially affected on account of improper rejection of nomination paper of 3 candidates. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has rightly held that the rejection is bad for non compliance with the provisions of Section 100(3) of the Representation of People Act, 1951. [969C] 2.1 The rejection of the candidature of 3 candidates in the electoral rolls cannot be said to have been made by any person other than the candidate of the candidate of one of the candidates. The rejection of candidate of 3 candidates having attained the qualifying off 25 years of age at the time of scrutiny and since the entries contained in the electoral Rolls indicated that they were below 30 years of age the returning officer would be entitled to be considered for purposes of the Act. [970D E] 3.2 The rejection of nomination of 3 candidates on the ground of non production of 3 candidates did not amount to any illegality or irregularity in the process of selection. The rejection was also vitiated by non compliance with law. [971E F]
2079: The appellants were convicted under section 353 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to various terms of imprisonment. They challenged the order of conviction on the ground that the two offences being fundamentally distinct in nature, could not be separately taken cognizance of. It was contended that the two sections applied only to the case of the first offence and not to the other. Held, that the second offence is one which can be separately taken for the same offence and cannot be separately taken into the first offence. In the present case, the second offence also can be separately held to have been taken for the first offence, but the third offence is not a separate offence under section 352 IPC. The second offence is not an offence under section 354 I.P.C. and it is not a substantive offence under section 365 I.P., Code. The second offences are distinct and separate in nature. The first offence is one under section 379 I.P.; section 537 I.P.) (1) The second offence does not apply to the first offence; and section 537 C.P. I.C. C.A. No. 852 of 1963, applied.

Mills claimed that the commission payment was not allowable as it was paid by the assessee in its accounts for the purpose of earning profits. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim of the appellant holding that the commission was paid to the branch managers and the commission was not admissible under Rule 12 of Schedule 1 of the Excess Profits Tax Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the appeal of the assessees. The High Courts are bound to take into account the true scope of the word "income" used in the definition of "income ' in section 2(4) of the Act. The expression "income " means income which includes income or gains included in the definition. It does not include income which includes the income of an assessee. The High courts are bound to give effect to the true scope and effect of the words "income", and they do not mean that the amount was actually paid to a branch office. The High. Courts have taken the view that the commission would be admissible under r 12(3),
6517: The respondent No. 1 is the owner of a Petrol Pump which was set up on a site in Dehradun, of which respondent No. I was the lessee. The District Magistrate issued an order under Rule 151 of the Rules for conducting the said petitioner 's premises and to grant a certificate of "No Objection Certificate" under Rule 144 of the Rules. Respondent No. 5 filed a petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order. The High Court held that the District Authority under Rule 151 could cancel the No objection certificate granted under Rule 144. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the District Authorities under Rule 151 can cancel only when the licensee ceased to have any right to use the site for storing petrol; and that the 'No objection certificate ' cannot be cancelled at all. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The District Authority under rule 151 can cancel the no objection certificate. [292B] (ii) It is clear that a 'No objection Certificate ' has been granted under Rule 151. If the licensee ceases to have any fight to use the sites for storing petrol he has no right to use them. [293E] (iii) The District Rese mits of the State Government or the State Government is not entitled to cancel the No Objection Certificate. [294F] (iv) The District Authorities are not entitled to refuse to accept the licence. [295D] (v) The District Collector is directed to consider the question whether the licence is still continuing to have any rights to use the land for storing petrol. The District Authority is directed to reconsider the matter. [296C D] (vi) The District Judge is directed to decide the matter afresh. [297H] (vii) The District Appellate Commissioner is directed to dispose of the application for granting a certificate. [308G]

6753: The appellant, a Sagar Mahila Vidyalaya was an educational institution founded by a section of the public of District Sagar (M.P.) by giving donations and is duly registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1939. On 17th November, 1933 one Govind Rao Harshe had mortgaged some agricultural land and house known as `Harhewada ' in which he had sold it to his wife. The said mortgages filed a suit for sale of the house property in dispute on 14th September, 1939 in the Court of the Sub Judge, Alipore, West Tripura, West Tripura , which was later transferred to the Court of Sub Judge, Apota, East Tripura, West Bengal. The decree holders applied for settlement of the debts on 14th Sept., 1943. The judgment debtor 's application was dismissed on 13th November, 1942. Thereafter, the decree holders filed appeals against the aforesaid order of the executing court. In the appeal before the High Court, the appellant contended that the judgment debtor had defaulted in carrying out the directions of the executing Court and as such the order passed by the Debt Relief Court granting instalments had ceased to exist and the whole amount had become payable in lumpsum. The respondent 's contention was that the judgment debtors were not entitled to execute the decree. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The decree holder was not a member of the family of the appellant and he could not be said to have been in default in carrying out any direction of the executing courts. [312 D] 2. Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act provides that where a person has entered into possession of any land or building belonging to another person, the person who is dead has no title thereto, then the decree holder will not take advantage of section 4(1)(b) of the Transfer. The decreeholder himself had to prove that the property belonged to him. He had also proved that the property was purchased by the respondent from the appellant. The respondent had failed to establish that the property had been purchased by the appellant. [313 C E] 3. The respondent having failed to establish the case that the property vested in the respondent in the respondent 's name in the year 1939, he cannot be said to be in default in paying

[717 C D] (ii) The words "shall" in section 2(1)(a) of the Act are wide enough to include all the powers of an officer in charge of a police station under Chapter XIV of the Code and they cannot be said to be in conflict with the provisions contained in the Act. The words 'shall ' in section 2 (1)(a), and (b) do not mean that the officer should be merely army officers. The words do not mean the officer who makes the complaint in writing. 5339: The assessee, a non resident company in the State of Gujarat, filed a return for the assessment years 1961 62 and 1962 63. In the return, it claimed deduction of Rs.26986 being interest paid to Barivallabnas Kalidas Estate on loans taken by her. The Income tax Officer found that out of the loans real investment was of a sum of Rs. 1250 only. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim of the assessee. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the amount of interest was not an admissible deduction under section 57(iii) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the portion of the loan was not intended to meet expenditure wholly and exclusively for the purpose of earning income. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that so far as the annual contribution is concerned the assessee had to make a annuity deposit and the earning of interest through such deposit was merely incidental. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Court rightly held that so far from the year of account relevant for the assessment year 1961 62 is concerned, it cannot be said that the income of the assessee was income derived from other sources. 1597: The appellant company was incorporated in the State of Maharashtra. In a writ petition under article 227 of the Constitution, the High Court set aside the award and remanded the matter for reconsideration of the question after examining the financial condition of the Company and came to the conclusion that the Company was in a very sound financial position and could easily bear the burden of payment of gratuity to the extent of Rs. 50,000/ or even more. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the provisions for gratuity scheme are not based on any statutory provision but have been evolved by industrial adjudication as a step to achieve social justice. The scheme is not based on an existing right of ownership or ownership of the industry which has its own life time. It does not require the workmen to pay gratuity to retiring them. The scheme cannot be said to be a mere technicality. There can be no doubt that the scheme is a piece of colourable legislation. The Act does not provide for termination of contract of employment between workmen and employers. The Act provides for termination of service of employees who had worked for long time to come. The Act imposes restrictions on the employer to make arrangements for the supply of electricity to the employees. The Act did not contemplate the supply of electrical energy. The Act merely imposed restrictions on the employers to make arrangements with regard to the supply of electric energy. The scheme was not based on a statutory provision. The Act also did not impose any new conditions.

199: The appellant was a resident of the State of Hyderabad in the State of Mysore. In the year 1951, the Indian Finance Act, 1950 came into force and the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 was enacted. Section 3 of that Act provided for the imposition of a tax on income or super tax. The appellant challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that it contravened article 14 of the Constitution as it was passed without authority to pass any order under section 3(1) of the Act. Held, that the Act did not contravene article 14 of Constitution. The Act was passed with an object of imposing a tax on the income of the assessee and the power conferred by section 13 of the Act was subject to the provisions of the Act which were not in conflict with the provisions of section 13. The Act did not provide for the levy of a tax upon persons who are not being assessed to income tax but only for the assessment years prior to April 1, 1950, and the assessment and collection of the tax on income, but only for some years after the commencement of the Constitution.

894: The appellant was declared elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. He filed an election petition for a declaration that he had been made a party to the petition but he never appeared at any stage. On the basis of the allegations contained in the petition, the Tribunal rejected the respondent 's objections and held that the appellant had not been able to prove that the respondent had committed any corrupt practice or that it could be said that the appellant was guilty of corrupt practice. The High Court upheld the order of the Tribunal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Court erred in holding that an election petition must be dismissed as it did not comply with the provisions of section 117 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. 3794: The respondent, an employee of the appellant State Electricity Board, was promoted on 30th December, 1966. 2301: The respondent Society was the owner of a plot belonging to the appellant Society. 4878: The assessee company was a public limited company. It had its registered office in the year 1958 and its assets were divided into two companies, namely, the first respondent, and the second respondent. In support of the return filed by the company it claimed that there could be no assessment to super profits tax on the company 's share sheet. The Income Tax Officer held that the amount paid up share capital as on the first day of September 1959 was not liable to super profits Tax under section 34(1)(c) of the Act. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the order of the Income Tax officer but the Tribunal allowed the appeal of the assessee and held that no assessment to Super profits tax could be made on a company in liquidation. The High Court agreed with the view taken by the Tribunal that after a company has gone into liquidation there cannot be said to be in the hands of the liquidator any amount that can be distinctly designated as paid up share Capital of the company or as 'reserve ' with respect to which the capital of the company is to be worked out as provided in Second Schedule to the Act in order to arrive at the amount or standard deduction, and dismissed the appeal of 'the assessee. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the amount of Rs. 1,00,000/ being the sum of Rs. 2,25,000/ received by the assessee from the firm 'and Rs. 4,45,000/ towards the balance of Rs. 3,50,000/ was not liable for super profits tax. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that a company in the liquidation could not be said to have paid up share, capital as on April 1, 1957 was not liable. [975B] (ii) The High Courts below have committed an error in holding that no assessment was made on a Company in liquidation. [976C D] (iii) The High court was wrong in holding that there could not be any assessment to super profit tax. [977E] (iv) The High courts proceeded on the basis that the amount payable by the assessee was not liable as the assessee was entitled to super profits.
5825: The accused persons were charged under section 302 read with section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, alleging that in furtherance of a common object of committing murder of one G.P.S.H.S.B., the deceased and injure others, all the rioters committed the murder of G.P., while the other four were armed with deadly weapons. [873E F] 2. The charge against the other accused persons including L.K.C. was not proved. The charge under section 302 IPC is that the accused caused hurt to whom the deceased was alleged to have participated in the commission or causing hurt to whom he was alleged to be present. 3872: The appellant was a sub tenant (Shikmi) under the Bhopal Act of 1932. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Board of Revenue. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition and set aside the order of Board. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant was not an occupant within the meaning of section 2(15) of the Bhopal Act, which is a person who holds land from an occupant and is, or but for a contract, would be liable to pay rent for such land to that occupant but does not include a mortgagee or a person holding land directly from Government. HELD: Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The appellant was not a person holding the land in question as a tenant. [584 C] The appellant was an occupant and the respondent No. 1 was a sub lessee under the Bhopal Land Revenue Act, 1932. He raised an objection that the complaint filed against him was not maintainable because the appellant was not holding a post where he could not be re moved from service except by or with the sanction of the Government. The High Court rejected this objection and upheld the order of magistrate. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the appellant is a public servant and therefore section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure would be attracted; (ii) the appellant cannot be removed from his service without prior approval of the Government; (iii) the appellant has no locus standi in the matter of his removal; and (iv) the appellant was neither holding a post nor held a post where the respondent was discharging his functions as such. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant is an officer who is discharging his functions under the control of the Union, and he is certainly not holding a Post where he can be removed from service for a period of 5 years. 1886: The appellant company was carrying on the business of construction of roads and drain. [635F G] (4) The question whether the contract is a contract of sale is a question of fact and not a question arising out of the execution of a contract. The question may be decided in the negative. The question as regards the validity or propriety of the agreement is one of fact and the remedy provided for in the statute is not a remedyable one. [637C D] (5 ) The question as regard
4291: The assessee was a firm of M/s. The firm consisted of M/t. Nathirmal and the assessee was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1957 58. In the course of its assessment proceedings the Income Tax Officer made enquiries about the payment of Rs. 1,07,350 in cash on the same day and directed the assessee to explain the nature of this transaction and to produce the relevant evidence of having accounted for it. On receipt of the information he issued a letter dated 9th February 1956 asking the assessee to show cause why the amount should not be recovered from him as an unaccounted money. The assessee replied that the letter was false and that the sum of Rs. I,07,0350 was sent by the assessee from Madras to the State Bank Limited for personal reasons. The assessee did not disclose any such letter nor did he make any reference to it in the letters dated 24th February 1955 and 4th March 1955 which he addressed to the assessee making inquiries about the remittance of Rs.1,07,000 and requesting the assessee to explaining the nature of these transactions and to produce relevant evidence of his own account. The assessee also made a similar request in the letter dated 9 2 1956 and 4th April, 1955. The assessee received a copy of the letter dated September 22, 1955 and the letter dated December 14, 1955. These letters were produced before the Income Tax Authorities who held the same to be the undisclosed income of the assessee. The assessee 's explanation was that the said letter was a forged document and the same was written up by the assessee. In the assessment proceedings for the assessment years 1957 58, 1958 59, 1959 60, 1960 61, 1962 58 and 1963 59, the assessee had admitted that the said letters were written up by him and those were signed by him. The assessee denied that they were read as a whole. The assessee further stated that the said entries in the books of account were not true and that the said statements were not correct. The assessee therefore filed an appeal against the order of the Income Tax authorities. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal holding that the said statement was not a genuine one and that the same could not have been relied upon by the assessee in any manner whatsoever. The Tribunal however allowed the appeal
6761: The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of wagons. In the year ending March 31, 1983 it had manufacturing goods from September 9, 1981. The wagon for which the goods were supplied to the Railway Board on payment of a price. The invoice value of the wagon charged by the appellant from the Railway Board did not include the value of the "free supply items". The respondent raised a demand that the appellant should pay the price at the rate fixed under the agreement. The appellant challenged the demand but the High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the demand. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The cost of the wagons sold by the appellant is not taken into consideration in fixing the price of the wago or its value. [962E] 2.2 The cost of wagon as a whole has not been mentioned in the agreement and the same cannot be conceived of without taking into account or consideration the cost of free supply. The cost of raw materials are required to be taken into account in determining the market value of the goods. The cost is to be taken as the price of raw materials sold. The cost has to be taken in accordance with the terms of the contract. The cost may be taken as a whole. If the cost is not taken as a part of the relevant and independent of the contract, then the value of such a part will form part of the material. [964C D; 965A C] 3.3 The cost of production of raw materials is to be paid by the assessee. The cost must have been taken as a full measure of the value of raw materials. The cost would not be the price of goods. The value of the raw materials is not taken in accordance therewith. The cost does not amount to any additional price. The cost can only be taken as an expenditure which is wholly and exclusively laid out for the purpose of the sale of the finished product. [963D E]
4107: The appellant was declared an evacuee and the house in question was declared as an evacuee property on 15 11 1951. On 11 11 1960 the Central Government granted a certificate under section 16(1) of the Evacuee Property Act, as the section then stood, for grant of a certificate. The appellant filed an application before the Assistant Custodian claiming compensation on the ground that he had been inducted as a tenant in the house by the Custodian after it was declared as a displaced person in his occupation of the house. The Additional District Judge allowed the application and directed the execution of the certificate. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant was entitled to compensation only under section 20A of the Act and not under section 20 A. HELD: (i) The appellant was entitled only to compensation under section 20. Section 20A deals with the right to compensation payable to the person who has been allotted or whose land is in the possession of the Custodian. It does not mean that the right to receive compensation must be taken away or curtailed by the statute. [999E F] (ii) The word 'possession ' in section 20A means actual taking of the total loss or damage caused to the evacuee property or part thereof. The expression "possession" in section 20 A includes actual taking of any other part of such property or part". The words "possession " in section 20(2) are wide enough to include physical taking of any part of the property or part of such other part thereof or part thereof being in the possession or part thereof". The word "possession ' occurring in section 20B of the Act is used in the widest sense and not in any technical sense. The word " posses sion" in section 2(5) of the Act means actual taking or relinquished possession of any part or part of the interest of any part thereof. [990H 991C] (iii) The word " posession" in the section means actual taking over and delivery of possession of any other person. The word ' posession ' in the section meaning of the word "possessed" in section 18(1)(a) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act. [986G H; 987A]
2018: The appellants filed a suit for possession of the entire land on the ground that she was the legal heir of Raj Kaur and the Raja of Faridkot. The suit was decreed by the trial court but the High Court dismissed both the appeals. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The suit was barred by time. [850 G] (2) The suit is governed not by article 141 of the Limitation Act, 1908 as it does not bar the limitation of time. The suit must be regarded as barred by time unless it appears otherwise expressly or by necessary implication that the period of limitation prescribed in article 114 of the Limitation Schedule has been extended to the date when the institution of the suit is alleged to have been instituted. [851 C D] (3) The suit must therefore be regarded as having been filed within time. [760 H; 761 A] (a) The suit will therefore be regarded under article 141 of Limitation Act. [852 E F]
4192: The appellant and his brother Bashir Ahmad filed a suit for possession of certain properties. The notice in question was issued by the Assistant Custodian, Deoria, under section 7 of the . The appellant challenged the notice on the ground that the information in possession of the Custodian was that they were evacuees under clause (iii) of section 2(d) of the Act and calling upon them to show cause why orders should not be passed declaring them evacueess under clause (iv) of section 3(2) of the . In appeal to this Court it was contended that the notice issued by the appellant was invalid as it did not contain any particulars of the tact containing the information in the possession of the evacuee. HELD: The notice dated November 29, 1955 was invalid as the notice issued had been issued without the knowledge of the appellant. The notice did not disclose any particulars of any particular transaction or the basis of the information. [625D E] The notice did no mention the names of the persons who were in possession of any property or part of the property. It was therefore not necessary that the notice must also be accompanied by a copy of the relevant portion of the notice which was served on the appellant. [626E F]
4919: The petitioners, who were the members of a public company, carried on the business of editing and publishing newspapers, periodicals, magazines etc., and other bodies carrying on the same kind of business. They also challenged the imposition of the import duty by the State Government under section 25 of the . The petitioners contended that the imposition was discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution as it had led to the increase in the price of newspapers and the impost of the import licence fee by the State of India. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned imposition is not arbitrary or mala fide. [525D] 2. The petitioners are entitled to be treated as violent and violative of Article 14 of the constitution. It is well settled that the power to impose a tax is discretionary and must be exercised sparingly and with circumspection and without any limitation. The power to impose such a tax is not arbitrary and excessive. [526E F] 3. The power conferred by sub s.(1) of section 25 of which is a general power to impose tax is subject to the provisions contained in the Act. It is not open to the legislature to delegate its powers to make laws in respect of matters enumerated in the First Schedule to the (51 of 1975). The power to legislate in respect of any matter specified in the first part of section 25 is confined only to the matters specified therein. The power so delegated can only be exercised in exercise of the power conferred by the second part of section 26(2) of the Act. The power of the legislature is limited only to the subject matter of the power to legislate. The power is not restricted either to the subject subject matter of any other law or to the subject. The power has been expressly made subject to the limitations imposed by the statute. The power does not mean to restrict the subject matter alone. The power cannot be exercised for purposes of the Act except for the purpose of ensuring that the object is to secure the maintenance of public order. [527F G] In the instant case, the power to levy a tax is specifically confined to the subject, namely, the subject matter, of the power of the Parliament. The power includes both the power and the subject matter to the subject
1604: The appellant, a Hindu widow and his brother, was brought on record in the Civil Suit No. 18 of 1973 filed by her for partition of the joint family properties between the four brothers. In the said suit the respondent who was the sole surviving son of the deceased daughter of the appellant, who was the only son of the younger brother of the deceased. The appellant 's father died on May 5, 1974. The respondents were impleaded as defendants in the suit. The appellant contended that sometime before his death, Pitchayya took Venkayya, the son of his brother, Chimpirayya, Pitched to the two grand children of the appellant and that he had no knowledge of the declaration of fixed intention to divide the property belonging to him, to enable him to hand over the property to his two grand children. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the question whether the recitals in the will in the will themselves constituted a partition in status could not be allowed to be raised as that point was raised only for the first time in the High Court. On appeal, the High Court held that the question of the recitals contained in the will was a question of fact and it was not open to the High Court to raise the question of adoption or partition. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court has rightly answered the question in favour of the appellant. [850D] (2) The High Courts have always decided that the question about the existence of a will is a question of law which can be referred only to the decision of the Supreme Court. It cannot be said that the question must be decided by the Supreme Court in the absence of any statutory provision or rules or by necessary implication. [851E F] (3) The question whether the will in question is a question under section 10(5)(b) of the Indian Evidence Act is a question which may arise when the parties are divided into two groups of persons, one having knowledge of the fact that the other is a matter which is not a question of the nature of the document but is a question relating to the effect of the execution of the will. [855H; 856A B] (4) The question of
4869: The appellant was the owner of a shop. He filed an application under section 12 read with section 16 of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act 1972 for declaration that the shop was vacant and he required the same for his personal need. The application was contested by the respondent tenant on the ground that he was the heir of Naubat Singh in his occupation. The Rent Controller rejected the application holding that the appellant had been living with the deceased Naubat. On appeal, the District Judge held that the appellant could not be an heir on the basis of the will executed by Naubat Singha, but that the appellant was entitled to get the benefit of section 14 of the U P.P. Act No. 13 of 1972. In revision, the District judge held that the landlord was not entitled to get any benefit of section 16(1)(d) of the Act. The High Court also held that the tenant was not a person against whom proceedings under section 7A of the Act were pending immediately before the commencement of the Act and that the appellant cannot be an heir after the death of the landlord. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant could not have been an heir on a validatedatedatedatedion of his tenancy rights. [892C] 2. Section 14 is a procedural provision and it has to be construed as directory and not mandatory. It is only when the legislature makes it clear that the legislature does not intend to prescribe a period of limitation for filing of a suit under section 14(2) of the U .P. Act. The word 'or ' means "a person" and not merely a person against which proceedings under section 6A of the U Act are pending immediately before such commencement. The words "for any period" in section 14(3) of the said Act are wide enough to include a person who is a tenant or who is a person against whose eviction proceedings are pending immediately prior to its amendment in 1976. [893E F] 3. The expression "for any Period" in section 15(3) means "in order to get the benefits of section 14(1)". The words "to get the benefit
951: The appellants were assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1952 53 and 1955 54. They filed a return under the Income Tax Act, 1922 showing a net return of Rs.4,78,5945 0 as assessable income. The Income Tax Officer did not accept the report and directed that immediate steps be taken to recover under the Income tax Act from the appellants. The appellants then moved the High Court by way of a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the Income Tax Officer had no power to assess or reasses the concealed income; (ii) the Income tax Officer could not take action under section 5(2) of the Indian Income Tax Act; and (iii) the IncomeTax Officer could not proceed with the assessment after the expiry of the period prescribed by the Act. HELD: (i) The Income tax Officer is entitled to take action under the provisions of the Indian Incometax Act if he has reason to believe that the income has been misappropriated or that the income is not liable to pay any tax. [501 B] (ii) The Income Tax officer had jurisdiction to make an order for the assessment year 1951 52 and the Investigation Commission had to examine the facts and circumstances of each case. The Commission had to consider the relevant facts and circumstances relating to the assessment before it. The Commission was therefore entitled to take into account the fact that the income had escaped assessment. [510 C D] (iii) The Income. tax Officer had jurisdiction to take action on the report having been conferred upon him by the Government of India. He had also jurisdiction to take proceedings against the appellants with a view to assess or reassessment. [511 E F] (iv) The Income and tax Officer had no jurisdiction to initiate proceedings under the Income and tax Act. The Income tax Officers had no authority to go behind the orders of the Commission. The Commission 's order was made without jurisdiction and the Income tax Officers could not have proceeded with the assessment. [509 G H] (v) The Income, tax Officer had power to revise the assessment proceedings. The Income andtax Officer could not act as if the Income andtax Officers had acted in his own discretion
3187: The appellants were operating routes from the State of Uttar Pradesh. The routes mentioned above were notified by the U.P. Government under section 68D(2) of the (Act 4 of 1939). The Regional Transport Authority, in pursuance of a scheme approved by the State Government, issued a notification dated February 20, 1962, under section 68C(1) of the Act, inter alia, exempting the services of stage carriages and other transport services on inter state routes as a result of which private operators including those who had been granted permits by the Regional Transport Authorities of Rajasthan were excluded from those routes. The appellants filed writ petitions challenging the validity of the said notifications. The High Court allowed the writ petitions holding that the impugned schemes were not valid because they were not covered by any provision for exemption or renewal of the services of the stage carriages and the same was not invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the impugned notifications were ultra vires as they did not provide for grant of facilities to the employees of the State transport undertaking at all levels. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The scheme is not one for carrying out the purpose of the Act and the same cannot be held to be invalid merely because it provides for grant of facility to the employees. [839E] 2. The scheme was not a complete code of business but only a part of the scheme. It does not say that the scheme should be framed in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The scheme must be read along with the objects of the Act itself. The scheme has to be construed strictly and there is no reason why it should not be so construed. [840B C] 3. The scheme cannot be construed differently. The scheme can be construed differently and there may be some ambiguity in the language employed in the statute. The words used in the statute are "may" in the definition of "shall". The word "shall" means "that the expression 'shall ' means "that he shall '." [841H; 842A B]
2711: The appellants applied for a permit to run a passenger bus service on the ground that the route for which they applied though one not yet opened, was necessary in public interest. The Regional Transport Authority rejected the applications and the appellants filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the order of the Tribunal contending that no appeal against the order of rejection of the applicants under section 64(a) of the Act was maintainable as the decision of the Appellate Tribunal was not final and that the decision of this Court was binding on the appellant. Held: (i) The question whether a proposed route should be opened or not is one of fact and law must be decided by the Tribunal. In the present case the decision of a Single Judge of the High Court was not final but it was open to the R.T.A. to decide whether a proposed stage when the "general order" passed under section 47(3) can be reconsidered, for, the order under section 48 is subject to section 47 including the provisions of section 47(1). The decision of the Supreme Court in the present case does not affect the question whether the decision of an authority below the High Court is final or not.
6655: The appellant was a manufacturer of paper and paper board. He imported the goods from the respondent company, which were manufactured by him. The excise tariff was contained in the First Schedule to the . The said exemption was granted to the appellant. The Assistant Collector of Central Excise held that 'egg trays and other similar products manufactured by the appellant were "articles of paper or paper board" within the meaning of Item 17(4) of the new Tariff. The Assistant Collec tor of Central Excise, Pune Division passed an order dated January 28, 1982 whereby he held that 'Celvay 's goods manufactured by the appellants were classifiable under Item 17(3). On appeal by special leave, the Customs, Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal set aside the order of the Assistant Collector holding that 'eg g trays and others manufactured by the assessee were entitled to the benefit of the exemption. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The duty demanded by the Assistant Collector for six months prior to the issue of show cause notice dated May 4, 1984 is legally sustainable and with regard to recovery of the duty for earlier period from March 1, 1986. [324D] 2.1 The exemption granted to the Assistant Collector was not applicable to printed cartons (including flattened or folded printed cartons) whether in assembled or unassembled condi tion. The duty demanded was not the first time as it was payable on all types of egg traso cidies. The duty was payable at the appropriate rate leviable on all types. The duty had been paid after considering the reply of the appellant to the said show cause notice. [325G H; 326A B] 2.2 The duty demanded under the relevant entry in the First schedule to the Act cannot be taken into consideration in these cases. [321F G] 312 In the instant case, the duty demanded by him was admittedly the duty demanded under section 11 A(l) of the Act. The duty so demanded was actually paid. The duty thus sought to be recovered from the appellant was not the second time as the duty was payable on the first time. [323H, 320B C]
1506: The prosecution alleged that on or about the 18th May, 1961, at about 6.30 A.M., the appellant and his party were armed with deadly weapons. It was further alleged that on the same day and at the same time and place the said members of the unlawful assembly carried out their unlawful object and in so doing, the appellants caused injuries to them. The trial court acquitted all the five accused persons but convicted them under section 302/149 I.P.C. and sentenced each one to death and directed that the other two accused persons be released on bail. On appeal the High Court held that the charge under section 302 was not proved against Baland Singh and Piara Singh as well as the sentence of death imposed on them had been confirmed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court erred in holding that the charge against Baland Sing vs Daljit Singh, Sukhjit Singh, and Pira Singh was not proved beyond a reasonable doubt and that the charge could not have been proved against Balanand Singh. HELD: (1) The High Court has rightly held that the charges against Baland singh were not proved against B. When the prosecution case is that on the basis of the evidence adduced by the prosecution witnesses, the High Court should not have interfered with the acquittal of the other two. [186 C D] (2) The High Courts have taken into consideration the evidence of the witnesses examined in the present case. The High Court was right in coming to the conclusion that the charge of the appellants had not been proved against B and that the appellants had committed the offence of rioting and causing injuries to them, because they had no licence to kill the deceased. [185 H; 186A]
3351: The appellant was convicted for an offence under section 420 read with section 511 I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year and fine of Rs. 2,000/ . The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the charge against him was not proved beyond reasonable doubt and that the prosecution had failed to prove the case beyond all reasonable doubt. HELD: (1) It is well settled that in a criminal case the evidence must be accepted as good and cogent reasons are given by the court which should be satisfied. [279B] (2) There is no reason why the High Court should have interfered with the acquittal of the accused. The fact that the accused was present along with the complainant party at the time of the occurrence would not affect the question whether he was present at the trial. The fact of the accused party was also known to the complainant party. The fact does not mean that the accused party knew the identity of the complainant party and the complainant party was not known to the accused. [270E F]
7070: The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court for a direction to the Government to approve and publish the list of District Munsifs prepared by the Public Service Commission. On May 28, 1984 the High Court intimated the Government that the list was approved and published on December 27, 1986. In the meantime, the High Court decided to issue directions regarding filling up of vacancies in the category of munsifs and requested the Government to initiate appropriate steps for selection of candidates. The Government thereafter issued a notification dated March 11, 1985 inviting applications from the public service commission and the third candidate was selected. The Government accordingly wrote to the Public Service Commis sion to select twenty candidates in the category. Thereafter, the High court directed the Government to prepare the list of eligible candidates in the ratio laid down in the order dated December 23, 1986. The State Government again issued another notification dated September 25, 1986 stating that the list of the remaining candidates recommended by the Public Services Commission should be approved and published in the subsequent newspapers. The Government also reported that the list had been approved and published. The Government again issued a further notification dated August 3, 1986 stating the list of other candidates recommended by Public Service Commission and the third respondent was selected. On July 11, 1990 the High Court directed the Government not to fill up the vacancies of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes candidates who were working as such. The Government then sent a communication to the Public Services Commis sions to the Public Serv ices Commission to the effect that the names of the appellants including the writ petitioners should be included in the list of qualified candidates in the list recommended by the Commission. The Government thereupon issued a further direction to the Public services Commission to approve and promote the names in view of the fact that the Government had already taken steps to fill up all the vacancies. The appellants challenged the said order before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the Government could not alter or modify the order of merit determined by the Commission and that the Government was bound to revise the earlier order. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Government has no power to alter or abrogate the order of the Commission. It is open to the Government, if it thinks fit, to do so at
2362: The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction against the respondent tenant under section 13(1) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 on the ground that the tenant had failed to pay rent and the tenancy was not in accordance with law. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it holding that the tenant was in arrears of payment of rent and permitted increases and as such not entitled to the protection of the Act. In appeal by special leave, HELD: The provisions of the Act are not attracted to the case. [312 D] The provisions of section 12(3)(a) of the Act do not require that the conditions mentioned therein must be satisfied before the expiry of the period of one month after notice referred to in sub section (2) of Section 12(3) (a). The conditions necessary for the applicability of section 12 (3) (b) are not present when the arrears of rent is due to the tenant or the landlord has paid or tendered the amount of the rent or permitted increases from time to time. The said conditions are not present. [313 C E]
7102: The appellant and respondent No. 3 were both appointed to the Service on May 26, 1975 on the basis of selection by direct recruitment. In the first instance, the State Government issued a notification dated June 14, 1977 that the post of District Magistrate should be filled up by direct recruitment in all the services from 20% quota for Scheduled Castes and backward classes. On the basis of the said notification, the appellant and respondent Nos. 3 was selected as a Muslim belonging to the Scheduled Castes and from amongst other backward classes. Respondent No. 3 filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the appellant and Respondent No.3 was not entitled to any relief. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The order dated May 5, 1975 made by the State Government relating to persons belonging to Scheduled Castes and Backward Classes was made applicable to the posts in the service. The order dated March 24, 1976 made by the Government of Punjab, Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Group 'C ' was made applicable only to the posts of Scheduled Castes in the State of Punjab. [516D E] 2.1 The appellant and Respondent Nos. 3 are not entitled to the benefit of the order dated May 25, 1975 made under the provisions of the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1976. They have been appointed in 1979. The appellant and respondents Nos. 3 to 7 were promoted to the post of Additional Deputy Commissioner on the basis that the vacancies to be reserved for Scheduled Castes had to be offered to them to the Scheduled Caste and from amongst those candidates belonging to backward classes. The appellant is entitled to the same benefits of the order of the State Government. [517E F]

In December, 1967 the Government issued a notification under section 27 of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1947 fixing minimum rates of wages for employees in scheduled employments. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that it was not applicable to the industry of the respondent but only to the industries which were carried on by the appellant. The High Court held that the Explanation indicated that potteries industry in entry 22 was intended to cover all possible articles of pottery industry. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The definition of "publication" in section 2(g) of the Gujarat Act is wide enough to include within its scope the expression 'uncars ' industry ' as defined in the Act. It cannot be said that the definition of "potteries industry" includes any other establishment or establishments which are included in the definition of 'publication '. [5H; 5A B] 2. The definition of 'discountories ' means "anything done in connection with the employment of any person". The definition of `publication ' has been made in the first part of section 2(h) of the Act. The definition is wide enough for the purpose of the Act and does not exclude any other activity from the definition of `Publication '. The definition does not make any sense to indicate that any activity of an establishment which is covered by the definition. The definition also does not show that the word 'publication" means an extension of the definition. [5B C] 3. The definition includes "alone", and "alone". The definition does no more than include "a process or blanish". The definition is very wide enough to say that "the process or blandish" is intended to cover the whole activity of the employer. The definition further indicates that the activities of the employer have to be taken into account in the course of the work of the employer and the nature of the work. The definition therefore does not contemplate any activity of the employee. The definition thus does not contemplate an activity of an employee. The explanation shows that the employee is employed in some other establishment which
8: The appellant, a Hindu, inherited his father 's estate in the east row of Vellalar kedi and his widow Parbari. He died on 25th April 1905 leaving behind him as his near relations his adoptive mother. In the suit for possession of certain properties, the appellant claimed that the properties vested in the plaintiff as the adopted son 's widow and her daughter and that the properties were given to Nagammal to the appellant. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed this decree holding that the properties had been given to Nagamal to the plaintiff as well as the defendants. Held, that the appellant was entitled to get the properties in absolute right after the death of the testator 's wife and mother. The property in dispute must be held to be joint family property. It is not necessary that the property should be divided between the parties or that the property must be divided between two or more brothers. The property must be regarded as joint family property and it must be held that the property has been given to the plaintiff in the present litigation.
2608: The Government of India, by a Notification dated December 19, 1961, exempted certain classes of persons from the operation of the provisions of the Goa, Daman and Diu (Administration) Ordinance, 1962. By section 1 of the Act, the Government of India was authorised to extend to Goa, other laws in force in India. Section 3(1)(a) of the Act provided that all authorities shall continue to perform their functions and all laws with such adaptations as were necessary, be deemed to have been done under the Act. The petitioner challenged the validity of the said order on the ground that it contravened article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as the provisions of article 19(5) (f) and (g) of the Constitution (Twelfth Amendment) Act, 1962, which was passed to enable effect to be given to the Union of India, had become a part of India and could not be enforced against the petitioner. Held, that the impugned order did not infringe any fundamental rights guaranteed by article 19(1)(f) of the Constitu tion. Article 6 of the Constitution of India provides that if any person is entitled to the right conferred by the Constitution or the law of the State, the right may be exercised by the President or the Governor, the President may exercise it or even without giving him an opportunity to show cause against it. The petitioner was not entitled to the protection of article 19 because he was not entitled either to the right or the law.
4946: The appellant, a trade union registered under the Trade Union Act, was employed in the Chambal Hydel Irrigation Scheme under the Government of Madhya Pradesh. The appellant raised three demands and served notices of these demands on the Deputy Chief Engineer, Central Government Road Construction Corporation Ltd., Bhopal. The demand was refused by the State Government. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of the State Government refusing to refer the dispute for adjudication. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that no reference was necessary or not. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The State Government had by refusing to refer it to the Tribunal. [312 D] (2) The question whether a reference is necessary or not is one which depends upon the facts of the case. If the claim made is patently frivolous, or is clearly belated, the appropriate Government may refuse to make a reference. But it would appear from the history of the case that the delay has been most due to the fact that the case was pending before various Courts. [313 C E] (3) The State Govern ment should have taken into consideration all relevant aspects including the fact that there was delay in making the reference. The State Government could not refuse to refer the matter to the Tribunal without examining the merits of the case and decide it. [314 A B] (4) The State of U.P. vs Shareekantan, [1968] 2 S.C.R. 642, referred to.
5318: The appellant company was carrying on the business connection with the Indian Company and its principal object of selling its goods in India. In the assessment year 1962 63, the Income tax Officer assessed the respondent company to income tax for the assessment years 1957 58 and 1958 59. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the non resident company had a business connection with it and therefore the Indian Company was rightly treated as an agent of the non resident companies under section 163 of the Income tax Act, 1961. On appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal confirmed the order of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the respondent had no business connection with them and so far as the only company under Group C is concerned, the assessee had no business connections with them and therefore the non resident Company in respect of the goods sold by it to customers in India. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court has rightly answered the questions referred to and relied upon the decision of this Court in the case of Commissioner of Income tax, Punjab vs R.D. Sharma, [1957] S.C.R. 724. [197 E] (2) The High Courts have taken into consideration the correctness of the view expressed by this Court in its earlier decisions. [197 G H; 197 A] (3) The High courts have accepted the view that no attempt had been made by the Revenue to traverse the facts stated therein, referred to and relying upon the decision in the case in Commissioner of Income Tax, Punjab vs M/s. R. D. Sharma & Co., [1957] SCR p. 950, followed.
2081: The appellants were convicted under sections 326/149, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years each. They were acquitted by the trial court on the ground that they had been convicted under section 302/149, I.P.C. but their conviction was upheld by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court acted without jurisdiction in altering the finding of acquittal of Lakhan as the charge under section 302 IPC and that the High Courts have no jurisdiction to interfere with the findings of acquittal of such a charge. HELD: (i) The High Court has not committed any error apparent on the face of the record. [647B] (ii) It is well settled that when an accused is acquitted of an offence under section 302, he cannot be convicted for having committed the offence of murder unless he is charged under section 302 or section 34. Section 304, I. P. C. provides that if there is more than one person than one who is alleged to have been guilty of the offence of causing the death of another then the person can be convicted under section 326, I. R. for being a member of an unlawful assembly. [648E F] (iii) The High Courts have taken into consideration the fact that the appellant was acquitted of the charge under s.302 read with section 149 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court therefore could not have held that the appellant had been acquitted of the charges under section 302. [649F G]
3944: The respondent assessee was a registered firm carrying on business in the manufacture of cloth and other parts of its factory. In the accounting year ending March 31, 1975 the Income Tax Officer assessed the respondent under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 for the relevant assessment years 1963 64 and 1964 65. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the assessment order. On appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal held that the commission paid during the relevant period was deductible under section 36(1)(iv) of the Income Tax Act and that the deduction claimed by the assessee was allowable as it had been paid after the expiry of the relevant assessment year. The High Court took the view that the expression "salary" as given in the Shorter Oxford Dictionary and Stroud 's Judicial Dictionary and upon the manner in which the term was defined in Rule 2(h) of Part A of the Fourth Schedule to the Act, that unless commission or bonuses are fixed periodical payments not dependent on a contingency, they are not covered by the term "salary". It further held that the deduction from the amount received by the assessee to its salesmen was not deductible. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The definition of "salary", as given in Section 2(h), is wide enough to include all allowances and perquisites and commission payable by the assessee. [790B] (2) The definition includes all allowances and adaptation, and also includes all other allowances and pero dition. The definition merely contemplates payment of salary in respect of an item of income. The definition does not contemplate any payment of salary. The definition has no reference to the nature of the work done or the actual work done. [791E F] (3) The definition is wide enough for the purpose of section 2(h). There is nothing in the definition which excludes the definition from consideration. The definition cannot be said to have been made with reference to the class of work done or employment. [799C] (4) The definition does no more than mention the word 'salary ' as used in Chapter IXA of the Act. The definition is clear and unambiguous. The definition itself indicates that the expression 'salary means the salary pay

3961: The respondent was dismissed from service by an order of the Deputy Inspector General of Police. 6954: The appellant company was incorporated in the United States of America on January 22,1987. In 1978 the Prize Chits and Money Circulation Scheme (Banning) Act, 1978 was enacted for banned promotion or conduct of prize chits or money circulation schemes. The said scheme was to be implemented with effect from 1st April, 1977. The scheme was to operate till August 31, 1979. On December 24, 1979 the Reserve Bank issued a circular that the scheme should be implemented with retrospective effect from July 8, 1980. The appellant company filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the notice dated September 23, 1979 as under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed both the writ petitions but appeals preferred by the Peerless General Finance and Investment Company Ltd., and the Company appealed to this Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the directions given by the High Court were contrary to the provisions of the Banning Act which had come into force w.e.f. 1st April 1977; that the directions contained in the Circular dated December 24,1979 did not affect the rights of the appellant; that the direction contained in the circular dated December 24. 1979 did not affect any right of the appellant to receive the benefits of the scheme; that the appellant could not claim any refund; that the High Court erred in holding that the directions were contrary to law; that the direc tions were contrary to section 14(1)(a) of the Indian Contract Act; that the provisions of section 15(2) of the Act were not inconsistent with the provisions of Section 19(3) of the Contract Act; and that the directions made by the High Courts were contrary to their statutory provisions. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The directions given by this Court in the instant case cannot be challenged on the ground that they were contrary to any provision of the statute or the rules framed thereunder. [830D] 2.1 The direction given by the Supreme Court in the present case is contrary to the law laid down by this Court. The directions are contrary to the statutory provisions of the Act and the directions are contrary thereto. The directions have been contrary to the provision of the Act. The directions were contrary and void.
125: The plaintiffs, the trustees of a will of a building in Bombay, obtained a decree for ejectment against the defendant on the ground that the suit was barred by limitation. The defendants contested the suit on the grounds that the suit had been filed after the expiry of the period prescribed under section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, which came into force on January 1, 1948, and that the suit as well as the suit was not a suit between a landlord and a tenant relating to the recovery of rent or possession of any premises to which any of the provisions of this Part of the Act applied, was barred by time. Held, that the suit having been filed after expiry of the said period, the plaintiffs were entitled to be ejected from the property in the suit. The suit was therefore not one for recovery of rent and the suit was therefore barred by limitation; it was also barred by limitation and the suit could not be dismissed on the plea of limitation.

3941: The appellant was a dealer in the purchase and sale of Vanaspati plant on the basis that it would be availing of the exemption granted by the State Government and would be charging sales tax at the rate of 31/2%. The State has power to make laws for carrying on trade or business or trade or trade in any part or of the territory subject to the provisions of article 19 (1) (g) of Constitution. The power to legislate in respect of goods specified in Entry 25 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution is not confined only to the operation of the impugned legislation but also to the operation thereof. [657 C] 4. The State cannot levy sales tax on the sale of goods brought from outside the State except in accordance with the procedure prescribed by the Central Acts. The State does not have the power to levy sales tax for a period of three years from the date of commencement of production. The State must therefore be free to impose restrictions on inter alia the right to carry on the trade of the class of dealers in the goods. [658 H 6
201: The petitioners who were displaced persons from Pakistan, filed a petition under article 32 of the Constitution praying for a writ of certiorari quashing the orders dated August 7, 1949, and the order dated September 5, 1948, terminating the allotment of evacuee lands to them. The petitioners contended that they had been deprived of their fundamental right of property and were unable to hold such land within the meaning of article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. Held, (per Sinha, C. J., Wanchoo and Shah, jj.), that the impugned order was not illegal or without jurisdiction on the ground that no notice of cancellation of allotment had been issued to them. It was not correct to say that the impugned Act did not require that the land should be allotted to them but that the order was passed by the first respondent on the 14th October, 1953, which was to the following effect: " Government have decided that in the case of persons who were able to secure possession of part of the land, the land shall be allotted to him, but an order made by the first re spondent on the 14st October, 1953 is the first order which is to the extent of the land so transferred to the person claiming possession of the land.
59: The petitioner, a company incorporated under the Indian Compa ny Act, 1882, and having its registered office at Bombay, challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that it was not liable to pay compensation. Held, that article 31 (1) of the Constitution contemplates a law being passed authorising deprivation of property in public interest by the State, so that the "depriation of property" is within the meaning of article 31(1). The words "depriate tion of property" in cl. (1) Of article 31(2) show that it is a prohibition of unauthorised compulsory acquisition or taking possession of it and required payment of compensation. It does not mean that the law must be made by the legislature. In the present case the impugned Act was passed by Parliament and the State Legislature could not have enacted the Act for the acquisition of property for the purpose of the Union. The Act did not provide for any restriction on the right to property except by the State itself. The Act was therefore ultra vires the Constitution.
