The appellant filed a suit claiming damages from the respondent on the ground that the contract was not binding on the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed this decision. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) It is well settled that where a contract is made in evidence by conduct or other circumstances beyond his control, it is difficult to hold that the parties intended that the contract should be fake or that the contract must have been executed in their favour. [950 C] (2) The mere fact that the parties had put forward a claim to the effect that the contract would become impossible if the contract was made operative. The question whether the contract was legal or illegal was immaterial because the contract was merely an act which the parties wanted to make it void. [951 D E] (3) The principle of res judicata evolved by this Court does not apply to the present case. [955 F G] (4) The principle that the parties did not intend that the contract will become concluded by the agreement. [956 H]
4724: The appellants were the Excise officials of the State of Assam. They had been granted a licence under the Assam Excise Rules, 1945 and the same was renewed by the Deputy Commissioner to be a mere benamidar of a prominent businessman of Dibrugarh. On the expiry of the period fixed for grant of the licence, the Government of Assam by its order dated February 11, 1982 directed the Deputy Commissioner that the matter should be referred to the Board of Revenue for decision afresh in the light of the observations made by it. Thereafter, the Deputy Commissioner passed an order on February 11,1982 whereby the appellants were held to be a single holder of a licence. The appellants challenged the validity of this order before the High Court. The High Court quashed the order of the Board of revenue on the ground that the appellants were not entitled to any privilege in preference to the appellants under the note beneath r. 223(2) of the Assam Excise Rule, 1965. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court has rightly held that the appellants are not entitled to the benefit of the proviso to section 35 of the Act. [830D] (a) The question whether the appellants are entitled to the grant of a privilege in preference is one of fact which must be determined on the facts and circumstances of each case. In the instant case, the appellants are admittedly carrying on the business of selling liquor from Jorhat in the State of Bihar. The Board of Revenue has taken into consideration the relevant provisions of the Assam Act, 1935, and the rules framed thereunder. The Board has taken into account all the relevant provisions in the Assam Excise and Sales Tax Rules, 1965. The Board took into account the relevant provisions relating to the grantees of licences issued to them. The Board did not take into account the material on record as to how the grantors of licences issued by the Government of India have been obtained. The Board had taken into account the evidence that the first respondent had purchased the liquor shop with the appellants ' father and his brother. The appellants were not given any opportunity to explain their conduct or conduct in obtaining the licence. The Board could not have taken into account any other material on record. The appellants are not therefore entitled to the relief claimed. [831
3219: The respondent, a Hindusthan Muslim Family Trust, was assessed to tax under the Income Tax Act, 1961. In respect of the assessment years 1955 56, 1956 57 and 1958 59 the income tax Officer included the income for the said four years in the assessment year 1957 58 and 1958 59. On the question whether the income from the aforesaid two trust deeds were not produced before the Income Tax officer when he made the original assessments for the four years in question, HELD: (1) The income tax Officer had no jurisdiction to assess the income for each year in question as the income chargeable to tax for the relevant assessment years. [650 E] (2) The High Court was right in holding that the income tax officer could not be held to have been properly computed for the assessment years. The High Court did not accept the explanation given by the Income Tax Officer that the income derived from the aforesaid three ladies had escaped assessment within the meaning of section 147 of the Indian Income Tax Act. [649 C] (3) The High Courts have taken into consideration the fact that the income has escaped assessment. It is well settled that where the income has been assessed to tax on the income chargeable under the head " profits" or income chargeable under any other law, it must be presumed that the income had escaped assessment. If the income has not been assessed to income tax, it would be difficult to hold that the income should be treated as having escaped assessment. [648 H 649 A] (4) The High courts have taken into account the facts which they found that the income was not assessable to income tax. The High Courts are bound to take into account all the relevant facts and circumstances of each case. [647 D] (5) The High court has taken into account all material facts necessary for completing the assessment years 1954 55 and 1955 57. The High court was wrong in taking into account the fact that there was no evidence to show that the income of the respondent was not assessable. [646 F G]
2587: The respondent firm carried on the business of buying and selling cotton and pressing cotton at Bamala. The respondent purchased unginned cotton and after ginning the cotton by a mechanical process and removing the seeds sold the ginned cotton to customers outside the State. In respect of cotton seeds sold by it to registered dealers, the respondent claimed deduction from the purchase turnover under section 5 (2) (a)(vi) of the Punjab Sales Tax Act, 1948. The assessing authority did not allow the deduction holding that the goods sold were different from those purchased. The High Court allowed the writ petition filed by the respondent. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have taken into account the facts of each case in which the matter has been referred to the Supreme Court. [501B] 2. The High courts have taken into consideration the relevant facts of each ease and are therefore entitled to the benefit of the decision of this Court. [401D E] 3. The facts of each one case show that the respondent was liable to pay tax under section 5(2)(a)(vi). The fact that the respondent had purchased unginning cotton and cotton seeds for manufacturing them could not be subject under section 15 to the provisions of the Act. [408G H] 4. The High court followed its previous decision in Patel Cotton Company Private Ltd. vs State of Punjab & Ors., [1963] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 791, relied upon.
2428: The appellants were the tenants of a portion of the land in dispute. They purchased the rights of the respondents and sought to be evicted under section 117 of the Transfer of Property Act, as amended by the Bihar Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1976. The appellants resisted the suit on the ground that it had not been brought within the purview of the Act and hence not maintainable. The trial court decreed the suit but the first Appellate Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed it. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the lease was invalid as it did not conform to the provisions of the Act, and therefore the lease was not valid. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts of Patna and Calcutta are well established that the provisions of Section 117 of the Act are not applicable to a lease of a homestead though that homestead is a part of an earlier lease which is admittedly an agricultural lease and to which the provisions of section 117 of Transfer of Property Acts are not applicable. [902B] 1.2 It is well settled that where a statute contains a provision dealing with a penal provision or the same rules or orders made thereunder, such provision cannot be said to have been enacted for the purpose of the Act. If the statute provides for the remedy of a penalty, the legislature has no power to amend or repeal any particular law. [903E F] 1.3 The decision in Arun Kumar Sinha and Ors vs Durga Charan Basu, ; , relied upon.
1859: The assessee, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act 7 of 1913, was carrying on business in the City of Madras and in particular in the Andhra country. In its accounting year the income derived from the said premises were utilised for the purpose of the assessment years relating to which the assessee had purchased a building and made substantial alterations, additions and improvements therein. The assessee claimed that the income should be applied solely towards the promotion of its objects as set forth therein and no portion thereof should be paid or transferred to the assessee. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was not a charitable institution but a charitable institution. The Tribunal accepted the assessee 's contention that the income was exempt under section 4(3) (i). The High Court in reference held against the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the income received by the assessee was exempt under the provisions of section 4(1)(i) because it was not exempt under section 6(3)(ii); that the income must be deemed to have been received by the appellant and therefore the exemption granted by the Income tax Officer was not allowable; and that the income could be said to be in the nature of income already received by the asses see. HELD: Dismissing the appeals, Held: (i) The income received by an assessee is exempt under section 3(2) (i) of the Income tax Act, 1922, and the income so received is exempt under the provision of section 4 (3) (iii) of the Act. The income received in the previous year cannot be said to have been exempt under section 9(3) of the Indian Income tax Act. The benefit of the exemption must accrue only when the income has been received by a person who is employed in connection with the purposes of the assessment year. [869 C D] (ii) The income which is sought to be taxed is exempt under Section 4(3)(i) of Act 2 of 1947. The income which has been utilised for the purposes of assessment under the head " profits or gains" is exempt under s.4(3)(iii) of Act 1 of 1948. The income thus received by the respondent which is a public trust, is exempt under Sec. 4
2736: The appellants claiming a share in the joint Hindu family property as successors in interest of one Kothandaraman alias Kumarasami Naidu, respondent No. 1, and respondent No. 2, were adopted by the appellant 's father. The suit was decreed by the trial court on the ground that the adoption was not binding on the plaintiff but it was not necessary to obtain the consent of the nearest sapindas of her husband. The first appeal preferred by the appellants was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The adoption is made with the consent of all the parties to the suit. It is not necessary to have the consent of any other person who has been impleaded as a party to the suit or to implead him in the proceedings. [503 D] (2) The adoption was made with the permission of the Court which granted the consent. The adoption was not made with the previous consent of the parties. The consent must be given in the plaint and the Court should give its own opinion whether the adoption was for public good. [504 C] (3) The adoption cannot be said to be an act done with the consent. There is no reason why the adoption should not be held invalid merely because the consent did not contain the wordings. The adoption must be taken as a whole. The consent may be expressed in the words "the consent" and not in the words which are used in the will. The consent can be implied from the words "that the consent may be express in the words of the words "and" which are used for the purpose of the Act. The consent cannot be implied from what the consent has been obtained. The consent does not mean anything more than what the consent may also be expressed in writing. The consent is only a formal document. The consent need not necessarily be such as would bind the parties to whom the consent is sought. [505 H; 506 A B] (b) The adoption must therefore be taken as part of the consent. [507 G] (c) The adoption does not amount to a consent. The consent of the adoptive assembly is not a consent. It is a consent if the adoption is found to be contrary to the law.
1201: The respondent was the owner of a village in which the Government granted lease to Raja Rama Krishna Rao, ancestor of the appellants. The suit was filed in 1920 by the respondent in 1920 with respect to village Timmapet. In 1918 the appellant 's case was that the village had been granted as bilmakta with a fixed pan makta in their favour by the Nizam and the respondent was only entitled to the said amount. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it on appeal by the first appellate court. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the appellant could not claim to dispossess the respondent from the village where the land was situated and the appellant was entitled to the same for the benefit of the jagirdar. The question whether the appellant was liable to ejected under section 9(1) of the Act is a question of fact and must be decided in the affirmative. The question of law has to be determined in the light of the provisions of the Hyderabad and the rules framed thereunder and the evidence adduced before the courts below would have to be very much influenced by the decision of the Privy Council in Pulukuri Kotayya vs The State of Madras [1917] I.L.R. , referred to.
2470: The respondent firm entered into a contract with the appellant for the purchase of timber from the respondent. The contract was to expire on 26th January, 1958 and the appellant filed a suit for damages for breach of the contract and also claimed damages for the amount paid by him as damages. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant had failed to perform its part of the contract. On appeal the High Court held that the appellant could not be allowed to claim damages for breach or wrongful act or wrongful act in connection with the contract. In this appeal by special leave it was contended that the appellant was entitled to damages for breach and wrongful act or unlawful act. HELD: (i) The contract in question is governed by the arbitration agreement contained in clause 21 of the form W.S.B. 133 which states as follows: "Arbitration" means an award and award and not an award and decree in any other way. The award is made under the contract and the award is to be final and conclusive and the provisions of the Indian , and of the Rules thereunder and any statutory modification thereof shall be deemed to apply to and be incorporated in the contract. [133 A B] (ii) The contract is governed by a contract of sale and the terms thereof are subject to the restrictions imposed by the contract. It is not a term of contract but a contract of transfer. The contract is one where the parties have agreed to pay the balance at the time of the contract, and the contract is one which may be called an arbitration. The contract does not require the performance of the contract by the parties themselves. The contract has to be in writing and in the absence of such a contract the parties must accept the same. The contract cannot be said to be in the present case. The contract merely provides for the payment of the balance of the price payable by the contractor. The contract itself does not require a contract of the performance of it. The contract being a contract of performance, the parties must abide by the conditions precedent and the contract must be construed as if they were in the usual course of construction. The contract in the present cases did not require the execution of the contract in the sense that the contract would be in writing. The contract did not require a formal contract of performance. The
3044: The Andhra Pradesh of Delhi is the State of Andhra Pradesh. In exercise of the powers conferred by section 3(1) of the Andhra Pradesh (other than the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes specified in the Schedule to the Constitution, the Andhra Pradesh Government issued a notification under section 4(2)(a) of the Act providing that the selections made under the Rules shall be subject to any rules or orders that may be made in regard to the reservation of seats for Socially and Educationally backward classes. Rule 24 provided that the selection shall be subject lo the rules and orders that may make provisions for reservation of seats in favour of persons belonging to backward classes. Clause (b) of this rule laid down that the reservation in educational institutions maintained by the State or receiving aid out of State funds shall be made in accordance with the criteria set out therein. The first appellant was a resident of the State of Madras. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said provision. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the impugned provision was discriminatory and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The reservation in educational colleges in the State of Hyderabad is not arbitrary and cannot be sustained. [301D] 2. The reservation of posts in educational institutions which are maintained by the States or receiving aid from the State is not unconstitutional. The reservation can only be regarded as socially and educationally backward classes and in accordance with such criteria prepare a list of such backward classes and make recommendations as to the special provisions which may be made by the Government for their advancement and for their advancement. [310B C] 3. The reservation must be made in the interests of the backward classes of citizens and the reservation should be made in consultation with the authorities concerned in the matter of making them. The reservation has to be made in public interest and it is not necessary that there should be some indication in the manner in which it should be made. It is only when there is a representation against any of the backward class that is to say, the reservation should have been made in consultation. If the reservation is in the interest of the backwardness of the backward communities, the reservation would be invalid and void.
3896: The assessee company was engaged in the manufacture of electric light and supplying water to the contractor. In the course of its execution, it had received from the contractor certain amounts towards the cost of stores/materials supplied by the Government. The said amounts were paid by the Government on behalf of the assessee. The assessee claimed that the cost of the stores/material supplied by the government was not to be included in the figure of cash payments received by the assessee under the contract for the purpose of 'an account ' and that the same always remained the property of the Government and that no profit could be said to have arisen to the assessee when such stores (material) was merely handled and manipulated by the assessee in the execution of the works under the contract. The Income Tax officer held that the cost was not to he added to the figure of income or profits derived by the contractor but directed the assessee to make a best judgment assessment. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. The High Court, however, allowed the reference holding that the cost should be deducted from the figure of the cash payment received by the appellant as part of the figure of Rs. 70 to Rs. 80 only. In support of his contention, the Revenue sought a reference to the High Court. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has rightly decided in favour of the assessee, and the Tribunal has also found that the cost is not to be excluded from the figure given by the assessee. [350E] 2. The High Courts below have failed to notice that the cost would be deducted from this amount. The High court has rightly held that the amount of Rs.70 to Rs.80 only was to be deducted from its total cash payment. [360B C] 3.2 The High Court was right in holding that the amount paid by the assessee was not to have been utilised in any manner in the execution and that the amount was not liable to be included. [340C D]
5927: The appellants are the LDA and their Authorities seeking leave to appeal from the Order in W.P. 3463 of 1986. The Writ Petitions before the High Court were pre ferred by the Authority for special leave to appeal, and the Authority sought permission to withdraw the two writ petitions. The High Court allowed the said two writ petitions quashed the impugned order dated 19.4.1986 and directed that the appellants be permitted to file fresh writ petition. In the appeals by Special Leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the lessees had no authority or power to revoke a permission; (ii) the notice dated 9.1.1986 issued by the State Government in cancelling the lease, was illegal as the revocation of the permission was without any basis; (iii) the appellants were not affected by the said order; and (iv) the appellants have been deprived of his right to move the High Court for an appropriate writ against the cancellation of the lease. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have failed to exercise its jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution. [316B] 2.1 Section 35(2)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent & Eviction) Act, 1972 provides that every person aggrieved by an order made under sub section (1) shall be afforded an opportunity of being heard with the object of making such an order. It is only when the order has been made under sub s.(1), that is, the order must be deemed to have been passed under sub section(1). The order of the High Court is set aside and the orders of the Single Judge are restored. [317D E] 3.2 The High Court has failed to exercise jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution, and the appellants have come within the purview of Article 32 of the Constitution of India. [318C] 4.1 The High Court should have exercised its own discretion in entertaining the writ petition and pass a decree for eviction. [319G H]
5965: The respondent assessee, a private limited company, carried on the business of manufacturing and selling pendi ners. In its agreement for the Assessment 1959 60 the respondent assessee claimed deductions in respect of the loss of the sale of certain shares of Bharat Starch and Chemicals Ltd. to M/s K.C. Co., Ltd. and Greaves Cotton & Co. Ltd. (the appellant) as a share holder. The Income tax Officer rejected this claim on the ground that the sale had been affected only to enable the assessee to claim the loss and could not be allowed as genuine. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the order of the Income tax Officer but the Tribunal held that the sale was not a trading loss and it was not a case of the Department that in arriving at its decision the Tribunal had taken into consideration any relevant material or irrelevant factor or that the assessee had shown some shares as investment shares in its books of account. On appeal by the Revenue, the Tribunal accepted the assessee 's contention that the sale having been affected only on the basis of the finding arrived at by the Tribunal, the High Court took the view that the sale in question was an allied concern of the assessee and that the same was not a finding of fact. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Tribunal has rightly decided that the loss incurred by the assessee in the sale of shares is a trading loss. [601E] 2. The High Court was right in holding that the loss suffered by the assessee was a trading loss within the meaning of section 2(4)(ii) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. [603F] 3. The High Courts have erred in holding that there was nothing to show that the assessee was carrying on any commercial activity. The assessee had failed to prove that the shares were sold within a much shorter period which would suggest, though by no means conclusively, that the sales were in the nature of a business transaction. [604D E]
4035: The appellant was detained under section 3 of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities, Act, 1985. He challenged the detention on the ground that it was necessary for the detaining authority to consider whether a person should be prosecuted before an order of preventive detention could be made against him. The High Court rejected the writ petition holding that the power of preventive detention is discretionary in nature and not with discretion. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the power to detain a person was not exercised by the detaining authority as a result of the failure of the detaining authority in making an order of detention, and that the failure of such authority to consider the possibility of launching a prosecution may in the circumstances of a case lead to the conclusion that the detaining authority had not applied its mind to the vital question whether it was necessary to make an order of externment. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 It is well settled that the power conferred on the executive authority to pass an order of bail is discretionary subject to the provisions contained in sub cls. (a) to (b) of article 22 of the Constitution. [548H] 2.1 The power of preventive detenus is generally not restricted either to the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authorities or the court itself has to see whether there are sufficient materials to justify the said satisfaction. If the authority makes an order of the preventive detention it is open to the authority to make an appropriate order. The power of the preventive Detention is not restricted either in the statute or in any other statute. The power to detain is not limited by the statute but only to the subjective subjective satisfaction of a concerned authority. The power is not restricted by the statute. The authority must necessarily be satisfied that the existence of prima facie case has been established. [549C D] 3.2 The power of arrest is not confined merely to the subjective facts and the subjective satisfaction must be judged by the subjective satisfaction. The power can be exercised sparingly and cautiously within the meaning of Article 22(5) of the Constitution and it cannot be exercised in the interest of justice and therefore the power of arrest must be exercised in accordance with law. [550D E] 4.3 The power of detention is not limited to the subjective
4920: The appellant was the owner of a land in a village. He sold it to his predecessor who purchased it under a registered sale deed. The land was not reserved for personal cultivation but was only a part of the land and the land was required by the State Government for the purpose of sub sec. (1) of section 7 of the Act. The Collector took possession of the land on the ground that the land was reserved for his personal cultivation. The Collector dismissed the application of the respondent holding that the land had been reserved for his own personal cultivation and that the land could not be resumed as the land was not available for the purpose. In appeal, the Collector held that the land in question was reserved for the personal cultivation and the land fell within the permissible limit and the land could be terminated under section 8(2) of the Act and accordingly he set aside the order of eviction. On further appeal, the Financial Commissioner confirmed the order of the Collector. The Financial Commissioner, however, held that the tenancy was not a proper one and that the lands were not "not" reserved for personal use or 'received '. The Revenue appealed to this Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the term "not being "notwithstanding the provisions of section 7(1) of the ," was wide enough to include the land in a manner which is likely rendering the land unfit for the purpose for which it was leased him. HELD: The words "notwithstanding anything contained in section 7(3) of the are used in the definition of "notwithstanding" in section 2(a)(i) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. [869 C] The words "provided for" in section 7 of Act 7 of 1868 are intended to give a different meaning from the word "not" contemplated in section 7. The words "subject to the pro visions of section 7 are intended to indicate that the land must be "not" notwithstanding the other provisions of the Act, and the words "not" merely refer to "received" and "reported" and they do not mean that the land should be "not". The words "according to the terms of the definition are intended to convey that the land may be "not", though the intention
6588: The respondents, the deceased and the deceased were tried for murder of one Partap Singh and causing injuries to others. The Sessions Judge convicted them under section 302 I.P.C. and sections 323, 325/149 I.P., I.P.) and Sections 323, IPC. The High Court dismissed their appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The prosecution has misdirected itself in not examining the witnesses examined by the prosecution. It is clear from the evidence that the deceased and his deceased had no enmity or hat ends to falsely implicating the accused persons. [869D] 2.1 In view of the statement made by the deceased and PW.I, the High Court was right in its conclusion that the sentence already undergone by the deceased should be set aside. [870B C] 3.2 In the instant case, the deceased was last seen in a quarrel which arose out of a minor incident. There was no prior enmity between the parties. The abatement of the occurrence was not explained by the prosecution witness. The deceased could have been injured even after the occurrence. The prosecution did not examine the witnesses examined. The High Courts erred in holding that the sentences awarded to the appellant, the deceased must have been reduced. [871E F]
4620: The petitioner, a member of the Indian Revenue Service, filed a petition for relief in the matter of his death. He alleged that the deceased had been murdered by her father in law and his wife, and that on receiving information a Sub Inspector of Police, he was compelled to give a child to the deceased and his daughter. The trial court dismissed the petition. On appeal, the High Court held that the evidence led against the deceased was not sufficient to warrant the conclusion that the appellant was guilty of the offence charged. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court has rightly held that the prosecution was not maintainable because the allegations made out in the charge were false. [113C D] (2) The High Courts have always taken into consideration the fact that the relations between the young husband and wife are vitiated by bitter discord. It is not possible to accept the contention that the conviction of the accused could be set aside on the ground that the prosecution had failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. [113D E] (3) The High courts have accepted the evidence which was not supported by any material or cogent reasons. There was no reason why the High Court should interfere with the order of acquittal. [113E F]
3175: The respondent, a professor of the University of Jammu and Kashmir University, was appointed as Professor and his probation for a period of two years. He was allowed to function as Professor and he was discharged by the Vice Chancellor under section 13(4) of the Ordinance (which had already been replaced on November 10, 1969). On November 10, 1970, the Governor issued an order that the respondent began to function as Principal of the University. The respondent challenged the validity of this order before the High Court. The High Court held that the order was not sustainable in law and quashed the order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (1) the order of the Governor was without jurisdiction; (2) the Chancellor could not have issued the impugned order; (3) the Chancellor was not competent to pass the order; (4) the Chancellor may make appointment of a professor, like the respondent, is the University Council; (5) the Chancellor might appoint him as Principal of a University; and (6) the Chancellor can make such appointments only on the recommendation of the Selection Committee created by section 36 of the Ordinance. HELD : (i) The Chancellor may make the appointment of a Professor or other person who has been given substantive appointment, transfer or discharge any functions which are being performed by a University Council. [258E] (ii) The Chancellor cannot exercise his powers under section 36 of Ordinance. It is only when the appointment is made to a post or office by a University council. The Chancellor may either direct or indirectly the appointment of another Professor or to appoint another Professor. The appointing authority is required to act according to the directions of the Executive Council. If the appointment is ordered by the Executive Council, the appointing authority is empowered to do so. But if the appointment is directed by the Executive council, the appointing authorities will not be able to act in future. [260B C] (iii) The Chancellor is expected to act in accordance with the provisions of the Ordinance and the Rules framed thereunder. The Chancellor is bound to act in conformity with the provisions contained in the Ordinance and rules framed thereunder. [270C D] (iv) The Chancellor does not act in terms of the Ordinance but merely makes appointments of
6448: The petitioner in the two appeals were auction purchaser of property bearing No. 112, executed on 13.4.1988 for sale of the said property. The purchasers filed a certificate of sale and the Collector of Stamps contending that the sale was not valid because the original sale certificate was liable for stamp duty as required under section 89 (2) of the Delhi Land Revenue Act, 1958. R.O ' has been defined in section 2(6A) of the Income tax Act, 1961. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The expression 'received ' has been used in section 84 (4). The word 't ' means "a T.R., or a T.M.; and if not, whether without an appropriate amendment of section 89(2) or (4) of that Act, the mere framing of a rule by the Central Board of Direct Taxes under the Income tax Rules, 1961 will be sufficient to oblige the registration officer to file a copy of the certificate of sale sent to him by the T.R./or the concerned officer under the Indian (18 of 1908) within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the whole or any part of the immovable property comprised in the certificate is situate. [316B C] 2. The word 'T.R. Or some of the words 't ' occurring in section 84 is used in the context of the purpose of the Act. The word "t" in section 84 has been used with reference to the nature of the power conferred on the legislature to make a provision for the purpose of making the provision. 1915: The respondent was a Hindu owner of a limited estate in the State of Madras. In the suit for maintenance and consequential reliefs, the appellant claimed that she was entitled to the estate left by her husband, but the respondent 's husband had no right to maintain the suit. The trial court decreed the respondents ' claim for maintenance and other reliefs and awarded them maintenance during their lifetime out of the estate of Lingayya. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the relevant provisions of the Act applied only to the estates of Hindus dying after the commencement of the Act, and that the right of the respondents to maintenance during their life time was not affected by the Act. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the respondent was not entitled to claim any maintenance from the estate of Jubbaras. HELD: (i) The rights of the respondents were not governed by the Hindu law as they belonged to the Hindu Community and therefore the respondent could not claim any maintenance. [950 C] (ii) The right of the respondent to maintenance during his lifetime under the Hindu Law is not an absolute right of alienation or transfer of property. It cannot be denied to the respondent that he was entitled to any maintenance from his estate. [951 D E] The right of a person to maintenance can be enforced only if he has been found to have been guilty of misconduct or conduct of himself in discharge of his duties. But the right of a party to the action must be held to be one which is against the terms of the contract. [955 G H; 956 A B] (iii) The right to maintenance is a personal right of the husband. The right of his wife is a personal and independent individual. The right to maintain a family marriage is a personal. The right may be enforced both by a husband and his wife. The right is not an existing right but a right of the wife is a right of a personal and distinct entity. The right does not involve a right of alienation. [956 F G] The right to the wife is not an essential ingredient of the offence of committing the act of murder. The right cannot be enforced in part merely because the husband has no right to sue for maintenance. [995 C] The
6061: The petitioners, who were members of the Indian Army including their families had been living in a country. They filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the legality of the orders passed by the Central Government and the Central Government granting reliefs to them. In the Writ Petitions, it was contended that the scheme approved by the Government of India had not been implemented and that the scheme had not been fully implemented. It was also contended that the directions given by the Government to the effect that the final order should be made by the Govern ment of India after consideration of the report submitted by the Ministry of Home Affairs, which had been taken into account for the purpose, had been communicated to the Ministry of Defence, Ministry of Home affairs, and that the approval of the Ministry of the Ministry was only an executive decision and not an executive decision. Disposing of the Writ Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Union of India has no power to make any order under Article 32 or any other law for the enforcement of any fundamental right against any person or persons. [57D] 2.2 The Union of the Union of India is entitled to make an appropriate order for redress of grievances of the aggrieved party. The jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is limited to the extent of ensuring that the rights of the citizens are affected by the action or action taken by the authorities concerned. [57F G] 3.3 The Union of Indian Union of India cannot claim that the jurisdiction of the courts should be exercised in accordance with law. [57E] 4.4 The jurisdiction of this court is limited to matters enumerated in Entry 7 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The jurisdiction is confined to matters specified therein. The jurisdiction must be exercised sparingly and properly construed so as to enable the court to exercise it in a particular manner. [57G H; 57A]
795: The appellant, a public charitable trust, made an application to the District Court for a decree against the respondent. The District Court held that the appellant was estopped from making the claim and that the deity was a private individual and that the suit was barred by limitation. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the appellant had no right to institute a suit under section 5(3) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the deity was not a family or private property and therefore the deity could not be treated as a public one; (ii) the deity could only be a 'an interest in the property 'and that the deity could have no right and authority whatever over the income of the deity was merely a family or individual, and (iii) the deity had no right and therefore the appellant could not sue for recovery of possession of the properties. HELD: (i) The deity was a public trust and the deity was entitled to recover possession of all the properties belonging to the deity. [256E] (ii) The deity is a trustee of the entire Hindu Community. It has no right to sue for any specific performance. There is no provision in the Act which requires the Court to entertain a suit for a declaration of title to immovable property. The Act does not require the Court to grant a declaration of the nature of the property. The Court will not do so in a suit for declaration of title but only apply to a plaint in respect of a declaration of his title. [255B C] (iii) The deity must be a "a" of a public trust" and the deity must be an "chostic owner". The deity must have been a trustee of a public Trust. The deity must also be a trustee of public trust. The deity should have been a 'an 'or 'in charge of the trust property. The deity may be a trustee for the purpose of carrying on the business of the trust. The idol, who is a trustee, is a trustee for its principal purpose. The deity is the trustee of a trust. The settlor is a trustee and he is a trustee. He is a trustee within the meaning of section 2(1)(d). The deity
2383: The appellants were dealers in the State of West Bengal. They sold their goods to their depots outside the Province of Uttar Pradesh, and they had sent their goods to them at their places outside the Province. The Sales Tax Officer assessed the sales tax under the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 15 of 1948, on the ground that the goods were not manufactured within the meaning of section 2(h) of the Act. The appeals were dismissed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Revisions under section 10 of the Act were also dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that: (1) The Explanation to Section 2(h), with reference to the High Court, was a mandatory provision; (2) The proviso to section 2(g) did not apply to the case as the goods were manufactured or produced in the State within the meaning Of section 2(j); (3) The Sales Tax Authorities could not levy sales tax on these goods but only levied sales tax on those goods which were manufactured or producing in U.P.; (4) The Sales tax authorities had no jurisdiction to assess the sales tax on the goods purchased by the appellants for sale. HELD : (i) The explanation given by the Sales Tax Authorities that the goods had been manufactured after the contract for sale were made, and that the goods might have been delivered to them at the place where they were actually delivered. [515 D] (ii) The Sales of Tax Authorities could make a reference only if the goods were ' produced in the prescribed form. The Sales tax Authorities could not make an assessment on the basis that the goods are manufactured or produced before the date of delivery. The Sales of Sales Tax Authorities must be held to have passed the proper order of the Sales Tax Authority. [516 C E] (iii) The Sales. Tax Authorities could act upon the terms of the agreement between the parties. It is only when the contract entered into between the parties that the dealer has to perform the work of manufacture and sale of the goods. If the contract is executed in accordance with law then the dealer cannot be taxed. [517 H] (iv) The Sales, tax Authorities could make an assessment only if there was a breach of the
183: The appellant was arrested in pursuance of an order made by the Chief Presidency Magistrate, Nainital, under section 7 of the Indian Penal Code. He was served with a notice on him requiring him to appear before the District Magis trate, Nainal, for being tried together for offences under sections 383 and 575 of the Indian Arms Act read with section 420 (1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The appellant contended that the said offence having been committed in pursuance of the provisions of section 7 of that Act, he could not be prosecuted and punished only under section 428 of the Code. Held, that the said offences were distinct and separate from those mentioned in section 7 of Indian Penal Code and were distinct and distinct. Held further, that the offence charged against the appellant was not one which could have been validly committed in pursuance thereof. Section 7 of the Code did not apply to the present case as the offence was not committed in pursuance Of any other provision of the Code and the trial commenced against the appellant could not be held to have abated.
2299: The appellants were owners of a plot in the area known as Hirab Kuzi. They filed an application under section 11 of the Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1953 for permission to sell the trees on their land. The Compensation Officer held that the appellants were estopped from contending that they had no interest in the trees standing on the land as defined in section 2(5) of the Act and that the compensation officer was not competent to grant proprietary rights in the trees. The Additional District Judge allowed the petition and issued a writ of mandamus directing the appellants to pay the amount of Rs. 62,568/ . On appeal by the State the High Court held that the trees standing thereon were 'land ' within the meaning of the expression 'as defined in section 3(1)(a) of the Punjab Alienation of Land Act, 1953. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the trees being planted on agricultural lands were "land" within the meaning Of the expression as defined in the Act and therefore their sale to the appellants was unlawful having regard to the provisions of that Act. HELD: (i) The trees standing on land are not 'land ' as defined in s.2(3) of the Haryana Act. The trees standing which are planted on agricultural land are not defined or defined in the Punjab Act. The definition of 'land ' is wide enough to include all kinds of land. It may be either acquired or acquired by the Government. But there can be no doubt that the trees are capable of being transferred along with the other trees. [559E F] (ii) The trees on agricultural lands are not ' permanently settled and the compensation officer has no power to direct the sale of the trees. There can be no dispute that the trees on agricultural land were "land". The trees standing thereon cannot be said that the trees stand created in the land. The trees are capable only of being sold and the trees have been cut off from the land. Therefore, the trees standing thereupon will become vested in the appellants. [556G H; 557A C] (iii) The trees which are planted after the date of the vesting of the trees are not 'present
253: The respondents in each case claimed exemption from assessment in respect of sales effected by them on the ground that such sales took place "in the course of export" within the meaning of article 1115, and therefore they were not entitled to the exemption. Held, that the exemption was limited to sales by export and purchases by import, that is to say, those sales took place 'in the course Of export ' within the meaning Of article 286(1) (b). The fact that the goods actually delivered as a direct result of such sale or purchase taken place in the course of inter State trade may be said to have taken place in one State does not make it an exposition of the goods in the course Of inter State trade. In view of the wide construction placed upon clause (b) of article 286(i), the words "any other class of the goods which are sold or purchased for the purpose of consump tion in that State", in the context of cl. (b) and sub cl. (c) of article 282, the words "for the purpose of consumption in any State" occurring in the definition of "actual purpose" in section 2(a)(b) of the , and the words "of the goods in question" means that the goods must be exported out of India.
2436: The respondent was a surety of the principal debtor in respect of certain amounts due to him. The surety agreed to pay and satisfy the liabilities of the principal debtors upo Rs. 12,000/ . The surety agreed not to pay any amount but to invest the amount with interest thereon. The surety also accepted the liability of the principal and executed a bond against the principal debtor. The surety died on August 15, 1951. The High Court decreed the suit for the amount due. In appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended that the decree passed by the Trial Court was bad because he had no right to restrain the execution of the bond and the principal debtor could not be restrained from recovering from the principal debtor 's liability. HELD: (i) The surety is entitled to enforce his debts in execution proceedings against the principal and the principal. [734C] (ii) The surety has no right to sue or defend himself. It cannot be said that the creditor must have been given an opportunity to seek the benefit of the principal. The surety is bound to discover at his peril all the properties of the principal, and sell them. He may then recover the amount from the principal. If he does so, he will be subrogate to the creditor. [735E F] (iii) The surety was liable to pay the entire amount. The surety was not entitled to receive any amount as he did not know about the debt. The surety had no right of executing the bond. [736B C] (iv) The surety had to prove that he had paid the amount to the principal. There was no evidence to show that he had made payment of the amount. The order of the surety was not binding on the appellant. [733F G] (v) The surety further failed to discharge the obligation under section 30(2)(b). The surety was therefore entitled to get back the amount from him. [737D]
2678: The appellant, a public transport undertaking, was granted licence for carrying on the business of motor car driven by a driver. The Municipal Council and the Chief Municipal Officer, Raipur, had not been registered as required under section 3(1) of the , to be registered as required by section 2(g). The appellant filed a complaint before the Special Magistrate and the Chief Judicial officer, Raipur. The Additional Sessions Judge held that the appellant was guilty of an offence under section 2(1) and that the appellant had been acquitted. The High Court dismissed the revision application. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of the Magistrate was an order of discharge and not of acquittal and that the appeal lay to be decided by the High Court. HELD: (i) The High Court was in error in holding that the appellant could not be convicted without giving him a clear finding of fact that he was guilty of any offence under section 4(2)(g) of the Act. [917 D] (ii) The High Courts have failed to notice that the appellant 's case must fail. [918 E F] (iii) The High court has erred in holding that there is no question of law or procedure in which the appellant can be convicted. [920 C] (iv) The High courts have failed to apply the provisions of section 439 Cr. P.C. and the High Court has failed to consider whether the appellant was liable to be tried. [919 G H]
4311: The petitioners filed writ petitions under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the Central Secretariat Service (Amendment) Rules, 1979 and the Regulations made consequent thereto by the Union of India for the purpose of holding a departmental competitive examination limited to candidates belonging to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The petitioners contended that the Central Secretariat Services (Amendment) Rule 12 of the Central Administrative Tribunal (Amendment) Regulations, 1979 were not applicable to the Union of Indian employees. Dismissing the Writ Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Government of India was not empowered to fill up the reserved vacancies by recourse to a departmental competitive Examination for candidates from the Scheduled Castes and scheduled Tribes. [1189C] 2.1 The Union of India is not authorised to fill up any such reservation in the Department of Personnel & Administrative Reforms in the Cabinet Secretariat in accordance with the field of selection. The first instance is that the Government of India should have derive their own wisdom on the subject matter of the said resolution. [1190E F] 3.2 The Government of the India has no power to fill up or otherwise direct recruitment to the posts in the Central Secretariat service. The Government of Indian has no power either to make rules or amends to provide for the amendment of the rules. The only power available to the Government of the Indian is to make rules which are inconsistent with the provisions of the Constitution. [1191D E] 3.3 The Government of Indus trial Commission has no power under the proviso to sub rule (2a) to make rules in respect of the matters specified therein. The Central Secretariat Service is an independent body of officers of the Public Sector Undertaking. The Government cannot make rules in the matter of promotion to the posts of members of the Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes. [1290B C]
3195: The appellants, small manufacturers of matches, had been subjected by the impugned notification to excise duty at the same onerus rate as has been applied to larger producers, wilfully indifferent to a fractional pretext. The appellants, medium manufacturing techniques, had been subject by the impugned Notification, to excise duty in respect of the said category. The appellants contended that the impugned notification having been issued without jurisdiction, it was illegal and void being violative of article 14 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The impugned notification is not discriminatory and cannot be sustained. [501E] 2. The impugned notification having come into effect from April 1, 1963, it is not open to the appellants to contend that the impugned notifi cation should have been made under the Act. The impugned notifcations are valid and invalid. [510C D] 3. The impugned Notifi cations were not based on any rational nexus with the object sought to be achieved by the impugned notifica tion. It is well settled that the object sought was to bring about a uniformity of prices for all the manufacturer 's goods. The impugned would therefore be justified. [511B C]
725: The respondent filed a suit against the appellant asking for a declaration that she was the owner of the lands. The trial court decreed the suit and on appeal, the High Court held that the custom of the family of the deceased widow could not be enforced against her. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) It is well settled that where a Hindu law has no such rule or the rule of succession it cannot be said that the rule of adoption is not a special custom of the tribe or family but it is only a rule of primogity of the statute that is applicable to the case of a Hindu law. [1109 D] (2) The rule of adoption in the present case did not apply to the facts of the present case. The rule of the adoption does not apply to a Hindu law but only applies to the facts and circumstances of each case. [1107 H; 1108 A B] (3) The rule is not intended to govern every case of a particular person who has failed to establish a special custom. But the rule must be applied to all cases of fraud or undue influence. [1106 C E]
5671: The respondents were prosecuted under the Customs Act, and were acquitted. The trial court convicted them but the High Court confirmed their convictions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the prosecution had failed to prove the offence of being in possession of gold by the customs authorities as a bar to the prosecution of the same. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 It is well settled that the presumption arising under section 114 of the Evidence Act is that the accused must be tried and the burden which he can prove his case must be on the prosecution. [134E] 2.2 The facts are not only those facts but also the facts proved against the accused. The accused could have been tried by a competent Court for the offence of having committed the offence under the CustomsAct. The prosecution has not been able to establish altogether different ingredients viz., (i) that the respondents had been tried by the Customs Authorities; (ii) that they had been tried with the result of the acquittal of the respondents; (iii) that they were sought to be prosecuted under the Gold (Control) Act, 1968. [136B C] 3.3 The facts show that the respondents were tried by a Magistrate under the Customs Tariff Act, and had been acquitted. The Magistrate found that the prosecution was barred by limitation. He therefore proceeded to commit the offence under section 85 of the Gold ( Control) Act, 68 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 and ordered the confiscation of the said property. The respondents had been acquitted and the order of the Collector of Customs was affirmed by the High Court. [136C D]
2637: The respondent filed a complaint under section 20 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 against the appellant and his servant. The trial court dismissed the suit on the ground that the complaint was not made by the person competent to file it under section 20(2) of the Act in accordance with a resolution passed by the Corporation in its meeting held on December 23, 1968. On appeal the High Court upheld the preliminary objection that the complaint petition was not maintainable as the respondent had not been given an opportunity of being heard before filing it. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the complaint did not contain any particulars of the alleged offence or the allegations made out therein nor were they contained in the original complaint which could have been presented within time. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the complaint is not maintainable because the provisions of section 537 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 applied to the Municipality. [869 C] (ii) The word "may" in sub section (1) of section 2 of the , does not mean that the Commissioner must either be the Municipal Corporation or the Municipal Officer. It means that the Commissioner may himself choose from the Corporation. The words "in writing" are intended to convey that the Commissioner has to act according to the intention of the legislature. The words 'in writing ' do not mean that he should have done so as to include the Corporation. Therefore, the word "may". in sub section(1) of Section 2 of the is not used in the expression "in writing". The word "shall" means that the commissioner may either accept the same or by means of a written document. The word "in writing " means that the officer who signed the copy of the document shall sign it and sign it. If the officer does not sign it, he cannot be said to be an officer of the Corporation. [870 E F; 871 D E] (iii) The word 'may ' in sub section.(1) of s.2 of the would only mean that the officer authorised to file a complaint under the Act can file it in the manner prescribed for the purpose. But the word "in such a complaint" means that he may file it in some other manner or
3983: The appellants filed a suit for partition of the joint Hindu family properties, claiming to be their share in the property. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court affirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the decree passed by the trial court was not executable as it had been obtained by fraud or undue influence; that the decree was void because the provisions of section 14(1) of the Act were not attracted in the case of a Hindu female who is in possession of the property of the last male holder on the date of the commencement of the Act when she was only a trespasser with out any right to property. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (i) Section 14(1)(b) of the provides that if a person has become a trespasser without the consent of his father, he will not get the benefit of the Act. [532E] (ii) It is well settled that where a Hindu female has no right to alienate the property in dispute, the question whether such a transfer can be made by a Hindu female is one of legal inference. But where a Hindu widow has no right of alienation, the question cannot be answered in the negative. [533F G] (iii) The word "possessed" in section 14(2) means actual physical physical or peramanies. The expression 'possession ' in section 14 is used in the widest connotation. The expression "possession" means actual physical and peramanies or impliedly. The expression includes actual physical physical and permanisnate or physical physical physical or other means. The expression may include actual physical physical physical and mental physical physical physical physical, physical physical physical ingenuity, physical physical and physical physical physical social, physical physical, or physical physical and other means. A person who is in actual physical physical possession of the land does not hold title to it. The expression would have reference to a person who is merely a trespasser from the possession of the lands but does not include actual physical possession of which he holds title. [535C D] (iv) The expression " posses sion of possession" in section 2(3) of the , is wide enough to include physical physical physical possession. The
707: The appellant, a candidate for election to the Legislative Assembly of the State of Madras from Alangulam Constituency in the District of Tirunelveli at the time of scrutiny of his nomination paper was declared elected. He filed an application before the Election Tribunal under section 100(1)(c) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 praying that the said nomination be rejected and the same be set aside. The Tribunal held that the question to be decided by it was whether there was a valid nomination paper and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to enquire into any ground of disqualification which was not taken before the returning officer. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question as to whether the rejection of a nomination paper is a matter of substance or not must depend on whether the candidate is duly qualified or is subject to some disqualifications as provided in section 36(2) of the Act. [625 F] Hari Vishnu Kamath vs Syed Ahmad Khan, ; , referred to. (ii) The decision of the Election Tribunal on the question whether the rejection is justified or not depends upon whether the candidate has been duly qualified or has been improperly refused admission to the election petition. [626 A B] Hari Vishnad Kamath vs Union of India, ; , followed.
1706: The appellants, who were the respondents in the appeal, made applications to the Collector for reference under section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The Collector made a reference to the Court for the apportionment of the compensation amount among the various claimants. The High Court accepted this contention and held that the reference was not made by the Land Acquisition Officer but only with respect to the amount of compensation which had been paid to the respondent. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the High Court acted without jurisdiction as no reference could be made by the Collector in pursuance of the applications made by the Government. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court has rightly decided that the matter is remanded to the trial court for disposal of the application. [869E] (2) The High Courts have power to consider the question whether there has been any omission or failure on the part of the Legislature to make a reference. The High Courts must act judicially and properly exercising its powers under section 18. [870B C] (3) The High courts are bound to follow their own procedure and they cannot do so in a manner that they should proceed to dispose of the application for making a reference. [871C D] (4) The High court has power to decide the matter in accordance with law. It is only when the High Court decides that the matter falls within the purview of section 18. If the High Court does not think proper to interfere with the decision of the Subordinate Judge, the High Court will not go into the question of the competency of the District Judge to make such a reference. But if the High Court proceeds upon a assumption that the matter has been referred by the District Judge, he would have disposed of the application before him. [872D E] (5) The High 675 Court has power to consider whether there has arisen an omission or failure of justice. [873H; 874A B]
4714: The appellant Corporation was a statutory body of the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation. The services of the employees were terminated by the respondent Corporation on the ground that they had been working in a buses for their own convenience and they were not confirmed in any manner. The services were terminated by way of disciplinary action, but the employee challenged the termination order before a Division Bench of the High Court which held that the termination was bad. On appeal to this Court it was contended that the termination of the employee was invalid because the termination was based upon an arbitrary order of discharge and the employee could not be made liable to pay salary or allowances. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The services have been terminated by way Of disciplinary action. The employee is entitled to reinstatement with full back wages and other benefits. [850D] 2. In the instant case, the services have been terminable under a State Act. The termination of service of the employee, therefore, cannot be treated as retrenchment. [851G] 3. The employees are workmen who are employed for the purpose of employment between the employer and the workman concerned. The services are terminated by wayof disciplinary action. [855C D] 3. Section 25F of the provides that if any dispute arises between the employer, whether the employee is a workman or not, the termination of service shall be illegal and void. The question whether the termination of services of the employee is illegal or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [853E F] 3. In the absence of any specific provision in the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, the termination has to be validated. The definition of retrenchment in section 2(oo) and as used in section 25F has no wider meaning than the ordinary accepted connotation of the word 'retrenchment ' means the termination of serv ice of the employee for any reason whatsoever otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of either disciplinary action,but does not include such termination in the present case. [891B C] 3. It is the stand of the employer that the employee is not a workman and the employee is only workman and not a workman. The employee has to establish that the termination is illegal. [892H
4687: The petitioner was detained under section 3 of the (hereinafter called 'the Act) on the grounds that he had committed a serious crime and his explanation to the Court was that he had no "full knowledge that the vessel was to be used for smuggling activity. The detaining authority, after considering the evidence produced by the detenu, passed an order of detention against him, and also held that the petitioner was guilty of the offence punishable under section 3(1)(a) of the Act. The High Court quashed the order of detention on the ground that the respondent had not at all, nor had any "full knowledge about the activities of the vessel". Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The order of detention passed against the petitioner is clearly erroneous. [825E] 2. In view of the fact that the maximum period of detention mentioned in Section 10 of the Act has expired, and as such the appeal has become infructuous. It may be mentioned, to appreciate the preliminary objection, that the order of the High Court is clearly erroneous, and it is not open to the petitioner to contend that the order is vitiated by non compliance with the provisions of section 10 of the . [826D E] 3. The order is clearly erroneous and must be set aside. [827B C]
6019: The appellants, a company, set up a lease of the land in question for a period of 15 years. The lease was granted to the plaintiffs respondents. The lease deed provided that the interest would be paid on the date of the expiry of the lease period and that the lessee shall have no right to hold any portion of the land or subse quent mine. The lease granted to the appellants ' predecessor in interest, but the lessor took possession of the land after the expiry of its lease period. The appellants filed a suit for declaration of their homestead rights and for confirmation of pos session or in the alternative recovery of possession. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the suit property was not a "land" within the meaning of section 2(1)(a) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the suit property vested in the State of Bihar and therefore the transfer of the land to the appellants could not be treated as a "land", and (ii) the High Court erred in holding that the suit properties were not in the nature of the original land and that the High Court had wrongly reversed the decree passed by the trial court and dismissed the suit. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The suit property is an immovable property and the mere fact that the property vests in the State in the State. It cannot be said that the property vested in a State. [950E] 2. The suit lands are adjacent to a coal mines which are adjacent to the coal mines. The suit land is a part of the land and the courts below have found that the suit lands are suitable for the purpose of the aforesaid mine. The courts below have failed to find out from the plaint schedule to the plaint schedule and have given evidence that the suit land is an agricultural land. The courts have found that there was no proper and valid notification under Section 3 of the Act. [951D E] 3. The High Court has rightly held that the land is an asset within the meaning Of section 2(I)(a). The High Court further held that the lease granted to appellant No. 1 to the appellants did not come into existence
3467: The appellant was the sole selling agent of a firm carrying on business in the name and style of "Hire" and was running its business. In the course of his business he used to engage thirty six trucks for the running of the trucks, but did not have any other truck for the purpose of the manufacture of the tru vehicles. The assessee 's contract with the manufacturing company commenced some time on October 12, 1963. The assessee used to engage 30 six trucks covered by public carrier permits belonging to various persons at different times for transporting the cement. The assessee had also paid the monthly bills of Rs. 10,000/ . The Income tax Officer assessed the income tax on the basis that the assessee had engaged the two trucks in the transport work and had obtained receipts from them for delivery of the goods to the stockists. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the assessment order. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee was not liable to pay the tax under section 4(1)(a) of the Act. The High Court upheld the Tribunal 's decision. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the assessee could not be said to be an employee of the firm because he was not a registered dealer under the provisions of the Act and that the firm was not registered under the Act. 1100: The appellant was the Mahant of a Hindu family. He had been paying land revenue to the State for the year 1948 49 and thereafter under the order of the Subordinate Judge he handed over charge of the estate to the appellant on January 8, 1950. On January 15, 1950, the appellant submitted a return of income of the estate from the estate. The Income tax Officer found that the appellant was liable to pay agricultural income tax for the year 1947 47 and therefore the appellant was not liable to be assessed to income tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the assessment but the Tribunal held that the appellant could not be taxed as an assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the income received by the appellant from the Receiver did not retain its character as agricultural income and therefore also the appellant was entitled to assess the tax. HELD : (i) The liability to pay agricultural incometax is imposed upon the owner of the property in question and the liability must be regarded as a statutory obligation created by law. But the fact that the receiver may, because he held the property from which income was derived in the year of account, be deemed to be an assessee does not absolve the appellant on whose behalf the income was received from the obligation to pay agricultural Income Tax. [908 D E] (ii) The liability of the appellant to pay agricultural profits tax is not a mere liability of the principal employer. It is a liability of the assessee to pay the tax. The liability is a statutory obligation and it cannot be said that the liability is a pure one of the principal debtor. The liability can be enforced only when the principal debtor has failed to perform his duties or performance his duty and the liability is not binding on him. The liability cannot be enforced against the owner of any other person. The liability must be viewed with reference to the nature of the liability. [901 H; 902 A B]

1208: The appellant, a private limited company, was assessed to sales tax for the year 1948 49 and in respect of the assessment years 1957 58, 1958 59 and 1959 60, the Provincial Legislature passed the Khandwa Ginning and Pressing Cotton Tax Validation Act, 8 of 1938. The appellant challenged the validity of the Act on the grounds that it contravened article 14 of the Constitution as it imposed a tax on the trade of ginning and pressing cotton by means of steam or mechanical process within the limits of the Khandwa Municipality which was constituted by the notification dated March 31, 1939, issued under section 3(2) of the Act, and the imposition of the tax was illegal and ultra vires. Held, that the Act was intra vires and valid. The Act did not provide for the levy of tax on the sale of the goods sold or sold by the State of Madras, nor was there any provision in the Bill of the Government of India Act, 1935, authorising the imposition of tax on such goods as were brought into the State of Bombay, to be made by the Act. The Act was enacted with a view to make certain provisions relating to the levy of taxes on the trade or calling of goods and the rules made thereunder. The Act provided for the imposition of a tax on goods specified in Schedule I to the Act and the rules framed thereunder. The tax was levied on the trade and callings of goods and not on the trade. The Act also provided for the payment of the tax on the goods purchased by the State. The Act, however, does not contain any provision for the payment on the goods sold by the Government of the State of Bihar. The Act is a law providing for the imposition and collection of tax on goods and the Rules made thereunder. It is a law imposing a tax on trade of ginned goods and not a tax on them. The Act provides for the imposition, collection and collection of the tax. The Act does not provide for refund of the tax paid by the State Government either in the prescribed manner or in relation to any matter connected with the imposition of any tax. The legislature has no power to pass an enactment for the imposition or collection of tax. The impugned Act is a legislation intended to serve a social purpose and therefore the Act must be held to be invalid

2624: The appellants, workmen of the Company, were carrying on the work of collecting tobacco and selling it to its customers. 490: The respondent company was carrying on life time business in the United Kingdom and had to prepare annual statements of profit and loss for the purpose of ascertaining its profits. 364: The petitioners, who were the owners of certain lands in Bihar, filed a suit for possession of the disputed properties and claimed that they had title to the property. The State Government issued a notification under section 3(1) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, declaring that the estate of the petitioners was vested in the State. On the question whether the properties belonged to the State or not, the High Court held that the State could not have any title to the same. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The State Government has no power to transfer the ownership of the property to the State. It is only when the State has acquired title to it by virtue of the provisions of the Act and the acquisition of the property by the State, that is, the State cannot acquire title to the properties which are subject to the provisions of section 4(a). [990 H] (ii) The State can transfer all the rights and interests of the owner of the property. But the State cannot transfer all the interest of the owner. The State does not take away the right of the owner to retain the property as office or cutchery for the collection of rent. The State cannot claim the title to the land or the interest of its owner. The title to the said property is the title of the owner and the State cannot claim title to the State merely because the title is extinguished. The State has no title to the suit. The State is entitled to recover possession of the property from the purchaser. [990 E G] (iii) The State cannot make an order of eviction if the State has taken possession of the land or part thereof. The State can also claim title to it. [991 F G] (iv) The State has not taken possession of any land or part of it. The State did not take away any land or Part of it. [991 D]
