5086: The appellants are a broad description of seven persons holding status of tenants in common under the Kerala Agricultural Income tax Act, 1950. They owned an estate from which they derived agricultural income liable to be assessed in the year 1963 64. In assessment proceedings for the year 1963 65 the assessees claimed a deduction of Rs.33,747.09 on account of interest on the amount paid by them during the relevant accounting period relating to the assessment year 1964 65. The assessing authority brought the amount to tax. The assessee contended that the amount was not agricultural income and therefore the deductions were not admissible. The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee and against the Revenue. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court has taken the view that it was immaterial that the assessees followed the mercantile system of accounting because the case was not one of an actual or constructive receipt or any receipt at all but only one of remission. [350E] (2) The High Courts have held that the amounts received by the assessees should be treated as agricultural income. The High Courts had taken into consideration the substance of the matter in each case. It is not disputed that the assessees follow the mercantile method of computation of the amount payable by the assessee. The High courts have taken into consideration that the amounts in question must be regarded as taxable in the hands of the assessees. [360G H; 360A B] (3) The High courts are not expected to take into consideration the nature of the business carried on by the assessees. The High court has taken into consideration whether the amounts in fact received by the assessee are not agricultural income. Court has taken into account the fact that the amount in question could not be deducted in computing the agricultural income. In the instant case, the High Court took into account the relevant facts of the case. The High 'Court has taken into conjecture the contention that the amount of rebate in the present cases could not be said to be agricultural income. 1432: The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 149 and section 201 read with section 34. They contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the findings of the Sessions Judge as they were not recorded by the High Court and that the judgment of acquittal was based on wrong interpretation of law. Held, that the High Courts have power to interfere with findings of fact arrived at by the trial court and even though it may not be necessary to find in favour of the accused, such a finding can only be said to be perverse or perverse. It is well settled that where the High Court has taken into account the evidence which is admissible in evidence, it should not ordinarily interfere with the finding unless there are some material to show that the conclusions reached are unreasonable and perverse. In the present case the High Court did not give any reasons for disagreeing with the opinion of the acquitting judge but gave its own reasons for disagreement with the opinion. Held, further, that the view of the acquit ings must be accepted and the conviction cannot be set aside.
3853: The prosecution case was that on the night of the 20th and 21st June, 1971 the deceased had been stabbed by the accused persons with a fire arm in his cot. In the morning at about 4 a.m., the appellant Deena was found guilty of murder and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted both the accused holding that the evidence of the eye witness was not reliable and that the doctor who conducted the medical examination did not find any injury caused by the injuries caused by fire arms. Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD: 1.1 The evidence of the two eye witnesses clearly established the guilt of the accused. The doctor found only one injury caused by fire arm but he could not have held that there was only one injury which resulted in the death of the deceased. [1017C D] 2. The doctor 's testimony is consistent with the innocence of the accused and it is not possible to accept the version of the eye witnesses. It is not safe to rely upon the testimony of the eye witneses for convicting the accused. [1019E F] 3. The conviction of the appellant must be upheld. [1010B C]

The provisions are not unconstitutional. [822G H; 823A]

The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of clause (3) of Article 371 D of the Constitution on the ground that it was beyond the competence of the State Legislature to enact the said clause. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The power of judicial review is not an appellate or revisional jurisdiction but it is a power which has been expressly conferred by the statute. But in order to understand the true scope and ambit of the controversy raised before us in regard to the constitutional validity or otherwise of any law passed by Parliament or a competent legislature, the exercise of such power must be deemed to have been made in conformity with the provisions of Article 371D. [885C E] 2.1 The President of India made an order on 19th May 1975 under clause (3), (5) of Article 370 D of the Constitu tion by which the President of India was to form a new form or by way of modification or annul any order of the Administrative Tribunal before it became effective upon its confirmation by the State Government or on the expiry of three months from the date on which the order was made. The President of the Andhra Pradesh Government in the exercise of the powers conferred on him under clause (4) of Article 372 C of the Constitution, was therefore entitled to make the order of the Tribunal dated 19th May, 1975. [886E G; 887A B] 3.2 The power of the Tribunal to deal with any matter coming within the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunals, so long as the Administrative Tribunal was not less effective or survived. It is not possible to lay down any inflexible rule that the power of the tribunal should be exercised only in respect of matters coming within the purview of Article 371 C. The power of this Court to interfere with the decision of the Administrative Tribu nal is vested in the Administrative Tribunal. But the power of judicial Review is not an inherent power of the High Court to substitute its own view. [890B C] In the instant case, the power of this court to pass an order modifying or abrogate the impugned order of the
5302: The appellants were the sons of a minor, aged six years. They had executed a sale deed in favour of their father. After he attained majority, they filed a suit for a declaration that the said sale deed was invalid and was not binding upon them. The trial court decreed the suit. In second appeal, the High Court set aside the judgment and decree holding that the appellants were tenants within the meaning of Section 2(d) of the Kerala Compensation for Tenants Improvements Act, 1958 (Act 29 of 1958). On appeal by special leave to this Court, HELD: 1.1. The High Court has rightly held that the alienation was not something which a man of ordinary pru dence would have effected had the properties been owned by him and thus held it not binding on the plaintiff. [692C] 2.1. It is well settled that where a person is entitled to a decree for possession or damages for any particular particular property, the question whether he is entitled to such a decree can be decided by the executing court only if there is no allegation of fraud or collusion between the parties. [693E F] 3.2. The question whether a person is a tenant or not depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. The question as to what is the nature of the transaction is not a matter of fact but what is the consideration of the claim has to be determined by the court. If the claim is bona fide and the evidence led to establish the same must be examined in the light of the surrounding circumstances, the court may interfere with the order of the executing court. [694F G]
5814: The petitioners, members of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Lok Sabha and the Union of India, filed a writ petition in this Court seeking to issue a Writ of Mandamus directing the Government to consider their claims for promotion to the next higher grade on the basis of seniority subject to the availability of vacancies. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the petitioners were not entitled to any relief. In the appeal by special leave it was contended that the petitioners had been discriminated against and the principle of equality enshrined in Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as they had an equal advantage of getting promotions to a higher cadre which would be available to them if they were denied equality before the law was passed by the State. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The policy contained in the letter dated 23.12.1983 is that the claims of the members of the scheduled castes and Scheduled Tribes should be taken into consideration consistently with the maintenance of efficiency of administration, in the making of appointments to services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State. [628E F] 2.1 The scheme of reservation of posts for Scheduled Castes and Schedule Tribes in the Ministry of Personnel & Administrative Reforms bearing O.M. No. 11/83 730 dated 18.11.1983 is not only vague but also contains the scheme of reservation for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Scheduled Tribes. It is not disputed that in many of the other departments of the Union Government the scheme of reservations for Scheduled Castes & Scheduled Tribes is in vogue in cases of promotions from the lower grades when they are done on the basis Of seniority subject to fitness and under the said policy the persons belonging to the Scheduled Castes & Schedule Tribes are enjoying a similar advantage of getting promotion to a higher grade much earlier than the employees belonging to the backward classes. [629D E] 3.2 The scheme of the reservation of posts by way of reservation for scheduled castes and scheduled tribes is in v spirit and cannot be implemented retrospectively. [632F G]
4741: The petitioners in the writ petition were carrying on the business of the State of Maharashtra and the Government of India, in giving permission for conducting State lotteries. They had also sought a writ of mandamus directing the State of Karnataka to permit them to sell their State Lottery tickets in respect of the lotteries organised by the Government of a State. The Government of India issued a notification under section 4(1) of the Bombay Merged Territories (Regula tion) Act, 1947, prohibiting the sale of any State except with the express consent of that State. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that it was ultra vires the power conferred on Parliament and that it was not open to the Government of any State authorising the Union to make laws with respect to "Lotteries organised" by the Government or the Government of the State. Held, that the expression "Betting and gambling" includes and has always been understood to have included the conduct of lotteries organized by the Government and the Government or a State". The expression "Belthoric" means an independent and separate body of persons who may be members of a particular group of persons. In view of Entry 40 of List I of the VII Schedule to the Constitution Parliament has exclusive power to make laws in respect of "Lottersies organised by Government of a state". The expression 'Belthery ' is defined as "A Undertaking of the Government of which is a State" and the expression "C undertaking is defined as a undertaking of the Government. The expression "Offenceer" in section 2(g) of the Act must mean "a undertaking of the undertaking". It does not include an independent and distinct body of persons. The expression 'Offenceers ' in section 2 (g) of Act 1 of 1951 cannot be construed to mean "an undertaking of the State". The word "Offences" in section 3(g) must receive the meaning of "income" in section 6(2)(g).
6018: The respondent joined service as a technical assistant in the Gujarat State Electricity Board. While he was posted at Surat, he made an application to the Additional Chief Engineer for cancellation of his transfer order on the ground that his mother aged years was ailing and it would cause great inconvenience to him if he was required to join at home on 30th March, 1974 in accordance with the service Regulation No. 113. The respondent challenged the validity of the order of discharge from service by means of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Gujarat. A Division Bench of the High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the order of termination was not justified and quashed the order of the High court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The order of discharge passed against the respondent is set aside and the order of dismissal is restored. [316B] 2.1 The respondent has been given opportunity of being heard in respect of his representation. He must be afforded an opportunity of being represented through counsel. He may have already been given an opportunity of hearing. He may also have already been granted an opportunity of making representations which he may have already received. He may still be permitted to avail himself of the opportunity of being considered for reinstatement. [317D E] 3.2 The order of termination of the respondent was illegal and void. It was set aside by the High Court. The respondent has not been given a reasonable opportunity of being informed about the passing of the order. The respondent cannot be allowed to stand in the position of the appellant. [318C D]
4976: The appellant was a Judge of the Rajasthan High Court. He was appointed as a District Judge and was elevated as a Judge of a High Court. His case for pension was not considered in accordance with the rules framed by the Rajasthan Civil Services (Rajasthan Amendment) Act, 1976. The respondent who had been working as a District Judges on a scale of pay for a period of 5 years , 9 months and 18 days ' service for pension was sought to be taken into consideration for purposes of calculating the pension payable to such a Judge. The appellant challenged the validity of the said order before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the impugned order was not justified and quashed the order. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court has rightly held that the impugned orders were not justified. [312D] 2. The amount of pension is to be arrived at on the basis of the rules framed under the Rajasthan Civil Service (Rajasthan Amendment), Act, 1976 and the retiring Judges ' (Conditions of Service) Rules, 1973 are not only the existing statutory rules but also the old rules which have come up before the Constitution Bench . It would be wrong to contend that the impugned rules have no retrospective effect. [313C D] 3. The impugned rules are not inconsistent with the provisions of the Rajasthan Civil Servi ties (Rajasthan Amendment). The impugned rules do not provide for any change or modification of the rules. The impugned Rules do not require the approval of the Government of Rajasthan in the matter of fixation of pension. The impugned rule does not make it obligatory on the part of the State Government to give effect to the same. The impugned Rule does not impose any new duty or additional pension. [314E F]
3344: The appellant, a private limited company, was granted stage carriage permits for a short route to the respondent. The Regional Transport Authority, which evaluated the relevant merits and awarded the permit to the appellant No. 6, who held the applicant No. 6 as the appellant No, 6, who had secured higher marks than appellant No. 3, and allowed the permit to Appellant No. 6. The appellant No. 5, who had obtained a copy of the permit, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Appellate Tribunal. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant 's experience in bus service did not entitle him to any benefit under section 47(1) of the Act. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in its view that the appellant having been admittedly a new entrant, was entitled to preference, the route being a short one, other things being equal, the High Court should have interfered with the decision of the appellate Tribunal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have always taken an approach to interfere with the decision given by the appellate Tribunal, but the High Court has always taken into account the fact that the rules or guidelines are not exhaustive so as to be interpreted differently from the point of view of the parties. [532D] 2. The High court has always taken an attitude towards the object sought to be achieved by the provisions of Section 47(1). There is no doubt that bus transport is calculated to benefit the public and it is in the fitness of things that the interest of the travelling public isanguage and not the general interest of the public. It is only when the number of applicants for a particular route is more than one. If the number of applications are more than one, then the number of persons who are eligible for a particular scheme would be the same. [533C D; 534B C]
2809: The appellant, a dealer in respect of certain goods, was assessed to sales tax under the Maharashtra Sales Tax Act, 1959. In the course of assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1967 68, the Sales Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the goods were not 'goods ' within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act. The High Court held that the goods fell within the definition of "goods" in section 2(14) of the Act and therefore the High Court had no jurisdiction to set aside the order of assessment. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the expression "goods" is defined as including all materials, commodities and articles" and includes stock and shares, growing crops, grass etc., or otherwise used or used in the contract of sale. The definition of " produce" in section 3(1)(a) of the , as amended by the Maharashtra State Amendment Act 15 of 1967, is wide enough to include forest produce and articles. That is why the word "goods" has been substituted in section 2 (12) of the . The words "goods" are not defined in the Act. The definition given in section 2 of the Act does not exclude any part of the definition of 'goods ' but only applies to a variety of circumstances which may be taken into account.
2835: The appellant company was carrying on business in shares and its dealings in shares and the business in other commodities were carried on by the respondent company. In proceedings for assessment of income for the assessment year 1952 53, the Income tax Officer computed the income of the company from its business at Rs. 3,39,899 and declined to take into account the loss suffered by the company in the share transactions. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the business activities of the company 's dealing in shares and business in other commodity were not the "same business" within the meaning of section 24(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Tribunal referred the following question to the High Court: "Whether there was any evidence in support of the Tribunal 's finding that there was complete unity of control and that shares formed a part of the commodities in which the assessee company deals regularly from year to year in the ordinary course of its business? " Held, (1) that the finding of the Tribunal that the business activity of the company was carried on by it as a result of the conception of voting, that shares formed part of the commodity in which the asses see company was carrying out of the business of the company and that the business was carried on with the object of maintaining the stock of goods and that the profits earned by the company were not taxable under the Income tax Act.
4235: The defendant, a tenant of the land in suit, filed an application for ejectment of the plaintiff on the ground that he had failed to pay the rent and the same was not paid. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the defendant had failed to deposit the arrears of rent and the interest thereon. On appeal the High Court held that the defendant was entitled to re enter upon the premises and the forfeiture clause also provided that upon forfeiture the plaintiff would be entitled to re entering upon the premises. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Court 's jurisdiction was limited only to adjudicate on leased premises under the Bombay Rent Act and therefore the suit was barred by time. HELD: (i) The Court has power to determine the amount of damages which may include the amount of rent payable or other charges which may include interest. [1010 D] (ii) The Court is not competent to give a decree for ejectment in respect of two plots of land but only in case of default, the Court has jurisdiction to try the suit. It has no jurisdiction to make a decree for eviction in respect of the two buildings constructed on the same plot. The Court has no jurisdiction in the matter of passing a decree for recovery of possession. [1011 C E] (iii) The Court cannot go into the question whether the Court has power or authority to pass a decree for a specific performance of a contract. The Court does not exercise its jurisdiction under section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rent Control Act. [1012 H] (iv) The Court can issue a decree for the ejectment in respect Of two plots of lands. The Court will have jurisdiction to decide the dispute between the parties. [1014 A B] (v) The Court will not go into the questions as to whether the Court is bound to act on the basis of the contract entered into by the parties. If the Court goes into the questions of fact and law at the stage of the determination of the controversy, the Court cannot go behind the findings of fact arrived at by the Courts below. [1015 G H; 1016 A] (vi) The Court must act with all the judicial discretion vested in it. The Court cannot interfere with findings of fact unless they are perverse. [1019 F
4259: The appellant was convicted under section 376 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. He appealed to this Court on a certificate granted by the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. A conviction based substantially on the testimony of the victim is not sustainable in law. [401D E] 2. In the instant case, there was no material to show that there was any evidence to show that the victim was fatal to the prosecution. There was no material whatsoever to show that he had been ever taken into custody or that he was arrested. The trial court 's finding that there was absence of corroboration of the testimony of a rape victim, that there was no other material to show the victim was either circumstantial or circumstantial evidence. [408B C] 3.2. The fact that the victim has been taken into custody may be irrelevant because the prosecution has failed to prove the guilt against him. The burden of proof is on the accused person to establish his innocence. [410C D]
6345: The appellants who were duly elected Directors of the respondent No. 3, the Joint Director of Sugar and Joint Registrar Co operative Societies, Maharashtra State, Pune requesting him to summon a special meeting of the Committee of the Karkhana for discussing the question whether the members of the Managing Committee are entitled to vote at a meeting of the Society in which they are members of the Board of Directors. The High Court directed the Registrar of Cooperative Societies to give fresh notice to the elected members as well as to the persons mentioned in the letter dated 13.9.89 issued by the respondent No 1. The appellants challenged the requisition notice on the ground that under the scheme of the Act read with Rule 57A and bye law No. 29 of the Bye Laws of the Society the High Court had no jurisdiction to issue such a notice. The High court held that the members of a committee were entitled to vote in view of the provisions of Section 73 of the Act and the bye laws of the Society. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the members of an association of the Society could not be said to have got a limited right to vote at the meeting; (ii) the members were entitled to sit and vote at the special meeting when the Committee considered the vote of no confidence under section 73 I.P.C.; (iii) the members who have got a restricted right to vote in the meeting were entitled to one membership; and (iv) the members whose rights were conferred upon them to vote at any meeting. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The members of the Committee are entitled as members of the society. [497E] 2. The members are entitled to sit or vote at any meetings of the Committee. The members have right to vote after the Committee has taken decisions of the members themselves. The members may also have right to take such decision as may be decided by the Committee. But the members cannot claim any right to vote unless they are given a reasonable opportunity to do so. [488B C] 2. It is not necessary that every member should be given a reasonable hearing before deciding the question. The members must have been given an opportunity to participate in the proceedings. The members can only defend himself if they are not given a
5717: The petitioners in the present Writ Petition, who were working as Excise Inspector, challenged the validity of the Notifications dated November 21, 1986 and September 25, 1988 issued by the Central Administrative Tribunal. They contended that they should be placed in the pay scale of Rs.650 1040 with effect from 1st January 1973, and their counterparts in the so called Secretariat & participating attached offices CSSS, that they could not be placed in pay scale of pay until they attained the age of retirement or retirement. Disposing of the Writ Petitions, this Court, HELD: (1) The method of recruitment in respect of Grade I stenographers in the Department is to say, directly recruited/admeasuring their seniority and promotion in the Department. But the method of recruitment cannot be said to be arbitrary or mala fide. [1010C D] (2) The mode of recruitment in regard to Grade I streiate officers in the Department are as follows: 1003 (i) they must have been given a lower grade pay scale of Class III (Rs. 650 for Grade II). (ii) they must rank in higher grade pay scale on completion of the prescribed period of service rendered by them as a result of which they would get at par with those who had put in regular work. (iii) they must be placed in a higher grade pay scales on completion of three years of service rendered after the date of their appointment to the post of Superintendent Grade II. (iv) they must receive a lower grade scale of Rs .650 10 40 and not on completion of any longer period of service. (v) they must hold a lower grade post on completion of two years of service. [1011D E] (vi) The mode in which the respondents were appointed to the post was to be regularised by the Government of India, and they were entitled to claim the benefit of the same. [1015E F] (vii) The mode under which the respondents had been appointed to the posts of Superintendent Grade 11 was not identical to the mode of recruitment of Grade I and was not similar to the mode adopted for the other cadre of Class III and was not identical. [1014A B]
5524: The State Government by its letter dated 24th July, 1973 directed the Commission that in view of the shortage of Munsifs in the State and since in view of their long absence, they should not be allowed to appear for the examination of the Commission under Rule 19 of the Rules. In pursuance of the said directions the Commission made an order determining inter se seniority of all candidates appointed on the basis of the 1970 Examination held by the Commission. On receipt of the IIIrd list of the candidates recommended by the Commission the State Government considered the names of the candidates selected and appointed them as the appellants who were unsuccessful at the subsequent examinations. The appellants challenged the validity of the said order contending that the said order was illegal and void as it had been passed without jurisdiction in violation of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order of the Commission was bad in law and quashed the same. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The order of the High Court rejecting the appellant 's representation and the consequent order of the State Government is set aside. [473E] 2. The order of promotion of the third candidate is restored. The State Government has no power to revise or modify any order of the nature of appointment or appointment. It is only when the State Government has a power to amend or modify any such order or order of the character of appointment or appointments or appointment. The power to make rules for the purpose of making such Regulations cannot be exercised unless the statute expressly so provides. The power of the State to make rules regarding the conditions of service of the employees is subject to the provisions of the Rules and the rules have to be framed. The rules are framed with regard to the minimum qualification of the candidates and the procedure prescribed therefor. The rules do not require the State Government to make rules in respect of the minimum qualification. The rules have to satisfy the requirements of the Rules themselves. The State can impose conditions precedent before a person can be promoted to the post of a Civil Judge. If the State has a right to fix the number of persons who qualified for the post, the State must give preference to those who qualified for such post. The State has a duty to give preference to the
1089: The appellants were under an agreement dated July 11, 1945, to pay the annual profits of the company for the years 1946 47 and 1949. In the assessment year 1945 46, the Income tax Officer treated the sum as having been paid by the assessee as received by it from the company. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the amount was not liable to be taxed in the assessment year 1946 47, but on reference, the High Court decided against the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The question whether the amount was received by the assessee in the previous year is a deductible item or not must be answered in favour of the assessee. [350 E] (2) The question as to what should have been the income has to be determined in the assessment years ending March 31, 1945, cannot be regarded as a deduction. The question as framed by the Income tax officer was one which was left open and it could not be said that the amount had been received by the asses see in the previous years. [360 H; 360 A B] (3) The question about the amount received by the assessees during the accounting period prior to March 31, 1946, was a mixed question of law and fact. The question of the amount received during the relevant accounting period was a mixed issue of law and facts. [310 D F]
2093: The appellant was employed by the respondent company in connection with a factory. In accordance with the terms of his appointment, he paid wages for the period of notice and retrenchment compensation under section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The appellant served notices of retrenchment upon out of its employees and paid them salary for the period Of notice and retrenchment Compensation under section 25FF of the Act. The appellant pleaded that retrenchment amounted to an unfair labour practice. The Labour Court held that the appellant required only four clerks in cluding the Accountant R. N. Juneja, Jai Narain, Budhpal Singh and Laljimal. The Labour court directed the appellant to pay the workmen salary for the aforesaid period of notice. The appellant contended that the retrenchment of the workmen was not illegal and that the retrenchment did not amount to an unfair Labour practice. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the retrenchment was not justified on the ground that the retrenchment had been effected by the appellant in violation of the provisions of the Standing Orders of the Government of India. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The Labour Court has rightly held that the retrenchment is invalid because some junior members of the staff were retained in contravention of the Standing orders of the Government. [783E] (2) The Labour Courts have found that the appellant had failed to discharge the burden of proving the retrenchment. The Labour Courts should not be too inclined to accept the contention of the appellant that the retrenchment must be deemed to be illegal or void. [784C D] (3) The Labour courts have found that there was no evidence to show that the retrenchment took place by the appellant. The Labour courts will have to find out whether the retrenchment was legal or illegal. [785D] (4) The Labour court has to see whether the retrenchment is legal or illegal and if it is not possible to hold that the retrenchment has been made without any reason. If the retrenchment has taken place by the employee, the employer cannot challenge the retrenchment. [786G H; 773A] (5) The Labour Appellate Tribunal has jurisdiction to deal with the question as to whether the retrenchment has to be upheld or not. It is only when the employer has made a reference to the Labour Court that the retrenchment can be challenged
5288: The respondent, a dealer in hides and skins and exports the same out of the territory of India has taken place on which the sales tax/purchase tax under the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948 was levied on him by the State. In the course of export the goods sold to the respondent who is a dealer in Hides and skinning and selling the same out in the territory of the country for export. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the aforesaid order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the transactions entered into by him which are such on which sales tax/ purchase tax could be levied on them under the U .P. Sales tax Act, 1948. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The transaction entered into by the appellant which are such as to bring within the purview of sub section (3) of Section 51 of the Central Sales Tax Act. [869C] 2.1 The mere fact that such a form has been given will not amount to a liability for payment of sales tax or purchase tax in respect of a transaction in the course of inter versation with sub section (2) of Section 5 of the , cannot become exigible to tax merely because a wrong form is used. It would be immaterial if the form is used at the time when the appropriate form had not been devised by the Rule making authority. [870H 871A B] 3.2 The mere fact of the form is not an element of the contract between the parties which may be regarded as validate one. The mere fact whether the form has been used or not must necessarily lead to the conclusion that the transaction is not one which is not connected with the transaction. [872D E] 3.3 The mere fact about the form is neither a correct nor proper nor proper nor any other material evidence can be relied upon. The mere reason of the form does not make it necessary for the party to show that the transaction has been made in the course or performance of the transaction. The mere existence of a particular form is not decisive of the question whether the transaction is one which is either wholly or partly. [873E F]
5543: The appellant joined the service of the Narang Bank of India Ltd. On July 12, 1976 he was dismissed from service by the United Bank of India. He filed a suit for declaration that the dismissal order passed against him was illegal and inoperative. The appellant contested the claim made by him in the earlier writ petition before the High Court. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the appellant had been impleaded as a party in view of the amendment to section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the appellant was not a party in the earlier Writ Petition; (ii) the appellant had no locus standi to file the present petition; (iii) the appellant could not be permitted to amend the petition; and (iv) the application for permission to implead the United Bank was barred by limitation. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The appellant was entitled to be impleaded as a respondent in the earlier petition. [1095E] 2. The appellant was not at any stage in the earlier proceedings. The appellant did not appear in the earlier proceeding. The appellant made an application for impleading the United Bank. The appellant had also failed to do so. The appellant 's application for impleadment was rejected by the High Court on the ground that the appellant was a party in a subsequent proceeding. The High court rightly held that the appellant has been impleaded as an employee of the United Bank and therefore the appellant cannot be said to have been impleaded as the appellant. [1096D E] 3. The appellant is not a party to the earlier proceedings which were pending on the date when the appellant made an applica tion for impleading him. The appellant could not have been permitted to withdraw the petition. [10100C D]
2744: The Rajasthan Medical Service (Collegiate Branch Rules, 1962 were framed by the Rajasthan Medical Council of the State of Rajasthan under section 30(4) of the Rajasthan Medical Services (Collegnaciate Branch Rules. Under the Rajasthan Medical Service Rules, 1962 a post graduate qualified or equivalent to M.B.S.S. Class II was appointed as Principal of Medical College, Jodhpur. In the first instance, the appointment was made on a purely temporary and ad hoc basis till further orders. The respondent challenged the validity of the rules on the ground that these rules could not have afforded a ground for the University to withdraw affiliation of the Colleges concernd, but it was not open to challenge either in the High Court or before us and his appointment as Principal alone was assailed in this Court. The High Court held that the rules could not override the provisions of Ordinance No. 65 which provided for the University of Rajputana Act, 1946, and that the Rules could not be read retrospectively. The High Courts also held that the Rules did not make provision for the University for giving effect to the decision of the High Court. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1.1 The rule of Rule 30 does not confer any power on the State Government to make only a temporary ' or officiating ' appointments and does not create new rights in respect of the service rendered by a person who has been working as Principal. [573C] 2.1 The Rules do not provide for the appointment of Dr. Rishiklal Jain in the matter of appointment of Dr, Rishik Lal Jain in connection with the selection of Dr. Ram Kishan is not entitled to continue to be in service. [572E] 3.2 The Rules do no play a vested an obligation upon the State Government. It cannot be said that the Rules were intended to supersede the Rules. The Rules do nothing about the appointment of Shri Rishikalal Jain in this case nor do they give any right to the respondents to continue in service. The Rules are silent over the period of the grant of admission to the post of Dr.Rishiklal jain in the speciality concerned. [571D E]
3779: The Punjab High Court, in a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution, held that the Punjab High Court had no jurisdiction to determine the tax on the total income of the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Punjab Act did not provide for the levy of tax on the gross income and that the expression "profits" in section 3(1) of the Act must be construed as including "benefit" and that the words "cenefit" should be interpreted as meaning "grade or profite". HELD: (i) The Punjab High Courts have clearly erred in interpreting section 3 of the Act in such a way as to make section 2(b), read with section 5 of the Act, useless in determining the tax in accordance with the grada tion laid down in the schedule 2 of the Act. [869 C] (ii) The Punjab Act does not contain any provision for the levy on the gross turnover of an assessee. It merely lays down the method of assessment of tax in accordance therewith. The definition of "profits", in section 3 of Act 2 of 1951 is wide enough to include the income from the business which includes the profession. The definition has been given by the Legislature in the present case, but the definition has been substantially reduced by the wording of the definition itself. The definition is clear and unambiguous and there is no reason why the definition should not be so read. [870 H; 872 A B] (iii) The Punjab Legislature has clearly erred in its interpretation of section 3 of 'the Act. [892 D E]
4798: The plaintiffs, who were the defendants, filed a suit for declaration of the right to be in possession of certain premises. The defendant contested the claim on the ground that the notice was not valid and that the suit was bad for want of a notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it holding that no further notice under s.80 was necessary as the notice had been served by the plaintiffs ' father Seth Lachman Dass. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) It is well settled that a notice must strictly fulfil its requirements. [235B] (2) The requirement of a notice is not mandatory but directory and it is only directory and not mandatory that the notice should not be given in writing or left at the office of the plaintiff. But if the notice has been properly complied with, it would be sufficient compliance of the section as to the requirement that it should state the name, description and place of residence of the plaintiff and the relief which he claims; and the plaint shall contain a statement that such notice has been so delivered or left at his office. [246E F] (3) The requirement that the notice must substantially satisfy the requirements of the section and the cause of action for the purpose of the suit is that the notice has not been properly served or that the cause of prosecution has been sufficiently sufficiently proved. The requirement is that the cause must substantially satisfy its true character. [247F G] (4) The requirement is not mandatory and the Court cannot go into the question whether the notice has complied with the requirements. The Court will have to ascertain the nature of the suit and the cause has to be ascertained from the facts alleged and circumstances appearing in the plaint. [249D E] (5) The requirement must strictly fulfil the requirements of section 80 of C.P.C. [240G] (6) The requirement has to be reasonable and the object of the section is that the requirement must be satisfied from the material particulars set out in the plaint and the manner in which it can be said to have been satisfied. [241H] (6)(a) The requirement does not necessarily mean that the notice is not invalid merely because
532: The respondent was dismissed by the District Superintendent of Police. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging his dismissal and the order passed by the District Superin tendent of Police on December 20, 1948. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the order of dismissal passed by the Subordinate Judge was not final until the Inspector General of Police took cognizance of the case and directed the District Superintendent to take steps against the respondent. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court had no power under article 226 to deal with the order of the District Superan tendent of police for his dismissal as such. HELD: (i) The High Court had ample jurisdiction to exercise its newly acquired powers under article 226 of the Constitution. [839 C] (ii) The High Courts have ample power to interfere with an order of dismissal which has been passed at a time when the Constitution of India had not come into force. It is only when the High Court can act upon the basis of the allegations made in the petition and if the High Court takes the view that the order passed is not final until then the respondent has exhausted all remedies available to him. [840 H; 841 A B] (iii) The High court has ample power under article 227 to interfere with the order passed under article 226 or under article 226. [838 E F]
2083: The Mysore Public Service Commission (Fole ery, , was constituted by the Mysore Government for the purpose of making appointments to the posts of Assistant Engineers. The Government appointed a number of persons who were working as Assistant Engineers in the Department of Government and who were not eligible for appointment to the post of Assistant Engineer. The Government made rules called the Mysore Public Service Commis sion (Fole ary, ,and Mysical Works Engineers Rules, 1957, which came into force on February 10, 1958. In exercise of those rules, the Governor issued a notification dated December 3, 1960, under section 4(1) of the Act, the Mysore Public Services Commission (Function) Rules, 1957 were published in the Gazette on December 1, 1960. The Government amended the Rules on January 11, 1958, but the said rule was substituted by the new Rule 2. The appellant who was an officer in the Department was served with a notice on March 5, 1961, calling upon him to show cause why his appointment should not be made to the post. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notice on the ground that it was violative of article 311 of the Constitution inasmuch as the rules did not provide for the imposition of any penalty or punishment, and that the Government had no power to make rules under article 309 of the Constitution. Held, that the appellant was not entitled to the declaration that he was not qualified to be appointed to the post, because, the Government had not been given the right to continue to hold the post till the rules were made in that behalf. The State Government could not have made the rules in question. The rules did not require the approval of the Government to make them. The rules were not approved by the Government. The Government had no authority to pass the rules in the matter of making appointments. The rules had no application to the appellant 's case.
1631: The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, filed a suit for the recovery of possession of certain properties. The suit was resisted by the first defendant on the ground that the document executed by Bhagavathi Valli had been fraudulently obtained and therefore the suit was not maintainable. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal the High Court reversed the decision of the two courts below holding that the plaintiff had not obtained any right in the property or in the alternative to redeem it. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the suit was barred by limitation. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The suit was barred under section 36 of the , because the plaintiff had no locus standi to file the suit. [902B] (2) The suit is one for damages for breach of contract and for breach of trust. The suit is for damages for default of payment of consideration. The suit has to be dismissed as time barred. The suit must have been instituted within six months from the date of the accrual of the cause of action. [903E F] (3) The suit having been filed after the expiry of six months from its commencement, the suit cannot be said to have been barred under section 6 of the Limitation Act. [904F G]
6788: The appellant, a manufacturer of goods imported from the respondent company, received complaints that the soda ash which had been supplied was of sub standard quality. The Assistant Collector of Customs rejected the refund application on the ground that the damage was discovered after the goods were out of customs control and not the price actually indicated by the seller at the time of filling the bill of entry. The Assistant Collec tor, however, rejected the refund claim. The appeal preferred against the order of the Collector of Customs was dismissed by the Collector of Central Excise. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the demand for the amount of penalty under Section 22 of the Act for reasons set out therein. The learned Single Judge allowed the writ petition holding that the value to be assessed under section 14 of the Act is the real price at which goods imported are ordinarily sold at the time and place of importation and not the prices determined on the basis of the real value of the goods. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The appellant 's claim under section 22 of the is not maintainable where imported goods are defective and has suffered losses. [803E] 2.1 The value to be payable by the seller to the buyer to the seller to whom the goods are delivered is the market value of the value of the consignment. The value to he has to pay the same is the market Value of the consignment to the buyer. The value is the real consideration of the value to the buyer is the market price of the consignment at the time when the goods are despatched. The value being the market value is the market rate of the value at which goods are imported. The value has to be ascertained on such other material as may be placed before the assessing authority or the appellate authority concerned. [804F G] 3.2 In the instant case, the value to he had to pay the customs duty of Rs.32,15,904.21 on 28.12.1990 was the real price of the goods imported by him. The appellant having failed to pay the said amount, the Union of India has filed an appeal in this Court. [805D E]
4749: The petitioner was drawing the amount as indicated in the communication of the Central Government, and the Accountant General of Madhya Pradesh authorised him to draw the amount as specified in the communication without prejudice to his right to claim the same. He informed the Accountant General that he was drawing the said amount as indicated by the letter dated July 17, 1982. On February 2, 1983, the Union of India wrote a letter to the effect that the petitioner be paid an excess of Rs. 2,220 which should be refunded. The petitioner informed the Accountant general that he was receiving the amount as also the subsequent communication dated July 17. 1982. The petitioner also informed the AccountantGeneral that he was entitled to payment of cash equivalent of leave salary in respect of the period of earned leave at their credit. The petitioner sent a representation to the Accountant General for grant of pension on the ground that the time limit had been prescribed under Rule 20B of the All India Services (Leave) Rules, 1955. The representation having failed, the petitioner approached the High Court by way of Writ Petition. Allowing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has rightly held that the rule is not applicable to the case of the petitioner. [560D] 2. In view of the provisions of the Rules, the limit has to be confined to five months ' equal to 150 days '. [566C] 3.1 The rule does not make provision for payment of the retirement benefit contemplated under Rule 20 B of the All Indian Administrative Service (Pension) Rules, 1981. The rule does no mention of the period for which the period of leave would be extended. [557E] 3.2 The rule does neither contemplate payment of the pension nor does it contemplate payment of any other allowance. It speaks of payment of the service or gratuity. [558G] 4.1 The expression " wilful absence" in the Act means absence of something like, or otherwise, which is not connected with the main object of the Act. The words "double dictionary or anything else" in the context of the Act, are used in the context and are intended to convey that the meaning given therein must be such as to include within itself the purpose of the Act and the rules made thereunder
6148: The petitioners, who were members of the Board of Directors of the Nationalised banks, challenged the validity of the Circular dated 23.8.1982 (Annexure A) issued by the Joint Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs, and the Natio nalised Banks (Management and Miscellaneous Provisions) Scheme 1980 (hereinafter referred to as the 'Act '). The scheme was approved by the Central Government on 23.8, 1982. By its letter dated 23.9.82 (Annexure A), the Central Government directed that the circular in question should not be given effect to. The circular in question was also not given effect to, but was followed by a similar circular. In the writ petition filed by the petitioners, the petitioners contended that the circular being contrary to the provisions of the Circular, the Act was to govern the existing practice of the Directors of the nationalised banks and the Nationa nalised banks would have been included in the list of members of the Association and therefore the circular was ultra vires. It was further submitted that the circular was contrary to the statutory provisions of the Scheme and was invalid. Dismissing the Writ Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The scheme is not discriminatory and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. [532C] 2.1 The impugned circular is contrary to the mandate contained in the scheme and is hit by Article 14 of Constitution. The scheme does not lay down any procedure for selection of the non member of the association or the members of the association. The scheme has to be construed strictly and in accordance with the provisions of Section 15(2)(c) of the Act. The scheme cannot be said to be arbitrary and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. [533D E] 3.2 The scheme is an integral part of the scheme and it is not open to the High Court to direct that the scheme should not be made applicable to the members of a society. The scheme is intended to serve the purpose of the Act and is not intended to be exhaustive of the scheme. The scheme can be amended only by the Parliament and the Central Government may amend the scheme. [534E F] 4.3 The scheme is a statutory one
3110: The land in question was situated on the main Ranchi Chaibasa Road, a strong piece of land. The land was assessed to land revenue for the purpose of the Act and the compensation awarded was Rs. 45,000/ per acre. In the appeal before this Court it was contended that the valuation report given by the Land Acquisition Officer, Ranchi, was not proper or adequate as the valuation had been made after the expiry of the period fixed for the acquisition. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court has rightly so, that after the termination of the Second World War in 1945 there was a rise in land values due to the increased demand of homestead lands for building purposes. [560B] (2) The High Courts have taken into account the fact that the sale price of the land is the same which was paid to the Government under the Act. The High Court took into account the relevant evidence that the sale deed was executed in the year 1945 and the sale deeds produced were not only a single piece of land but also a small portion of the land. The High Courts did not consider the value of the land at all. [566C D] (3) The High court was right in holding that the sale deeds were not properly considered. [557E] (4) The High courts have taken into consideration the market value of the acquired land. The market value of land is the basis for determining the market value. The High courts should have adopted some measure of uniformity in awarding compensation. [575F G] (5) The High 693 Court has taken into account all the factors which are taken into account while deciding whether the market value or the market value should be arrived at by taking into account the market value as claimed by the parties. [565H; 566A B] (6) The Highcourt has rightly held that the sale of the land in question being a sale deed could not be said to be vitiated because the sale deed itself was not a document of title. [570G H] (7) The High wills relied upon by the High Court cannot be regarded as good evidence. [568D]
1550: The appellant was convicted under section 419 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for two weeks. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the concept of fraud ' in section 24(1) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, had no application to the case as the intention of the appellant was not to cause injury to the respondent. HELD: (i) The concept of fraud is a thing which every person must act with property or property. But when such acts are done by some persons other than those who have been responsible for their conduct, they can be said to have acted in the course of the common good faith of the owner or the doing of the act. [595 C D] (ii) It is well settled that where a person has acted in connection with the benefit of another person, the intention of defraud is not proved, but where the act done by one person does not amount to an act done by another person, then the intention is not to attract the provisions of section 464 unless he is guilty of deceitting him. [596 H; 597 A B]
273: The respondent, a resident of Pakistan in 1947, was allowed to migrated to India in November, 1947, to Pakistan. He filed a complaint against him under sections 380 and 454 Indian Penal Code and also under section 412 of the Code before the District Magistrate of Gurgaon. The trial magistrate rejected his plea that he had no locus standi for the prosecution as the respondent was not a native Indian subject but only a resident of India within the boundaries of India and therefore could not be said to have acquired any nationality by merely staying on there from. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the respondent was a native foreign Indian within the boundaries and was therefore entitled to the protection of article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. HELD: (i) The words "any person" in cl. (a) of article 19 means a person who has been convicted of an offence under the . [701 H] (ii) The word "person" in cls. (a), (b) and (c) must mean a person who is not a party to the proceedings or is a party to them. The words "for any other purpose" are wide enough to include persons who are not in India or who have been convicted of any offence under the , and they cannot be read together with the words "for " any other purpose". The words "to which the person concerned is a party" indicate that the person is not a 'another person" within the meaning of the words "to whom the person is accused of an offence" and not a "another person". The words 'may ' do not necessarily mean a person in India or a person who was not in India. The words 'shall ' mean a person whose name is registered in India. It may include a person who had been convicted of offences under the . But the words "in India" in the context of the expression "for "any other purpose" would refer to a person who were not in India and who had been found to be a "unit". [802 D E]
387: The appellants were convicted by the trial court and sentenced to six months ' rigorous imprisonment each. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction but made a reference to the High Court under section 307 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Held, that the High Court was in error in holding that the charge against them did not amount to an offence of committing mischief by fire as alleged by the prosecution. It could not therefore be said that the charge was invalid merely because it had taken the other view that the charge might have been proved. The High Court was right in its view that the High Courts should not interfere with the findings of fact arrived at by the jury unless they are satisfied that they are perverse. In the present case, the High Courts below had found that the evidence adduced was sufficient to establish the guilt of the appellants. Held, further, that the finding of the High Court that the charge had been proved was not correct. Held, also, that the charge having been framed by the trial Court, the High court was wrong in holding that it was not open to the High Courts to go into the question whether the charge was defective or not.
6683: The appellant, a public servant, was charged with offences punishable under the and (2) under the Gold Control Act 1968. After examination of the prosecution as well as the defence witnesses and recording of the statements of the accused under section 342 of the old Code (corresponding to Section 311 of the new Code), the prosecution examined two witnesses, who were not present at the trial on the date fixed for examination. The prosecution filed two separate complaints against the appellant in the court of Judicial Magisrage, First Class, Anjar, being criminal cases Nos. 929 and 930 of 1973 for offences punishable under section 34 of the . The learned Magistrate allowed both these applications and directed the Trial Court to recall the two other complaints on the ground that the prosecution had failed to examine the three witnesses as prayed by the complainant. In the second revision petition filed by the respondent, the High Court allowed the two other revision petitions filed by the respondents and quashed the first one. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 It is clear from the language of section 342 of Criminal Procedure Code that the prosecution has to be able to establish beyond reasonable doubt that the prosecution is primarily based upon the evidence adduced by the prosecution. [717C] 2.1 The second part of section 342(1)(a) of the Code provides that the prosecution shall rely upon the evidence already recorded or relied upon by the prosecution witness and if such evidence does not disclose any offence which he may have committed or abetted him to commit it. If the evidence appears to be essential to the just decision of the case, the Court will not allow the party to say that he is entitled to make out his case, but if he thinks that he is not prepared to prove the prosecution evidence, he must record his statement before the Court. [716E F] 3.2 The second part which is mandatory imposed an obligation on the Court to summon any person as a witness or to recall or re examined any person already examined. The second part cannot be said to have been directory. [718D E] 4.3 The second part does not operate as res judicata because the former part does not apply to the latter part. [719G H; 720A B]
1878: The workmen of the Company were dismissed after a domestic enquiry. The workmen challenged the dismissal order before the Labour Court on the ground that the enquiry was not proper and some of the witnesses were re examined before the Tribunal whose verdict was against the Company and hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the Appeal, HELD: (1) The Tribunal has no jurisdiction to interfere with the findings of the Industrial Tribunal or in the Labour Union Agreement for the employees. [256E] (2) The Tribunal had no power to interfere with those findings except where they are based on evidence and it is not open to the Tribunal to go into the merits of the case. [257B C] (3) The Tribunal could not have gone into the merits as the evidence adduced before it was not sufficient to support the finding of the Tribunal. [258C D] (4) The Tribunal should have taken into consideration all the relevant facts and circumstances of each case. The Tribunal has not considered the material which would justify the conclusion of the Tribunal that the enquiry held was not proper. The Tribunal did not consider whether the evidence given by the employer was correct or not. [259D E] (5) In the present case the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to reverse the findings of fact arrived at by the Tribunal. The Tribunal could have acted upon the evidence led by the parties without any reference to them. [255F G] (6) The Tribunal was not justified in holding that the enquiry conducted was not proper because the evidence led was not sufficient for sustaining the finding of fact arrived by the Tribunal and hence the finding of misconduct was not sustainable in law. [251H]
6474: The appellant, a private limited company, entered into an agreement with the respondent State of West Bengal for the purpose of setting up and working as the Berubari Union, which was situated in the State of West Bnadaro. In pursuance of the said agreement, the appellant made an announcement that it had been decided to continue the operation of the said Union and that all the provisions of the said Agreement would be amended and there being no "appointed day" within the meaning of Ninth Schedule to the Constitution. On 30th June, 1947, the Governor General made an announced that the Dominion of India was to come over and the name of the appellant in the list of States, namely, West Bengal, and the name Lindrats, including the name Linder Bengal, and that the name Lendrana, in respect of the territories in the Eastern India, be added to the name Lender of the appellant. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that the said notification having been given retrospective effect from 1st April, 1948, it was not competent to the appellant to challenge it by filing a writ petition under article 32 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the notification dated 30th June was valid and quashed the impugned portion of the notification and directed the appellant to pay the entire sum of Rs. 10,000/ .of the amount of compensation payable to the State of Bihar. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the notification issued by the Governor General was invalid because it was not published in the Gazette of the State of the State. [913C] (2) The High Courts have taken the view that the notification was not published and that the appellant could not challenge it. [914E] (3) The High court has rightly held that the Notification dated 30th September, 1949, which was issued by the Government of India, did not come into force on the date when the Act came into force. [915B C] (4) The High courts have taken the correct view of the matter. [916D] (5) The High 675 Court is justified in taking the view that
3303: The appellant, a displaced person from Pakistan, was allotted certain land in the State of Punjab. He filed a suit for possession of the land on the ground that he had acquired title to it and that the land was not 'deemed '. The suit was dismissed by the trial court. In appeal the High Court upheld the decree. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The object of the Act is to provide for the acquisition of land in excess of the permissible limit of ceiling on land revenue. It does not say that the land should be acquired or transferred to any person. [631E] (2) The statutory provisions are intended to give effect to the policy underlying the Act. The object of legislation is to secure the protection of social justice and the object of the land is to promote the social welfare and the economic development of the country. The object is to provide adequate measures to protect the life of the society. The aim of the Act has been to provide adequate measure to protect the family life of the Society. The object being to provide adequate means to help the society, the Act has to be interpreted so as to enable the society to meet the ends of justice. [632F G] (3) The object is not to make the land lord either to acquire the same under the Act or to make other provisions for the land. The object and purpose of the Act must be gathered from the language employed in the Act itself. The object which is to provide the land required by the society for the purpose of providing adequate compensation to the society for acquisition of the land in excess. The society is primarily intended to serve the society for a better living value than the market value of the property. The society has to be looked into with the result of the land lost. The society cannot be equated with a society like a public limited company. [633B C] (4) The object and pur pose of the land was to provide adequate compensation to society for rehabilitation and rehabilitation. The society can claim compensation for the land only if there is an existing structure or a building or a building owned or held by him. The society does not have any direct or substantial interest in the land. There is no provision in the Act for the acquisition
3630: The appellants purchased raw hides and skins, locally as well as in the course 'of inter state trade. The goods were sold to them by the State Government. The Sales Tax Officer assessed the sales tax on the ground that the sale price of tanned hides and kins was not taxable under the State Act. The High Court upheld the contention of the appellant that the sales tax was not levied on the amount for which the goods had been sold but only on the value of the goods supplied by the State. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the sales were not sales tax within the meaning of Entry 86(a) (c) of the State List; that the rate of tax was the same as the tax on the goods manufactured by the State; and that the levy of tax was not a tax under the State Acts. HELD: Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The sales tax is leviable at the rate of 1 1/2 per cent. [1067D] 2. The sales are made in accordance with the provisions of the Central Acts. The rate of tax is fixed by the State Legislature and the State Legislature has power to amend or modify any law in respect of such turnover. It is only when the State legislature has done so. The State Legislature has also empowered the State Legislature to amend or modification any law in regard to the levy of the tax. [1068E F] 3. The State legislature has also to make provision for the imposition of tax in respect of those goods which are liable to be taxed at the rate applicable to the goods produced. The State is entitled to impose the tax on goods imported into the State. [1069G H] 4. The State cannot levy the tax on sales of goods which are exempt from payment of tax. The State has also to provide that the tax shall be payable on the goods produced in the State. The State may not levy the tax if the goods are delivered to the State. But the State has also not to pay the tax on such goods. [1070H 1071C]
6931: The State Government, in exercise of the power under section 68D of the approved a draft scheme published by the State Transport Undertaking for the route No. 1 of the approved scheme and excluded the said four routes from the scheme. The State Government issued a notification under section 68C(2) of the approved Scheme. The respondents filed writ petition challenging the self same scheme contending that the non exemption of the routes represented by the State Government to give it free access to the operators on the notified routes and exclusion of private operators from the scheme, was discriminatory. The High Court upheld the contention and held that the exclusion is discriminatory. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The State Government has exempted four routes from applying the scheme for an area or route or part thereof. The scheme for an existing or potential private operators from one route or part of the route or part thereto is not discriminatory. [754E] (2) The scheme for the first route is for the first portion of the route. The State may have exempted two other routes from the Scheme. The State can pass such a resolution only after considering objections and giving opportunity to the objectors and representatives and also to the State Transport undertaking approved the scheme. [755B C] (3) The scheme cannot be struck down as arbitrary. It is open to the State to pass such a Resolution only after considering the objections and giving hearing the objector and representatives of the State Transport Undertakings. [756G H; 773A B] (4) The State has no power to make any scheme either under section 68 D(2) or under section 68 C(2). [757H; 758A] (5) The State is entitled to take into consideration the scheme for the second portion of the scheme. But the State has not taken into consideration the entire scheme. The scheme is not discriminatory and does not violate any fundamental right guaranteed under Article 14. [759F G] (5)(a) The State cannot act arbitrarily or discriminated against its employees. The State has not acted mala fide. [757E F] (5). The State has neither acted mala fide nor discriminately. The State had made the scheme for some of the routes. The State could not
3971: The appellants imported goods in the warehouse on December 22, 1965. They were cleared on July 7, 1966 and paid for the same. The customs authorities, however, rejected their claim for refund of the amount of duty which was payable under the amended section 15(1) of the , as amended by Act 4 of 1969. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the determination of the rate of duty applicable to the imported goods. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the goods were not "invalidable" within the meaning of article 19(6) of the Constitution. [869 C] (ii) The High Courts have power to take away the correct rate of duty on the imported goods in question. But, as it is not in dispute before us that the goods are 'invalidably different from those of the other two cases. [870 E F] (iii) The High courts have power to interfere with every case where the goods are brought to the customs authorities or where they are actually removed from the warehouse after the amending Ordinance has come into force. The new section 15(3) does not apply to the facts of the case. [871 D] (iv) The High court has power to interfere if the goods are not "in Dao" but "invaliding them to be "as soon as they are found to be "invalised" and the words "the rate of duty" should be read together. [872 H; 873 A B]
555: The appellant was appointed as a Civil Judge in the Rajasthan State and was later transferred to his service. He was subsequently promoted to the post of Civil Judge. In the former State, he was posted as Civil Judge and was then transferred to the Rajasthan Civil Court. On December 9, 1949, the appellant received certain orders from the Government of Rajasthan under article 143(1) of the Constitution. The appellant 's pay was fixed by the Chief Justice of India with effect from January 1, 1950, but before that date, the appellant had been asked to retire on probation for two years. The appellant challenged the order of the High Court on the ground that it was passed without jurisdiction because (i) the appointment of the appellant was not made to the Judicial Service of Rajasthan according to the Constitution of India; (ii) the appointment was made to the judicial service of the Judicial Service even after the commencement of the Constitution of the Constitution, and (iii) the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the confirmation of his appointment in accordance with the provisions of article 143(3). Held, that the appellant was rightly retired from service on July 31, 1951, and was entitled to all consequential benefits including salary and allowances admissible to him till the date of his retirement. The appellant was not entitled to any protection under article 311(2) of the Constitu tion of India. The appellant could not be said to have been dismissed from service on the ground of his being in illegal or vicious, because, he was not entitled at the time when the appointment was terminated.
7045: The petitioner, a resident of the State of Bihar, was taken from his home in police custody at about 8 a.m. On the night between the 1st and 2nd December, 1987, he had been arrested by the police custody. He was taken to the house of the Police Inspector, who searched the dead body of the deceased, and thereafter his dead body was thrown on the railway track. The respondent No. 6, Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police, who conducted investigation into the case, filed an application before the District Judge, Sundergarh, for award of compensation to the petitioner, the mother of Suman Behera, for contravention of the fundamental right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the prosecution failed to prove that the death of the petitioner was not in accordance with law. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The order of the High Court dismissing the petition is set aside and the matter remanded back to the trial court for fresh consideration. [825D] 2. The High Courts have always been alive to the fact that the fatal injuries were inflicted to the deceased, which resulted in his death. In view of the controversy relating to the cause of death of the deceased and the nature of the injury caused to him while he was in police custody, the question whether the death was inflicted or not arose out of the direct result of the death of one person. [826E F] 3.2 The burden is on the respondents to explain how Suman Beara could possibly be treated as a custodial death. It is not possible to say that the burden is on them to explain how the scribe of the alleged incident was really discharged. [827B C]
