On 15th April, 1986, the respondent wrote a letter to his bank on 21st January, 1986 informing him that his resignation would become effective on 30th June, 1986 and that the respondent would be relieved from the service of the Bank on the same day. The respondent thereafter filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the purported acceptance of his resignation and for a direction to the bank to treat him as in service of the appellant bank up to 30th June. The High Court held that the respondent 's resignation letter dated 21st January 1986 had been accepted by the authority competent under the Service Regulations, and hence the order passed by the respondent was illegal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the respondent 'testa bleed was not entitled to the benefit of the said order; (ii) the respondent was not entitled for protection under Article 311(2)(b) of the Constitution; (iii) the respondent could not have been treated as an employee of the bank; (iv) the respondent had no right to continue to remain in service till the date of his retirement; and (v) the respondent cannot claim any protection against the termination of his services. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The respondent 's letter dated 21.1.1986 is a validated letter and has been written to the bank. It does not contain any reference to the letter. [616C E] 2.1 The clause in the letter clearly indicates that the respondent may terminate the services of the bank after giving one month 's notice. The respondent 'tested his intention to retire from service on the ground of his bona fide illness. He was also informed that his resignation will become effective only on the 30th June 1986. The respondent did not take any action pursuant to the letter or the letter. The respondent was not at liberty to accept the resignation. The respondent had no power to alter or modify the terms of the letter. There was no force in
4879: The appellants are teachers in the service of the State of Punjab. They were teachers in the appellant 's service. In respect of them, they were entitled to the higher grades and their pay scales were fixed on the basis of the qualifications prescribed by the order of the State Government. The State Government issued a circular letter dated July 29, 1967 that the posts of teachers in the grade would be available for the existing teachers in the State of Haryana. The appellants challenged the validity of this circular as violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellants had taken graduate degrees and, therefore, were entitled to their claim to the higher grade. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The State Government has no power to make any new rules or bye law providing for the selection of teachers in a particular grade. [839C] (2) The State is bound to frame rules regarding recruitment, appointment, pay, pension etc., and other conditions of service. The State cannot make rules for promotion from one class. It may provide for a teacher or a teacher in a particular class. But it does not say that the State should frame rules for promotion to the higher posts. [840E F]
3182: The respondent landlord let out the premises to the appellant on a rent of Rs. 125/ per month. On an application under section 14 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 for eviction of the appellant on the ground that she had sub let the entire premises to one Sohan Singh who was running a business under the name of Royal Dispensing Chemists and Druggistn. The Rent Controller held that the appellant was the legally wedded wife of Sohan Singh. In appeal the Appellate Tribunal set aside the order of the Rent Controller holding that the appellant had sub let his entire premises to another tenant. In second appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that two substantial questions of law and fact were involved in the appeal one relating to the status of the appellant as wife and the other whether on the facts found the ground of sub letting had been established. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has dealt with the case as if this is a matrimonial proceeding in which the status of a husband would be under direct challenge. [527D] 2.1 The question whether on the evidence found the ground or not is a matter of law and whether the High Court was in error in interfering with the concurrent finding of the Rent Control authorities, there is great force in the contention that even if it is assumed that the appellant is the wife of So thanhan Singh, he would be entitled to possession of the shop premises as a tenant. [528G H; 529A B] 3.2 The High Court was right in interfering with findings of fact arrived at by the Rent Control Authorities. There is no substance in the contention raised by the appellant that the High Court has acted upon any extraneous material. It cannot be said that the High Courts have committed errors apparent on the face of the record. [530C D]
5094: The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1966 67. In respect of the assessment years 1966 67 the Income Tax Officer assessed the assessee 's share of income. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Authorities but the Tribunal held that the amount standing to the credit of the deceased partner in his individual capacity was not her asset within the meaning of section 2(4) of the Act and accordingly set aside the assessment made on the ground that the amount had been acquired as an asset of the assessee ' Hindu Undivided Family. The High Court upheld the view taken by the Tribunal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the income from assets inherited by a son from his father from whom he had separated by partition could not be assessed to income Tax under the Income Tax Act, 1961. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1) The income from assets occuring in the hands of a son from whom he has separated by partition cannot be assessed to tax under the Income tax Act, 1961, because, the property of a male Hindu dying intestate devolved on him by partition. [256E] (2) The income derived by a son or a minor daughter from his father 's estate is not liable to tax under section 3(3)(a). But the High Court was of the opinion that under the Hindu Law when a son inherited separate and self acquired property of his father, it assumed the character of joint Hindu family property in his hands qua the members of his own family. It was not correct to say that the income received by the son inherited by the son from his parents from which he had separated. [255G H; 256A B] (3) The income of a son inheriting by a son in his individual capability must be computed in accordance with the provisions of the . [256B C] (4) The income so computed cannot be said to have accrued to the assessee. [257C D] (5) The income thus computed cannot be added to the income of the assessee. The income so worked out does not cease to be income within the meaning Of section 2(14A) of
2567: The appellant company was in financial difficulties in 1954 and was unable to meet its obligations. In 1955 the Government of U.P. sanctioned a proposal for the purchase of land by the respondent company, and the price fixed by the Collector was Rs. 8,38,176 13 0. Sardar Jagjit Singh, Chief Engineer, Indian Institute of Sugar Technology, Kanpur, valued the movables belonging to the Company at Rs. 23,75,000/ . On August 8, 1956 the Government of Uttar Pradesh issued under section 46(2) of the Act, the Government of that U.P., appointed the Collector, Deoria, as the Authorised Controller of the Company. The Collector, Denor, after making enquiries regarding the claims made by the appellant company, passed an order on July 14, 1954, directing the sale of the holdings and the property of the Company for realizing Rs. 8 ,38,175/ . The appellant company challenged the order before the High Court. The High Court held that the sale was not illegal because the proceedings were initiated against the appellant company and that it was not proved that there was any material irregularity or mistake in publishing or conducting the sale or that any substantial injury had resulted to the company. The High court also held that the amount of Rs. 8.38,174 13 0 was paid to the appellant company. The State appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the sale is not illegal because it has been made without authority and acted upon. It was not proved by the record that there was no material irregularity or mistakes in publishing or carrying the sale or the valuation or the amount paid to the person who entered into the transaction. [470 D] (ii) The High Courts have taken the view that the amount paid by the appellant Company could be treated as a sum of money which would be payable to the appellant Company. The amount of Rs, 8,38 and the amount of the amount received by the appellant was really income tax and was therefore taxable. The amount was liable to be deducted from the amount of compensation. 5438: The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the appellant tenant on the ground that he was a sub tenant with knowledge and consent of the landlord and as such could not be said to have consented to the bargain. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the agreement was not binding on the tenant. In appeal, the High Court held that the respondent had no right to enter into possession of the premises in question and dismissed the suit. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. The High Court was right in holding that the respondent was not a sub tenant and as such he was bound by it. [869C] 2.1. It is well settled that where a person has been given an opportunity to defend himself and there is no parting of possession of the demised premises, there is only a right to enter in the premises in dispute and not a right to take any other action against the landlord. Therefore, the respondent cannot claim any protection under section 14(3) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956. [870D E] 3.2. There is no force in the contention that the respondent did not give any notice to him to appear before the Rent Controller or the Rent Control Tribunal. The respondent could not have been called upon to produce evidence of his defence. The respondent did not even object to the plea raised by him. [871E F]
6267: The landlord 's premises let out to the appellant tenant on a monthly rent of Rs. 10,000/ . The landlord filed an application for restoration of possession of the premises in question. The Rent Controller dismissed the landlord 's application dated October 12, 1986 for restoration of posses sion of the premises. The Rent Control Tribunal confirmed the order of eviction passed by the Rent Controller. In appeal, the High Court held that the permission granted under section 21 of the Act was invalid and set aside the order of the Rent Controller holding that the landlord had failed to perform his personal need of the landlord 'S ' family; and that the premises were constructed in 1972 and the second floor of the building was never occupied by the landlord since 1973. On this basis it was held that creation of tenancy for limited period of three years w.e.f June 8, 1976 under section 21(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, was not valid. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, HELD: 1. The landlord 'should be deemed to have been in possession of the tenant 's premises as required under section 21 (1) of Delhi Rent Control (Amendment) Act, 1976. [837E] 2. Section 21(1)(a) of the Act is not applicable to the facts of the case. It is only when the tenant has sought permission to renounce the landlord 'turnover the premises in dispute or the landlord does not require the suit premises for a limited period of 3 years. The landlord has thus failed to establish the requirement of the landlord for the grant of permission to ren attorate a tenancy for limited periods of three years. [838H; 839A B] 3. The landlord is entitled to get the benefit of the provisions of section 21(2) of the , which provides that where a tenant has obtained permission to ren dered the landlord 'it shall not be entitled to evict him on the expiry of the period of six months from the date of expiry of the prescribed period. [840B C] 4. The landlord must be deemed to be in possession of a residential accommodation within the meaning of section 21 (3) of the . [836C]
6924: The respondent State of Gujarat was a manufacturer of liquor. In the writ petition filed before this Court it was contended that since the entire judgment of the High Court proceeded on privilege theory it could not withstand the principle laid down in Synthetic & Chemical 's case, it could not be said that the impost was excessive and arbitrary. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The impugned levy is not justified because the element of fee levied by the State is clearly covered by Entry 33 of List II of VIIth Schedule to the Constitution. [58A] (2) The impugned imposition is not justified on any ground for interference. [58E] (3) The impugned levying is not justified as there are no levy of fee under Entry 8 of List II. Nor such levy can be justified on any basis other than the one made under Entry 33 of the Concurrent List. [58F] (4) The impugned Act is within the legislative competence of the State Legislature. [59D] (5) The impugned legislation is not saved by article 31 A of the Constitution. It does not provide for refund of tax or excise duty which may be collected from the person who pays them. [59E] (5 ) The impugned levy cannot be sustained. [59H; 59B] (6) The impugned provision is not justified. [59C] (7) The impugned notification is not justified in law. [59G] (7)(ii) The impugned provisions are not inconsistent with Article 31 A of tho Constitution. [59F] (8) The impugned enactment is not justified when it has been passed without complying with the mandatory requirement of the proviso to section 58A of the Act. [59B] (9) The impugned statute is not intended to operate against the appellant. [59A] (10) The impugned law is not affected by the provisions of Article 31 A. [59 E]
2993: The assessee company was incorporated on October 11, 1941. In 1956 the managing agency of the New India Industries Ltd., was renewed for a period of five years in view of the provisions of the . The object clause in the memorandum of association contains the usual string of objects. (p) of that clause empowers the company to take part in the formation, management, supervision or control of the business or operation of any company or undertaking and for that purpose to appoint and remunerate any director accountants or other experts or agents. Under section 23A of the Income tax Act, 1922, the income from its Managing Director 's office or office shall be deemed to have been income from its Directors ' office or office. The assessee company had a business consisting wholly or mainly in the dealing in or holding of investments within the meaning of cl. (a) of the second proviso to s.23 A of the Indian Income tax Act. The Income tax Officer held that the assessee company was a company whose business consisted mainly in dealing in or hold of investments and at the rate of 30 per cent. In appeal by the assessee company, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. On reference, the High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Court has rightly answered the question against the assessee. [950 C] (2) The High Courts were wrong in holding that the assessee is a company whose affairs comprised entirely of the dealing in and holding of investments and not merely as an "investment company" but also as an "income" used in the definition of "invest". The High Court did not give any reason whatsoever why it should have refused to answer the question whether the assessee company is a company which carries on business or carrying on business. [949 F G] (3) The High court was right in holding that there was no evidence to show that the assessee Company was a company which carried on business. The High Court was in error in holding that it was a company 'as defined in section 2(g) of the Income. tax Act. [951 D E] (4) The High courts are justified in holding that a company is a Company
4400: The appellant, a registered dealer under the Gujarat Sales Tax Act, 1969, was assessed to sales tax on the turnover of sales of goods specified in Part B of the Schedule to the Act. In the assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1970 71, the Tribunal referred the following question of law: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, and on a correct interpretation of sub section (33) of section 2 of the Gujarat Sales tax Act, 1969 the Tribunal was right in deciding that the applicant was liable to pay purchase tax under section 16 of the Gujarat Act read with Rule 24(4) of the Rules framed under the Act, stating that the raw materials purchased by it would be used in manufacturing taxable goods which would be sold by it in the State of Gujarat. The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The definition of 'consigible ' in Section 2(k) of the Gujarat General Sales Tax Act is inclusive and includes within its scope. It is not intended to include any sale of goods or resales of goods from a registered dealer who is not a Registered dealer. [890B] 2.2 The expression 'consigible means the purchaser 's goods as defined in the Act. The word 'consigible" means the purchaser to state that the goods will be used in carrying out the purposes of the Act. If the goods are so used, they must have been converted into manufactured goods and that is why they should be so altered. But if they were so converted, they cannot be said to be a registered dealer. [891E F] 3.3 The definition of "consigible" in section 2(k), is wide enough to include all goods brought into the State of Gujrat, and the word "consigible", has reference to goods which are not included in Schedule I. The word "consATI" has no reference to goods other than those falling in Schedule I and the word 'consATI ' has no reference thereto. [902D E]
4960: The appellant was a licensee of a piece of land. He let out the building to the respondent for a period of ten years and he had let out the premises to the respondent after the expiry of the period. The respondent became a sub tenant of a piece. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the respondent became a licensee and that the respondent become a sub tenant under the original owner. The trial court decreed the suit but the first appellate court reversed the decree holding that the respondent had purchased the property from its original owner by sale deed dated 27 8 1979. In second appeal, the High Court held that the appellant should not be allowed to file a suit for eviction on the ground that the respondent has no right to sue for possession since the suit was in effect one for possession though couched in the form of a suit for mandatory injunction as what would be given to the plaintiff in case he succeed is possession of the property to which he may be found to be entitled. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant should not have been denied relief merely because he had couched in a suit for ejectment against the respondent. [869C] 2. The appellant must be granted relief only when there is some delay. There is no reason why the respondent should not be prevented from seeking relief in a suit to obtain relief in a situation where the suit is in effect one. [870H; 871A B] 3. The appellant cannot be allowed to claim protection of the suit merely because he has failed to get relief in a case where the suit has been dismissed for default. [867E F]
1255: The appellant was the owner of a forest land in Bihar. He entered into a registered agreement with the State for the purpose of cultivation of the forest and the forest area was to be allotted to him. On the basis of the agreement, he paid the price of the forest on the basis of which he had worked the jungle before his enjoyment. In the meantime, the Governor of Bihar issued a notification under section 14(2) of the Bihar Private Forests (Validation) Act, 1949, which provided that no proceedings or action taken by the Government shall be deemed to be invalid or shall be invalid only if it was made after the expiry of one year from the date of the commencement of the Act. The appellant filed a suit against the State for a declaration that the notifications issued under section 14 were invalid as they infringed their rights under article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : Under section 14(3) of the Act, the provisions of Chapter III of the Act are not mandatory but directory and must be complied with. It is well settled that the provisions of the Act do not require that the provisions should be complied with must be complied strictly. [701 B C] The provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure do not require the compliance with the requirements of the Act to be complied with; but the rules framed thereunder may provide for the remedy of an election petition in order to prevent abuse of the process of the Court. The provisions of Chapter I of the Act have to be read together and the procedure prescribed therein has to be followed. The provisions contained in Chapter II of the Act cannot be said to have been complied with except in certain cases where the provisions of chapter I have not been complied with. The provisions also do not require any specific reference to the procedure prescribed by the Code of Criminal Procedure. The provisions in Chapter II have to be complied again with. But the rules framed under the Act do hot have to be observed in the present case. [702 D E] The provisions in Ch. IV of the Act did not require that a notice should be given to the person concerned in charge of the forest area should be served on him. The provisions
5139: The appellant company was incorporated in the State of Uttar Pradesh. In July, 1974, it filed a petition under section 15A(1) of the Companies Act for winding up of its mills on the ground that the company had been carrying on business as a textile undertaking and had failed to pay the tax payable by it. The company challenged the validity of the order of the Central Government dated August 25, 1975 and the High Court dismissed the petition. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The company has not been carrying on any business or profession of trade or business within the meaning of section 2(d) of the . [942 G] (ii) Section 18A of the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 is not applicable to the present case. [943 C] (iii) The company 's contention that the company was not carrying on any work or employment in connection with the manufacture of the textile undertaking was negatived by the Central Government. The company could not be said to have taken over by the Government. [941 D E] (iv) The company was entitled to take over by the State Government under section 18A of that Act. [940 H] (v) The company had no power to make any law for the time being in force in the State. The State cannot make an order directing the company to take over the management of the undertaking. [945 B] (vi) The company is entitled to take such action as may be necessary under sub clause (i) of section 2 of the , to take over any other person or body of persons who are appointed before the appointed day. [946 F] (vi). The company is not entitled to take action under section 18 A of the Act. [1048 C] (vii) The company can go into liquidation only if the State Government has made a declaration that it has become a sick industry. [947 C]
5268: The appellants, a member of the Army (C.R.P.) applied to the Andhra Pradesh High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution for a direction for his absorption in the Force. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent was not entitled to be absorbed in the Force and that he had been appointed after they have attained the age of superannuation in civil posts. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court was in error in saying that there was nothing which stood in the way of absorption. [386E] 2. The scheme of the rule is indicative of the position that in regard to that category of officers benefit of absorption was not admissible and that the arrangement was on temporary basts. Even though under sub rule (2) of Rule 107 as it stood, the respondent would be governed by the said provision from time to time. [387B C] 3. The scheme is indicative and specific in clause (b) of Rule 6 of the Central Reserve Police Force Rules, 1955. It is a fact that the respondent has been given a promo tion and in the promotional post he has worked for about 16 years. On the basis of such promotion on temporary basis the respondent would not be entitled to claim absorption. [398D E]
6438: The appellant was detained under Section 3(1)(i) and 3(1) (iii) of the COFEPOSA Act, 1974. He challenged the detention order on the ground that the grounds were vague and that there was no material to show that the authority making the order must communicate to him any reason whatsoever; that the detaining authority had failed to do so in his reply that he had been informed that if he desired to make a representation against the order, he would be given an opportunity of being heard in accordance with law; that the said failure did not amount to violation of Article 22(5); that the detaining author ity having passed the detention order without considering the representations, it could not be held that the authority has acted mala fide or for unduly long delay in passing the order. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. It is well settled that the power of the Central Government to revoke the order cannot be exercised unless there are cogent reasons to exist. In the instant case, the detaining authority has made the order on the basis of which the order has been made. [890B] 2. The order dated 10.12.1988 is set aside by the High Court and the same is restored. [891C D] 3. The right under clause is two fold, namely, that the authority must communicate to the detenu the grounds on which the order had been made, as soon as the order is made and secondly, that the detenu must also be afforded the earliest opportunity of making a representation against such order. In the counter affidavit it is stated that the authority had communicated to the detenu 's representation to the State Government. The said communication does not mean that the authority should communicate to the deten tion to the detenu. [892E F] 4. The authority has to consider the representation within reasonable time and has to consider whether there is sufficient cause for making a representation. If the authority makes its report within 90 days from the date of receipt thereof, then the order of detention can be quashed. [895D] 5. The right of the detenu is not absolute and the authority must inform the detenu the reason for making the order. The authority must act according to the procedure prescribed by law. [893F G] 696
4364: The appellant, a workman of the respondent, was employed in an industry, for nearly 15 years. He applied to the Labour Court for permission to terminate the services of all workmen who had been in continuous service for not less than one year and the termination of their services were given under the provisions of section 2(OO) of the . The Labour Court granted permission to the appellant to terminate the service of all workmen on the ground that they had been in continuously working for not less then above the age of 60 years. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the expression 'retrenchment ' means the termination by the employer of the service of a workman for any reason whatsoever; (ii) the termination of services of all employees without notice or compensation is arbitrary and discriminatory and violative of Article 14; and (iii) the expression "re fictionally accepted notion of retrenchment in an existing or running industry by the employer does not mean that the termination of service of all employees must be deemed to have taken place as a measure of punishment and therefore the termination of the services of the workman after serving him must be held to be illegal. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The definition of " retrenched workmen" in section 2(oO) of The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 includes the termination of employment of all workmen in an industry when the industry itself ceased to exist on a bonafide closure or discontinuance of its business by the employer. [887C] 2. The definition merely gives effect to the ordinary, accepted notion of retirement in an existing and running industry by making it clear that the intention was even to include a bona fide closure or discontinuance. It cannot be said that the definition has no application to the definition of retrenchment. [890E F] 3. The definition is wide enough to include the termination of serv ice of all workmen except the workmen who are in continuous service. The definition has been made with reference to the definition in section 2 (OOO). The definition is intended to give effect to the definition so far as it provides that the definition is concerned, but the definition is not intended to give retrospective operation. [891D E] 4. The definition does not make any distinction between the employer
159: The appellants were convicted for offences under sections 297 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code. They contended that the offence was committed by them in the course of their duty as a criminal act, which was punishable with imprisonment for life. Held, that the offence charged was not one under section 182 or section 21 1, Indian Penal Code, but it was an offence under section 526 of the Criminal Procedure Code and therefore the convictions and sentences were bad. The offence was committed after the giving of the report. The fact that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to take cognizance of the offence was immaterial because the offence was alleged to have been committed by the accused. In the present case the offence was said to have been done by the appellants before they could be tried for the same offence. The question whether the offence was such as a criminal offence within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) Of the Indian Penal code is a question of fact which may arise when the facts proved are not sufficient to hold that the offence has been committed by him.
2605: The appellant, a workman of the respondent, filed applications under section 33C(2) of the , before the Labour Court for the recovery of certain sums as due to the various workmen who had filed their applications under section 20(1) of the Act. The application was rejected by the Labour Court on the ground that the jurisdiction of the Labour Court was barred by the law of limitation. In appeals to this Court, HELD: (i) The Labour Court and the High Court did not accept the plea put forward on behalf of the appellant and dismissed the writ petitions. [869 C] (ii) The Labour Courts have no jurisdiction to deal with claims of the workmen under section 20 of the Act and they are bound to decide such claims. [870 E F] (iii) The Labour Appellate Tribunal has power to try all these claims which can be made by the employer in respect of those matters. The jurisdiction of the Tribunal is barred by the Act. [871 D] (iv) The jurisdiction of an Industrial Court is ousted when the Act provides for relief in such cases, the jurisdiction of an industrial court is excluded from the jurisdiction of it. [872 G H] (v) The jurisdiction is barred by section 20 of Act No. 11 of 1948. The Act does not provide for relief in any case where the Act provides that the jurisdiction is barred either by the Act or by the Act itself. It does not say that the Act is repealed by the Act providing for the remedy of a claim which may arise under the Act. If the Act provides otherwise, the jurisdiction is not barred by the statute. [873 A B]
5889: The appellant was a teacher in the college of education. In the year 1984 he applied for permission to various private bodies and individuals for starting colleges of education (B.Ed.) courses. He also applied for permission from the University for the said teaching staff. The Government granted permissions to various private private bodies and teachers who had been given permission for the course of studies. The appellant filed writ petition No. 812 of 1986 before the High Court challenging the cancellation of permission. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the cancellation was not as arbitrary, as the grant of permission was only for one purpose and did not amount to any violation of Article 14 of the Constitution. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the Appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The order of the High Court is set aside and the matter remanded back to the High Court for compliance with the directions issued by the Government. [897C] 2.1 The Government Order dated September 20, 1985 declaring the college to be closed on the ground that the college has ceased to exist with effect from the last working day of the academic year 1985 86. The Government Order does not provide for approval of the college or its college. It merely gives power to the Principal to give permission to the college for the period of six months. The college cannot be regarded as a minority institution or not. The college has no right to continue to function as a student. [898E F] 3.2 The order of cancellation of permission is quashed. [899A B]
3809: The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Court for murder of his two minor children. The High Court confirmed the death sentence and hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. In a case where there is no statutory provision to provide an opportunity under section 235(2) Cr. P.C., if the minimum sentence is imposed, the question of providing an opportunity under Section 235 would not arise. [813D] 2. The conviction of the appellant cannot be sustained. [814B] 3. The sentence of life imprisonment awarded by the trial court and confirmed by the High Court is set aside. [815E] 3. There is no reason why the sentence of life sentence should be substituted in place of death sentence awarded by the Trial Court and confirmed by this Court. [816F G] 4. The sentence must be reduced from one year from the date of the judgment of the trial court. [817H; 818A]
4605: The appellant was appointed as Principal of the College. He was not given any substantive appointment or withdrawing any power to appoint a Principal of that institution. The Committee had recommended his selection and the appellant was selected. The appellant challenged the order of the State Government in a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court held that the Teacher in question had no power to appoint the appellant as Principal, but only the authority to appoint him as Principal was not valid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the language used by the High Court in the impugned order did not warrant the conclusion that the appointment of the appellant was neither illegal nor justified. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have rightly held that the teacher in question had been validly appointed under section 16F of the Intermediate Education Act, 1921. [973E] 2.1 The High Court has rightly held that since the appellant had been appointed by the State Government, he could be said to be appointed as Principal only if he had been appointed as Principal. The High court accordingly dismissed the Writ Petition. [974C D] 3.2 The High Court was right in holding that the teacher was not entitled to the post of Principal. It is well settled that the expression "Forfeiture" occurring in Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure means 'the appointment of a Principal of an institution. The expression "Forsely" means "forfeiture". The expression "Promotion" means "to facilitate the promotion of teachers including Principal and therefore, the Committee of Management of the college had no power of appointment of such staff as Principal. [976D E]
5006: The appellants were carrying on business in foreign currency. They had been residing in a hotel in Punjab. On the night between August 24, 1967 and May 14, 1968 they made various representations for return of documents including foreign currency. Thereafter when the appellants made various representations to the Directorate of Enforcement, the respondent No. 2 was directed to deliver such rooks of accounts and other documents and goods seized during the search to the requisitioning officer as the documents and material seized during the seizure. The appellant 's writ petition challenging the legality of the action taken by him was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the power of search warrant under section 132A of the Income Tax Act, 1922, was not exercised in a fair and just manner and to effectuate the purpose for which it was conferred as is evident from the language employed in section 132A(1) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power of search is vested in the Central Government or any officer of Enforcement not below the rank of Assistant Director of Enforcement has been delegated to the Central Government. [869D] 2. Section 132A does not confer power on any officer of the Enforcement Officer to search for and seize any document which in his opinion will be useful for or relevant to any investigation or proceeding under the Act. It cannot therefore be said that the power to search and seize any documents which in his own opinion would be useful for the purpose of the Act, if he thinks fit. [870H; 871C D] 3. The power to search without making an order under section 132 A is not an empty formality but is intended to be used in a summary way. It is only when the power is exercised in a particular manner and the power is exhausted. It is not possible to say that the power is not exercised in the ordinary course of law. [872E F] 4. The power conferred on the officer of Enforcement may be exercised in a different manner and it can also be exercised in the same manner. But the power to make a search and seizure must be exercised in accordance with the rules of natural justice. [873G H]
6378: The appellant workman was employed by the management of a private limited company. He was assigned work in the first shift for picking up certain employees of the second shift and general shift, and for drop, ping school children at various scheduled points. On the same day, the management sought approval from the Industrial Tribunal for the said work. The Tribunal held that the work was not done in the previous year but on the other hand, it had taken into consideration the fact that the work had been done in the earlier years. The Tribunal rejected the claim of the workmen to pay gratuity at the rate of Rs.607.90 as wages for one month, before hand a sum of Rs. 607.90 being the amount already paid to the workman. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that (i) the Tribunal should have considered the evidence adduced by the employer; (ii) the Tribunal ought to have taken into account the fact that there was no evidence to show that the employee was actually worked in the earlier year; and (iii) the Tribunal could not take into account the evidence of the employer that he was actually worked out on the basis of the material placed before him. Dismissing the Appeal, HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal has rightly held that the respondent was entitled to the benefit of the payment of the gratuity pay. [976C D] 2. The Tribunal has also found that the respondent 's salary for the period prior to the date of his employment is not admissible under section 33(2)(b). [977E F] 3. The finding recorded by the Tribunal cannot be challenged in this Court. [977D]
5478: The appellant was appointed as Principal of a College. On January 29, 1986 the District Magistrate issued an order of suspension of the appellant and directed that the appellant be allowed to function as Principal. The appellant 's writ petition challenging the order of suspension was dismissed by the High Court on the ground that the charges against him did not warrant his dismissal from service and that the charges were not proved. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the order of dismissal passed by the Vice Chancellor was illegal and void because the order of the Vice Chancellor could not be set aside unless the High Court had laid down certain guidelines for the exercise of power under section 68 of the U.P. State Universities Act, 1976. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The order of the appellant dated March 7, 1987 is quashed and the order of discharge passed by the respondent passed by the appellant must be set aside. [312B] 2.1 The appellant has been given an opportunity to show cause why he should not be removed from service. He must have been given an adequate opportunity before passing any such order. The order of discharge is not a punishment but a penalty. It is always open to the appropriate authority to pass such an order in accordance with law. [313D E] 3.2 The order of suspension passed by the appel lant was passed by the Deputy Controller of Agriculture, U.P., one dated July 18, 1986 and the order was passed by him on December 31, 1986. The appellant was afforded an opportunity to explain his conduct and if he did not appear before the High Court he would have been denied the opportunity of being heard. [314C D]
2126: The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was running a temple of the temple. In the year 1962 he filed a suit for declaration that the properties in suit were public religious endowments and were not public religious endowments within the meaning of the Act which applied. The Commissioner of Hindu Religious Endowments, Orissa, held that the properties constituted a 'religious endowment ' within the meaning Of section 4(1)(c) of the Act. The Commissioner further held that the property in suit was a 'math ' as defined in the Act and that the properties were public religious trusts. The appeal to the High Court was dismissed by the Commissioner. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i) the Commissioner had no jurisdiction to decide whether the properties in dispute were public religious endowment or not; (ii) the Commissioner could not have decided the question whether the properties were private properties or public religious endowments; (iii) the Commissioner was not competent to decide the question whether any particular property was a public trust or a public character, and (iv) the Commissioner acted in violation of the provisions of the Act and therefore the appeal must be allowed. HELD : (i) The Commissioner was not a statutory body under the Act. It is only a tribunal of law and does not function as a court of law. [440 B] (ii) The Commissioner can act as a judge of a civil or revenue court and cannot act as a tribunal of fact. The decision of the Commissioner being a quasi judicial one is final and binding on the parties. The Commissioner has no jurisdiction to determine whether the properties are public religious endowments. The Commissioner is not a tribunal of the nature of the appointment. The Commissioner may be a tribunal of status and status of a public character. The Commissioner can only act as a judicial authority. The Commissioner acts as a tribunal. The Commissioner merely acts as a judicial body. The Commissioner does not act as a court. The Commissioner cannot act as such. The Commissioner exercises his functions as a judicial tribunal. The commissioner is an appellate authority. The Commis sioner is a tribunal of its own. The Commissioner means a person who holds a public office and is appointed as a judicial officer. The Commissioner, however, acts as a judge. He
3656: The appellant, a teacher of a school, was dismissed from service by the Deputy Commissioner (Education) and his appeal to the Administrator was unsuccessful. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Deputy Commissioner, Education, as well as the order of dismissal passed against him. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the disciplinary authority had failed to record its findings on the charges, and that the dismissal was not justified. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the impugned order of the High Court was vitiated as the disciplinary authority has neither recorded its findings with respect to the charge drawn up against the appellant as required by regulation 8(9) of the Regulations nor has it given its reasons for passing the order. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The order of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 is invalid as it did not expressly and specifically indicate either the conclusions of the dismissing authority or the finding of the Enquiry Officer or that the dismissal of the employee under Article 311(2) of the Constitution is based on no such conclusion. [10B] 2.1 The impugned order of dismissal of the appellant was bad in law and therefore the appeal must be allowed. [10D] 3.2 The order of dismissal cannot be sustained merely because the disciplinary authority, having regard to its findings on these charges, is of the opinion that any of the penalties specified in regulation 8( 9 ) of the Regulations, can only be imposed upon the person found guilty of misconduct after giving an opportunity of being heard in accordance with the rules of natural justice. [10F G]
4018: The respondents were owners of certain lands in the State of Gujarat. After considering their objections under section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 the respondents amended their plaint adding a relief for quashing the notification under section 6(1) of the Land Acquisi tion (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967. The respondents challenged the validity of section 4 as violative of article 14 of the Constitution on the ground that they had no opportunity to file any return before the date of hearing. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the impugned notifications were invalid because the provisions of section 4(1) were not attracted. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the impugned notification was invalid because the legislature has now provided that in respect of a notification issued after the commencement of the Act the impugned notification would be validated if it was held that the impugned provisions were not likely to have been made with retrospective effect. HELD: Dismissing the appeal: (i) Section 4(1)(a) of the Act does not authorise the State Government to issue a declaration under section 6 of the Land Act. [969 C] (ii) The words "in respect of a declaration under s.6" are wide enough to include the operation of the provisions of the Act. It is only when the legislature has enacted the law that it has done so. The legislature has then enacted the law to provide that the declaration under section 4(2) shall be made after the expiry of two years from the commencement of Act. The legislature did not intend to make any such declaration under section 3(1). [970 E F] (iii) The word 'shall ' in cl. (a) means "the declaration under section 2(1)". The words "may" in cl. I(b) means "in respect thereof". The words 'may ' mean "in respect whereof" and "were not intended to include "in respect", which the declaration under s 6 can be made, the apprehended arbitrary exercise of power is made. The words "shall" in cls. (a), (b) and (c) indicate that the declaration may be made by the party concerned. The words 'shall ' mean "for any particular time" and "every
547: The appellant, a standing order of the respondent company, made an application to dismiss the respondents on the ground of misconduct. The Industrial Tribunal held that the appellant had alleged misconduct against the respondents and could not be allowed to adopt the expedient of terminating their services by giving notice for the requisite period or payment of salary in lieu of notice. The Labour Appellate Tribunal dismissed the application under section 33A of the Act. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the Industrial Tribunal was right in holding that the appellant was guilty of misconduct. In the absence of any evidence adduced by the appellant, it must be presumed that the appellant has been guilty of misconduct and he should have been given an opportunity before his dismissal. The Industrial Tribunals were, therefore, justified in entertaining the application for amendment of the prayer of the original application in which the appellant wanted to dismiss the respondent. The Industrial Court was of the opinion that the appellant 's action was in breach of the provisions of the Act and the discharge of the respondents by the appellant amounted to retrenchment and retrenchment being one of the matters specified in sub section (1)(b) of section 7 of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act 1950, the respondents had a right of appeal to the Labour Appellate Tribunal.
6237: The appellant, a displaced person from Pakistan, filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution challenging his election to the State Legislative Assembly. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant was not a specified landlord within the meaning of section 2(hh) of the Act and that the appellant could not be a specified landlord. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to him and that the respondent was entitled to recover possession of the premises in question. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The definition of "specified" in section 2(j) of the Punjab Urban Rent Restriction (Amendment) Act, 1985 is wide enough to include a person who has been declared to be an "unti fictive tenant". [95E] 1.2 Section 2(h) of Act provides that where a specified landlord at any time within one year prior to or within one year after the date of his retirement or after his retirement but within one year of the date of commencement of the Act, shall be deemed to have been made by such person as may be appointed by the Government in this behalf. The definition of 'specified ' in section 2 (hh) is very comprehensive and includes a person who had been declared to have been so declared as the person who had held an appointment in the public service or post in connection with the affairs of the Union or otherwise. The definition is wide enough for the purpose of section 2 (j) of Act. It would therefore be clear that the definition of "esses" contained in section 2 is wide enough so as to include a landlord who has been selected for being chosen from service or post of a person who is not a member of the armed forces of the Union. [95F G] 2.1 The word "esses", in section 2A of the Act means "not" and does not mean "every person who has ceased to be a member of any other armed forces." [95H; 95A B] 3. The definition cannot be confined to persons who are not falling within the definition. The definition has been amended by the Amendment Act, 1976. The definition does not cover a person who was a member of an
347: The appellant was convicted for an offence under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. He filed a petition for enhancement of the sentence. The High Court dismissed the same holding that the appeal had been heard by it in the absence of the appellant 's pleader, even after calling for the records of the case, would be to determine whether the conviction could be sustained or not. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court has no power to alter the decision of the trial court on any ground which may arise out of the order of dismissal passed against the accused. [1010 D] (2) The High Courts have always taken into account the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure and their decisions are not binding upon the High Court. But if the accused had an opportunity of showing cause against his conviction and sentence either by a substantive application made by him under sub section (6) in the first case, for the reason that he had an opportunity to show cause against his acquittal but nobody will contend that the order of the High Court is vitiated by its failure to exercise his right of appeal or revision to the High Court he was entitled in a subsequent application by the Government for the grant of special leave. [1011 H] (3) The High court has jurisdiction to deal with the matter as a result of the decision of a single judge of the High court. If the accused had a right of appeal and the High Court had jurisdiction to decide the question referred to it, the judgment of the lower court must be set aside. [1012 G H; 1013 A B] (4) The High courts have always taken care to find out whether the order of a single Judge of the High, Court is erroneous or not. It is only when the High Court decides that the order is erroneous that it can pass such orders. The High Courts cannot act merely because the order of an appellate court is not subject to the restrictions imposed by the statute. [1015 C E] (5) The High judges who have decided that the order should be set aside, cannot take advantage of the fact that the High Court has given a direction to the High court to dispose of the appeal without hearing the parties to the appeal.
1969: The assessee company was carrying on the business of land development in Calcutta. In the assessment to income tax for the assessment year 1948 49, the Income Tax Officer included the value of goodwill alleged to have been transferred by the vendor firm in lieu of the sale price of the business as a whole, there was no profit in the amount of Rs. 2,50,000 represented the surplus on the sale of the entire business. The Appellate Tribunal held that the entire share capital of the vendee company was taken over by the vendor 's partner of the firm and therefore the profits arising out of the sale were taxable income. On appeal by the Revenue, the High Court held that the total income of the vendees was not assessable under the Indian Income Tax Act. Dismissing the appeals to this Court, HELD: (1) The question whether the assets of the firm transferred to the assessee company or not is one which must be determined with reference to the total income from the property of the firm. [613 D] (2) The mere fact that in the schedule the price of the land is stated does not lead to the conclusion that the profits arising from the sale are not taxable but only those profits arising from such sale are taxable. If so, there is nothing in the name of Mugneerarm Bangur & Co., that would constitute income. [614 C] (3) The mere reason that the profits accruing from the sale proceeds of the business would not make any difference between the sale proceeds and the profits arising therefrom. [615 E] (4) The mere existence of the profit in the transaction does not lead either to the inference that the profits in the transaction fall within the definition of "business" in section 2(5)(ii) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. [616 H] (5) The mere circumstance that the profits earned by the assessee company cannot be considered as dividend received by it. [617 A] (5). The mere fact of the sale of some of the shares did not lead to any change in the figures given in the agreement for sale. [618 B] (6) The mere taking of the sale proceeds from the assessee company does not lead directly the inference that profits arising from it were taxable.
4656: The appellant was convicted for murder and sentenced to death. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the constitutional validity of the death penalty imposed by the provisions of section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the offence charged was not one punishable under the Indian Penal Code but only under the Indian Arms Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the circumstances found by the Courts below would be "special reasons" for awarding the death sentence; (ii) the circumstance that the appellant was already convicted for murder or some types of murder in most of the civilised countries in the world, if the framers of the Indian Constitution were fully aware as to why they should have been unable to obtain any bailer; (iii) the fact that the appellant had been convicted for murder, and the sentence awarded by the High Court was illegal because the appellant was not given an opportunity to explain his conduct and conduct during trial; (iv) the circumstances relied upon by the courts below showed that he was guilty of murder and the sentence passed against him was illegal; (v) the circumstances set out in the judgment of the High Court did not warrant interference with the sentence passed by the High court. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The law is clear and unambiguous and its true intention is that the circumstances must be considered in each case independently of the facts and circumstances of each case. [165B] 2.1 The circumstances mentioned in the judgment are cogent and sufficient to establish the guilt of the accused. There is no reason why the circumstances mentioned in this judgment should not be taken into consideration while considering the question whether there has been miscarriage of justice. [166C D] 3.2 The circumstances mentioned above do not lead to the conclusion that the appellant has been guilty of murder or some type of murder in many of the years. The circumstances mentioned are relevant to the present case and they are all relevant to the facts and the circumstances of the case. The circumstances relied upon are material to indicate that the appellant intended to avoid the death penalty which was imposed on him. The circumstances referred to are material to show that the appellant wanted to escape from the
2373: The appellant, a company owning several houses in the municipal borough of Godhra. On appeal by the respondent, the Judicial Magistrate fixed the valuation of the properties at Rs. 90,000/ . In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the value of those properties for the purpose of the Companies Act and the rules made thereunder were not relevant for determining the capital value of those lands and the valuation on the basis thereof was wrong as the High Court had committed an error in holding that the value should be taken into account only on the reliable data as the valuation on which the value is arrived at. HELD: (1) The question whether the value of the properties mentioned in the rule is correct depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [717 C] (2) The principle laid down in section 4(1) of the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925 is that the value must have been ascertained on the materials available before the Court has to determine the value of such property. The value of the property is determined on the material available on the materials or the market value of the assets. The value is to be determined on the materials produced and the market value is to take into consideration the value of all the assets acquired under the Act. The value has to be determined by the Court 's valuation. The value means the value of each item of the value actually received from the assessee and the value of any other assets acquired under a different kind of assets. The market value of those assets for the purpose for which the value has been determined is the value of which the value of some other assets acquired by the assessee is the value paid by the assessee. The value so calculated is the value which the value may be determined on such reliable evidence as would be required by the Court. The value should be determined on that basis. The value was to be determined in accordance with the principles laid down in the Bombay Municipal Market Rates Control Act, 1947. [720 E G; 721 A B] (3) The value of all assets which are included in the assessable value cannot be taken into consideration for determining the value of a particular asset. The value being the value of property which is included in the total assets of the assessee, it is not liable to tax
4079: The appellant was a member of the Indian Army and was put in a civil court for trial. He pleaded that he had been convicted under section 146 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The Magistrate rejected his plea and directed him to be released on bail. On appeal, the High Court held that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to attach the subject of dispute within the limits of the jurisdiction of the Civil Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Magistrate should have made an order under section 145(4) of the Code before making the order under section 3 of the Act. But it is not necessary that the Magistrate should have passed the order under Section 145(1). [145 C] (2) The Magistrate must act with all judicial powers and judicial functions. It is only when the Magistrate has acted upon the complaint or if he thinks fit and if no award can be given by him, that would amount to a criminal contempt. [145 E] (3) The Magistrate may also exercise any other power under section 145 Cr. P.C., but the Magistrate cannot go behind the order under s.3 of the Act, because, the Magistrate has not done so. [145 A B] (4) The Magistrate has to make such orders as are necessary under section 145 of the Code. Therefore, the Magistrate 's order under section 5 of the Act is not a valid order. [145 D] (5) The Magistrate does not act as a court. If he considers the case one of emergency, he proceeds to commit the offence. [145 C]. (6) The Magistrate is bound to give the accused an opportunity to show cause against the order. [146 F] (7) The Magistrate merely gives the accused an option to apply for the same relief in respect of some of the offences committed by him. The Magistrate does so. [144 H]
6363: The Karnataka Contract Car riages (Acquisition) Act, 1976 was enacted to provide for the acquisition of contract carriages and certain other categories of public service vehicles. Section 20 gave the Corporation the exclusive privilege of running contracts carriage within the State to the exclusion of any provision under the Act. The Act provided that the Corporation shall not be entitled to take any action against the State in respect of any matter relating to the same matter or the same thing as is done by the State Government. The Act was amended by Act No. 21 of 1976 which provided that the State Government may make a declaration that the Act was an 'acquisi tion Act ' within the meaning of Entry 42 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The petitioners contended that with the enforcement of the 1988 Act, the provisions of section 20 were ultra vires the State Legislature. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The Act is intra vires the State Legislative Assembly. [625C] 2. The Act does not contain any provision in the Act for the acquisition or acquisition of contract carriage within the state. It is the State Legislature which has the power to legislate in respect of the same matters including the law providing for the acquisition and for matters incidental thereto. The Act makes provision for the acquisition, the regulation and the control of the State is subject to the provisions contained in the Act. [626E F] 3. The Act provides for the acquisition by the State of Karnataka and the State of Tamil Nadu. The Act also provides for the imposition of a tax on the person who takes part in the business of the State. The Act gives the State Government the right to impose a tax on persons who are members of the public. The Act has made provision for the imposition and collection of tax on persons whose property is taken over by the State. In the absence of any provision in this Act, the Act cannot be said to have been passed without the authority of law. [627D E] 4. The Act, therefore, by operation of the provisions contained therein, must be construed strictly and except where the Act provides for its imposition, the Act is declared void. [628F G]
6452: The appellant was a religious minority institution. He applied for the post of Principal in the degree Section of the college. The Principal in its letter dated 5.10.87 stated that he had been teaching experience of Hindi and English as well as of Sri Justice S.K.P.S.Makhan Singh, who was one of the students of the College. The appellant challenged the decision of the University by way of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Lucknow Bench of the Allahabad High Court on the ground that the college being a minority institution any interference by the University under the Act is violative of Article 30(1) of the Constitution of India. The High Court rejected the contention of the appellant that the college was a minority institution and not a minority institution. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The college being a majority institution does not cease to be a minority institution within the meaning of Article 30 (1) of Constitution of India, and is an autonomous body under the provisions of the Constitution. [316B] 2. In the view which we are taking in this case it is not necessary to go into the argument based on Article 30(2). [317C D] 3. The college is a minority institution which has been recognised by the State of Uttar Pradesh. It is a minority Institution which has been established by the Act. The college has been recognised under the provisions contained in the Rules framed under the Act. [318D E] 3. There is no provision in the Act providing for appointment of teachers in a college or a student belonging to such a category. The college cannot be said to be a separate unit or distinct from the college. [319G] 4. The college does not belong to any particular class of teachers. The college merely holds a minority institution in the instant case. The college was a majority institution. The college itself was a minority society. The college did not belong to either party or to any member of the college or to any other person. The college also does not belong only to a minority institution but also to a minority candidate. [420E F]

The ceiling area allowed under section 82(1) of the Act for a family consisting of two or more but not more than five members was 10 standard acres which should not be less than 12 and more than 15 ordinary acres in extent. On 28 March, 1974 the respondent executed three deeds of gift transferring a total extent of 12.83 acres to his three children. The ceiling areas allowed under section 83(a) and the ceiling area allowed thereunder for a family con stituted the land specified therein. The respondent flied an objection on 5 April, 1974 stating that he had no authority to transfer any excess land. The Revenue Officer rejected the objection holding that the land was not 'sitable ' within the meaning of section 84. The respondent preferred an appeal before the Commissioner of Land Reforms. The Commissioner dismissed the appeal. The respondent moved the High Court by way of a writ petition challenging the order of the Commissioner. The High Court held that the provisions of sections 83 and 85 were not applicable to the lands covered by the valid transfers. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) Section 82 of the Act provides that where any person acquire any land after the date notified under section 83 by gift, purchase, mortgage with possession, lease, surrender or any other kind or transfer inter vivos or by bequest or insistence or otherwise and in consequence thereof the total extent of land owned or held by such person exceeds the ceiling area, such excess shall be surrendered to such authority as may be prescribed. [955B] (2) The words "such lands" have been defined in the Act. In the present case, the lands covered in the first part of section 82(l) are included in the term 'temporal '. The lands covered by section 82(i) are not covered by the first part. The lands are not covered either by the second part or by the third part. The land is not covered either in the first parts or by the fourth part. The ceiling in the present case was not fixed at the date
940: The appellant claimed exemption under section 14(2)(c) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, as it stood before the amendment in 1953. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the income tax law was not a taxable territory before April 1, 1950, and therefore, no tax for a period prior to that date could be demanded. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the order of the Income tax Officer but the High Court held against him. In appeal by certificate, Held: (i) The contention that the exemption did not operate to obliterate the exemption had been granted after the amendment of 1953 and the amended section 14(1) was applicable to pending proceedings before the Income tax authorities from whom the assessment year 1950 51 was completed and the question whether the said exemption would have retrospective effect is decided by this Court in the case of C.I.T., Bombay vs M. P. Chaudhuri, ; , followed. (ii) The definition of "tax" in section 2(m) of the Income Tax Act, 1922 includes the expression "income" and does not include any income which may arise during the accounting year.
4507: The Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961 was enacted to provide for the development of surplus land amongst those who were not entitled to hold as the ceiling area. 470: The appellants were married to the respondent on May 10, 1938. They had a house in the village of Darbhanga in which they had been living in the village. In the first instance, the respondent made a "sankalpa" of the gift of four houses at Asansol in the village, and the appellant 's husband was given possession of the house. The respondent filed a suit for maintenance against the appellants and the appellants. The appellants contended that the respondent was not entitled to claim any maintenance from the appellant. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal the High Court held that the appellants were not entitled to maintenance as claimed by them. It further held that the respondent had nothing to do with the settlement of the terms of marriage or with any control or management of the marriage ceremony; and that the appellants had no right to claim any such maintenance. The High Court also held that the appellant was not entitled under section 11(3) of the Hindu Marriage Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended that even if there was evidence that the parties had entered into a transaction of sale of the house in question, the fact that the parties did not make the arrangement or arrangement, would not arise. HELD: (i) The High Court was wrong in holding that the appellants are entitled to claim the benefit of the agreement dated May 10, 1939. [459 E] (ii) The appellants were not liable to pay maintenance because the agreement was not a valid document. The appellants were only interested in the property of the respondent. The appellants had no interest in the property. The appellants could not claim any maintenance. [451 C] (iii) The appellants had not proved that the respondent ever took the property in the past. The appellants have failed to prove that the respondent bad anything to do with his transfer. The appellants did not show that the respondent made any arrangement or arrangement with regard to the property. [455 H; 456 A]
256: The appellant and respondent No. 2, a candidate for election to the Lok Sabha Constituency was declared elected to the general seat of the Congress (I)6,604. Respondent No. 3 filed an Election Petition challenging the election of the appellant on the ground that he had been guilty of corrupt practices in the matter of securing votes under section 100(1)(c) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court held that the act of the Returning Officer in accepting the nomination of any other candidate was not proved. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the petition as the election was void because the appellant was not a party to the petition. HELD: (i) The Tribunal has no power to interfere with the decision of the Election Tribunal so far as it concerned and does not provide for any further appeal but that cannot in any way cut down or affect the overriding powers which this Court can exercise in the matter. [878E] (ii) The Tribunal is not entitled to go into the question whether the election of any other person is void or void. It is only when the Tribunal takes a contrary view, that question will be decided by the Election Tribunal. [879H; 880A B] (iii) The Tribunal must have the power to decide whether the election is void or illegal. The Tribunal has jurisdiction to decide whether any other person has been duly authorised by law to do so. If the Tribunal takes the contrary view then it would be open to the High Court to set aside the election of a returned candidate. [877B C] (iv) The Tribunal can take up the whole case either before it can decide whether the Election Commission is bound to give effect to the decision of such election. The Tribunal may decide whether the result of the election should be declared to be invalid or illegal. [876D E] (v) The Tribunal cannot go into the merits of the election of another candidate who has been selected by the candidate. The Tribunal is bound to follow the procedure prescribed by the Rules. [869C D] (vi) The Tribunal does not function as a court of appeal and does not make a finding upon the correctness of the findings of fact arrived at by the Tribunal

In appeal to this Court it was contended that the impugned Act was void because it was passed after the merger of the State of Kathiawad area into the United State of Saurashtra and the State became vested in the United State. 176: The appellants were convicted under sections 120 B and 161 I.P.C. for the offence of criminal breach of trust and for an offence punishable under section 120 B, and sentenced to one year 's rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1,000 each under section 120B. The conviction and sentences was upheld by the High Court. The impugned Act is a law relating to "public order" and is not a law relating merely matters of private individuals but also a law relating inter alia matters of public policy. [902 H] (ii) The impugned Act was passed with a view to protect the public interest and the appellants were not entitled to be convicted of offences under the Penal Code as they were not parties to the proceedings before the court. [903 D E] (iii) The impugned was not a law within the meaning of article 20(3). The impugned Act did not provide for the exercise or operation of any right conferred by the appellate Court. 1614: The appellant was a public officer and the Chief Minister of the State of U.P. The Chief Minister was the cashier of the Municipal Board of Hardwar and had been working as such since 1932. 5785: The Andhra Pradesh Public Service Commission (Roads and Building) Engineering Service Rules, 1960 were promulgated. The first respondent who was an Assistant Engineer in the State of Andhra Pradesh filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said order on the ground that the classification was arbitrary and violative of the prescription of the Rules. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the classification had been made without complying with the provisions of the Rules and that the procedure prescribed by the Rules did not violate any statutory guarantee or guarantee to the employees of the State Government. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The State is entitled to make direct recruitment to all the cadres of Assistant Engineers, and the quota prescribed by Rule 3(3)(b) of the Rules is to be worked out. [513C] 2. The State has not been able to satisfy the requirements of the Rules, but it has failed to make direct recruit ment to the posts. It has failed to do so because the prescription of Rule 3(4)(b) is not inconsistent with the prescription of Rules. [514D E] 3. The State cannot claim that the classification is unreasonable. [515E] 3. There is no merit in the contention that the classification has been made without following the procedure prescribed for filling up vacancies in the category of Section 4(1). The State has failed to provide for direct recruitment and have therefore failed to make the direct recruits. [516B C]

1769: The petitioners challenged the validity of the sales in question on the ground that they were inter State sales and had, therefore, been subjected to the provisions of article 31(1) (a). Held, that the petitioners were not entitled to the protection of article 14. The petitioners did not fall within the definition of a State 's 924 carry forward business or carry forward business but only those who carried forward their business or carrying forward business or carrying out their own name or names. The petitioners were not liable to be taxed under the relevant provisions of the Sales Tax Act. The petitioners are not entitled to protection of article 31A because they have not been actually registered as dealers in respect of transactions covered by article 31(2) of the Constitution. The petitioners cannot claim the protection of Article 31(1)(a) because it is not open to them to rely upon the decision of this Court in Pritam Singh vs The Commercial Tax Officer and Others, [1955] 1 S.C.R. 781, referred to.
