On June 21, 1966 the State of Madras issued another Notification under section 3 of the Act declaring that the list of backward communities prepared by the Director of Medical Relief, the State should not have included therein any caste or community in the list. The Government of Andhra Pradesh accordingly issued another Notification dated July 29. 1966 amending the first Notification under section 4 of the Act. The Government also made its recommendations which were considered by the Council of Ministers on July 4, 1966 and approved the list of the order of priority as directed by the Cabinet Sub Committee. The Government then passed an order on July 29.1966 amending the first Order of priority as stated by G. O.M.M. S. 1685 dated July 29; 1966. The Government again issued another Notification in September 1966 amending the second Order of priority. The Government thereafter issued another Notification of priority as provided in the Order. The Government thereupon amended the first Order in respect of the two categories viz., (i) Scheduled Castes and (ii) Scheduled castes and Scheduled tribes and (iii) Scheduled castes. The Government further issued another Notification withdrew the first Order and by its subsequent order. The Government however did not pass any order in respect of those categories. The Government made its recommendations that the former was to give preference to the Scheduled Castes and scheduled tribes for the remaining two categories viz. Scheduled Castes and Schedule Tribes
6607: The respondents filed a suit for obtaining leave to institute a suit under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 on the ground that the relief prayed for in the suit were such that leave could be granted without such opportunity having been given. On appeal by special leave, the Division Bench held that the grant was an administrative order of the Court and no notice had been issued to the respondents. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that the relief sought in the suit is not a lawful one. [850D] 2. In view of the language used in Section 92 of CPI (ffa) of the Code, the relief sought for in the suits must be granted in the plaint. It is only when there is a specific provision in the statute which confers power on the court to grant a suit, that is, it can be granted without the application of the rule of res judicata. [851E F] 3. The question whether a person or an individual is entitled to file a suit is a matter of public nature within the meaning of section 92(1)(ffa) and whether he is a party or an individual would have obtained the leave of the court before they instituted the suit. [852B] 4. In the instant case, the relief claimed in the suit was not a lawful claim but a right to sue in the nature referred to in section 92 of Code of Civil Proce dure, as the relief sought could not be granted in a suit. [760H; 761A B]

3367: The appellant purchased the managing agency of a company in the year 1953 54. In 1944, the appellant was the managing agent of an Indian company. The managing agency agreement with the managed company for a period of seventeen years provided that the remuneration payable by the managing agents as per the terms and conditions relating thereto shall be paid to the company. The company was assessed to tax under section 10(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The question was whether the income from the managing agency business which ended on June 30, 1954, could be taken as an 'resumptive purpose ' within the meaning of section 10(5A). HELD: (i) The income from the Managing Agency business which ended in June 30, 1955, was not the previous year for the managing agency capital of the company but was the previous year only for the purpose of determining the annual income of the managing agency. [558 C] (ii) The income derived from the managing agent was taxable in the hands of the managing agent. The remuneration received by the managing agent as remuneration was not the commission or salary of the managing agents but it was the remuneration received by them. The remuneration was received by the Managing Agents as remuneration for services rendered by the managing agency company. The remuneration had been received by the respondent company in the accounting year 1953 54 and the remuneration received in the accounting years were the remuneration received at the time of the managing Agency. The remuneration thus received was received by him by the managing Agents as remuneration. The remuneration paid by the managing Agent was received by them after the commencement of the relevant accounting year and the remuneration was received in the assessment year 1954 55. The remuneration came into no legal existence when the managing agency was closed and the remuneration paid by it became the property of the managing Agents. The remuneration though received by the Directors as remuneration was received after the commencement and the remuneration would have become the property of a managing agent. [559 D E; 560 B C] (iii) The remuneration received in respect of the managing Agent as remuneration for service rendered by the Managing Agent was received in accordance with law and was therefore taxable under section 10 (5A) of the Indian Income Tax Act. The remuneration so received by the Director could not be said to be the remuneration
208: The respondent company was incorporated in the State of Bombay under the . The appellant company claimed relief under article 32 of the Constitution on the ground that the provisions of the section were violative of articles 14, 19 and 31 of the Constitution. Held, that the provisions Of section 3 of the , are supplemented by what is subsequently provided for in section 12 which provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any law or in the memorandum or articles of association of the company, it shall not be lawful for the shareholders of the company or any other person to nominate or appoint any person to represent the company or appointed any person to be a director of the company. The provisions of section 12 of the Act do not confer upon any power on the Central Government to make rules for the appointment of directors as contemplated by section 12. The provisions are supplemented with the powers conferred by section 12 which provide that notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith, the State may make rules for making rules for the management of the company and for the management thereof. The provisions in section 12 of Act do not impose restrictions on the right of directors to make bye laws for their conduct and acts of themselves or of persons connected with the administration of the company but have the effect of enabling the directors to exercise such powers as they think fit to carry out the purposes of the Act.
6304: The petitioners in the writ petition were dealers registered under the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948. They challenged the constitutional validity of notification No. Act XV 48 order 85 dated 26th December, 1985 issued by Uttar Pradesh Government u/s 4A of the U. P. Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1976 and section 4A of that Act as it stood at the relevant time was a law which was enacted to provide for the imposition of tax on goods imported from other States or the Union territories or the Union Territories except in respect of such goods. It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the impugned notification was discriminatory and violative of article 301 of the Constitution inasmuch as it discriminates between goods so imported and goods so manufactured or produced in those States and non manufacturers of the same goods and thereby discriminate between goods so manufactured and produced; and that the impugned notifications being violative of Article 301 of the Constitu tion, the Legislature of a State has not been competent to pass any such provision. Dismissing the Writ Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The impugned notification is struck down as arbitrary and violative of Article 14. [803E] 2.1. In view of the fact that the impugned Notification is made with a view to give preference to all the dealers who are similarly situated in the State, the impugned notification is also struck down as invalid. [804F G] 3.2. The impugned Notification is held to be ultra vires. The impugned Act is not discriminatory and violative. [805D] 3.3. The impugned Finance Act does not contemplate any discrimination between goods so exported and goods so imported. The impugned provisions of the impugned Act cannot be said to offend Articles 301 and 304(a). [801B C]

508: The petitioners who were the displaced persons from Pakistan, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the allotment to them. They contended that the allotment was contrary to the provisions of the East Punjab Government and the instructions of the Financial Commissioner, Rehabilitation, or the Custodian, Evacuee Property, East Punjab, and that the allotment made by the Custodian was contrary to any of the terms of the allotment; that the allotment had been made under the instructions of a general authority; that the Custodian had failed to cancel or vary the terms of an allotment for the implementation of resettlement schemes and/or rules framed by the State Government; that the order of cancellation was bad as being violative of the principles of natural justice; and that the petitioners have contravened article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the orders of cancellation are not invalid on the ground that the orders were passed without jurisdiction and that the orders are not based upon any violation of the principles contained in the principles of equality before the law. The orders of cancellation were quashed by the High Court on the ground of violation of principles of equality.

The property was not liable to be sold but only when the person who was the owner of the property was the sole proprietor, and the property was transferred to his brother Fazal Bhi, and the deed of sale was executed on January 1, 1941, and the firm was registered in the name of Fazal Bhhidas. 5483: The appellant was a tenant of the respondent company. HELD: (i) The suit was governed by article 49 of Civil Procedure Code. The suit was therefore governed by article 46(1)(c) of the Code of Civil Procedure. [813 D] (ii) The suit must be instituted within three years from the date when the award is signed by both the parties. The suit has been filed after such a long lapse of time. The suit must therefore be held to be barred by limitation under article 46(2). [814 C E] (iii) The suit is one for the recovery or enforcement of a claim made in respect of a debt due to the appellant. The suit is not barred by time and the suit must accordingly be dismissed. [815 H]

3943: The State of Jammu and Kashmir, in exercise of the powers conferred by section 133(2)(b) of the Constitution of Jammu and sought to make appointments to civil services and posts. 247: The appellants, who were the mortgagors of a decree in 1933, obtained on the 13th December, 1937, a personal decree under Order XXXIV, rule 6 of the Civil Procedure Code for the balance due to them. On the 16th August, 1947, the decree holders purchased the properties at auction sale and got possession thereof. The mortgagees were put up for sale in execution proceedings in 1930 and the decree holders filed a suit for re maining the mortgaged properties. The appellants ' contention was that the suit was barred by limitation as the decree had been passed after the 15th August, 1948, when the High Court dismissed the suit. Held, that the suit having been dismissed long before the dismissal of the appeal it could not be said that the suit had been filed within time. The suit was therefore barred by limitation. The suit having been filed after the dismissal of appeal the plaintiffs did not come forward to file the present suit. The suit being one for re mained and the suit was therefore not barred by limitation; the suit was filed within time and the suit having become infructuous the suit was still pending.

1707: The petitioner challenged the election of the respondent, who was declared elected. [831C]

4136: The appellant company was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling shares in a private limited company. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner accepted the valuation of the shares made by the Gift Tax and the Wealth Tax officers did not accept the figures of valuation given by the assessees on the basis of the profit earning method of valuation of shares without making any adjustment in the profits of the company. The High Court upheld the contention of the assessee that in the case of an investment company like Mafatlal Gagalbhai Pvt Ltd., the proper method of valuation would be to take the mean of two values, one arrived at by applying the profit earning principle, since in their submission that was the only method which could be applied for valuation of shares of a going concern was the only way which could be adopted for valuation of the assets of the company, and that the value of the shares should have been ascertained from the market value of the assets. The Tribunal had no power under section 6 of the Act to interfere with the decision of the authority below on any ground which may be raised as a jurisdictional error. The Tribunal could not do so without making the reference to the question as to whether the action of an officer was ultra vires. [305D E] 3. In the instant case, the Tribunal has no power to interfere with his decision. The Tribunal was not right in holding that the action was unauthorised and illegal. [306B C]
2374: The appellant obtained an order for eviction against the respondent from the Rent Controller under section 3 of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1948. The decree holder applied for execution to the Court. In the execution proceedings the Court delivered a judgment debtor 's possession and after the decree was upheld in appeal by the District Judge. The High Court dismissed the appeal on the ground that the decree holder had not challenged the proposition that the court could not order delivery of possession without the requisite sanction for the dismantling of the factory. The High court held that in view of the order passed by the executing court the decree holder could not be granted posses sion in execution of the decree and dismissed the appeal by order dated January 8, 1954. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the Court could not order the delivery of possession of the property. The Court could not grant the possession of the premises without the requisite permission for the dis city of the establishment. The Court would have no doubt that in a " case like this where there is no collusion between the decree holder and the judgment debtors" the State Government would not prosecute the judgment debtors or refuse to accord sanction for the disposal of the suit.
4013: The appellant company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling electricity to the respondent State. In its industrial policy, it had been using electricity at Renusagar plant and its factory for the manufacture of 20,000 metric tonnes of aluminium ingots per year. On October 29, 1959 the State Government sanctioned a scheme for the supply of power on a firm, continuous and uninterrupted basis at a rate of 1.997717 paise per unit for a period of 25 years from the date of commencement of the supply. As the Company failed to comply with the said scheme, the Company filed a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the impugned order. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Company was not entitled to claim any relief. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court has rightly held that the Company is entitled to claim the benefit of the relief which the State Government has no right to claim the same. [825D] (2) The High Courts have found that the Company has been able to establish a new unit of electricity and the State Government had no authority to grant the relief to the Company. The High Courts are bound to give effect to the policy decision of the Government. [826E F] (3) The High courts have found that there is no justification for the grant of relief to the company. The High courts should not be sanctified in granting relief to the State Government. [727F G] (4) The High court has not given any directions regarding the issue of relief to any party. The High court cannot go into the question whether the State Government is entitled to grant relief to the parties or whether the State should refuse to grant relief in favour of the company. [728B C] (5) The Highcourt has rightly held against the State Government as well as the State Government to grant relief. [729C] (6) The High will not make any direction to the State to grant relief either in favour of a company or in favour of any other company. [70A B] (6)(a) The High has not made any direction to grant relief under section 23 of the Act. [
6979: The appellants and the respondent Ramshri. She filed an application under Section 145 of the Code before the Sub Divisional Magistrate, Sadabad in which she claimed ownership of the suit property. On 31st May, 1976 the Magistrate passed a preliminary order under section 146 directing that the attachment would continue till the competent Civil Court determined the rights of the parties with regard to the said property. Thereafter, on 19th July, 1977 the Magistrate issued a final order under Section 146 attaching the property in dispute. The appellants and respondents were convicted for offences under Sections 147, 148, 323 and 323 IPC. In appeal, the Sessions Judge held that the appellants had no locus standi to file the present petition for quashing the order of attachment as well as the order of the High Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of attachment dated 25th July, 1978 upto 10th August, 1978 is not illegal since the order of confirmation dated 31st January, 1978 was made after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed for filing the same. [532E] 2.1 The order of appointment of the appellants as the appellants as co accused was not challenged before any authority within the meaning of section 141(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The order dated 25th October, 1978 passed by the Magistrate revived the earlier order of attachment. The appellants have been rightly discharged from the date of the order of appointment. [533C D] 3.2 It is clear from the facts that the order of detention passed against the appellants has been confirmed by the Additional District Magistrate. The order granting interim stay does not mean that the appellants are bound to be released on or without their surrender. [534D E] 3.3 The order of the Magistrate dated 25th March, 1978 is set aside and the order of his release is restored. [535B C]

On appeal the High Court accepted the testimony of the eye witnesses as against the appellant 's guilt and observed: "The appellant was accordingly acquitted. The State appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The evidence of the two eye witnesses as to the appellant was corroborated by the evidence of the other witness. The High Court accepted it. [549E F] (ii) The High Court was right in its view that the evidence of these two witnesses should be accepted as correct. The High Courts have committed error in accepting the testimony of these two eye witnesses. The High court was right in holding that the evidence was not sufficient to convict the appellant. [550B C] (iii) The High court has failed to record a finding that the appellant had been guilty of the offence charged. The High 'Court has held that the appellant could not be convicted under section 302, I.P.; nor can it be said that

But the definition does did not make any difference between cases where the words are not defined. The definition further contemplates cases where the expression 'chattels ' has been used, but where the word 'chattles ' has been employed in order to mean cases where the phraseology used is different from the context of the definition. 1385: The appellants were the youngest brother of the late Nalini Ranjan Sarkar who was a paid employee of the Hindusthan Co operative Bank. On March 17, 1956, an application in revision to the High Court under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for special leave from this Court was made by the appellants. The appellants applied for special leave to appeal against the order of the High Court and obtained leave on February 13, 1956. The appellants contended that the provisions of section 195(1)(b) of the Code had no application to the prosecution as it did not contain any provision for the prosecution which would enable the accused to make out his case in respect of the alleged offence. Held, that the provisions contained in section 195(2) of the Cr. P.C., were applicable to the prosecution of the appellants. There is nothing in section 195 (3) of the Act which makes it obligatory on the part of the prosecution to state the facts or circumstances of each case whether there has been a breach of the mandatory provisions of the Code or not. In the present case the appellants were not guilty of the offences charged.
3425: The respondent was promoted to Punjab Education Service (Class l) on October 1, 1949. In June, 1961 he received a copy of letter No. 5137 ED I 60/9269 dated May 2, 1962 addressed by the Secretary to Government, Punjab, Education Department to the Director of Public Instruction, Punjab, Chandigarh, conveying sanction of the Governor of Punjab to the grant to him i.e. the respondent of superannuation pension and death cum retirement gratuity at the rate of 50% of his basic salary in lieu of the said date. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the aforesaid decision of the Government to apply a cut of 10% in his pension and gratuity under clauses (a) and (b) of rule 6.4 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules Vol. II read with para 9(1)(a) of the New Pension Rules, 1951. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition holding that the impugned decision of the State Government to apply the cut in his pension amount from the date of the order imposing the cut in the year 1964 was an administrative order and the case did not fall within the purview of Article 311(2). Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have no jurisdiction to interfere with the impugned decision as it has been rendered without any authority to decide or determine whether or not the impugned order is justified or not. [316C] 2. The impugned order cannot be sustained merely because the decision of the High Court is based upon the facts and circumstances of the case. It is not open to the High Court to go into the merits of the matter. [317E F] 3. The impugned judgment and order dated December 19, 1966 passed by the High Court cannot be sustained. [318B C] 4. The impugned decision of Government to apply any cut in his age limit for the purpose of employment of teachers in the service of the appellant in the present case was not in accordance with law as superannuation pension was a bounty and was given only as an act of grace, that ground was not available to the appellants in view of the decision of this Court in Deokinandan Prasad vs The State of Bihar & Ors., ; , relied on.
87: The plaintiff 's case was that Budparkash Das and Nandkishore Das had two sons, Bud parkash Das and the other D. Nishore, who was a minor son of the plaintiff, and the plaintiff, as his father, was in possession of his share of the properties, as the daughter of Budparant, and the defendant, who was the son of the deceased, filed a suit for partition against the plaintiff and the defendants. The trial court dismissed the suit holding among other things, that the plaintiff had no cause of action, and that the parties were not Sudras, and that he had no cause to be made the subject of partition. In appeal, the High Court held that the plaintiff could not sue for partition because he was in joint possession of the properties by metes and bounds, but that the parties are only co sharers and not the plaintiff. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court erred in holding that the plaintiff was not entitled to sue for partition. [869 C] (2) The finding which the High Court has been found on evidence is not correct. The High Court should have taken into account the evidence adduced by the parties and the circumstances appearing in the oral evidence. [870 E F] (3) The High Courts have failed to take into consideration the evidence adduced on behalf of the parties. The High Courts will not interfere with the findings arrived at by the trial court unless they reach any reasonable conclusion or perverse. [871 H; 872 A] (4) The High courts have failed to exercise their jurisdiction under section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High courts will not interfere if it thinks that the evidence given by the parties is sufficient to establish that the plaintiff has not proved that he was the son or the son of a party to the suit. [873 G H] (5) The High court has failed to take note of the evidence adduced in the case and the High Court erroneously reversed its decision. [875 D]
2200: The appellants, who were dealers in Punjab and outside for the manufacture of yarn, filed writ petitions under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the sales tax on purchase of oil seeds. They claimed that the sales tax was not a tax on goods purchased by them but only on the sale price of the goods supplied to them, and so it was not liable to be levied as an excise duty. The High Court dismissed the petitions. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) Section 5 of the East Punjab General Sales Tax Act, 1948, which amended section 5 with retrospective effect could not breathe a new life into the said Act. [439 B] (2) The words "for any reason" in cls. (f), (g), (g) and (n) of section 2(ff) are wide enough to include the levy of excise duty. It is well settled that the word " rates" in the definition of "tax liability" in cl. (g) means the rate or maximum rate of the amount of tax payable. Therefore, the expression " rates" would have been used in the definition. The words " rates" mean the rate or total value of the goods sold at more than one stage. The words ' rates ' in the definition may be construed according to their ordinary meaning and they cannot be read in the context of the purpose of the Act. The words used in the charging section must be given its normal meaning and not given its normal language. The words, therefore, when read, should be interpreted according to its ordinary meaning and not in the popular sense. The words which are used in the taxing statute are not defined in the Act. [453 C D]
1307: The appellant, a decree holder in execution of the decree for recovery of money against the mortgage decree passed by the first respondent. The decree was executed on September 7, 1940, and on that date, the decree was transferred to the Court of Subordinate Judge, Midnapore. On August 16, 1941, the Subordinate Judge, midnapore, decreed the suit and directed that a new decree be drawn up and that the amount due under the personal decree be paid in three annual instalments. The Subordinate Judge, thereupon, filed an appeal before the District Court, Midnapur, which was dismissed. In second appeal, the High Court held that the decree was not fully satisfied by the first day of January, 1939, but that the decree had been made absolute and that the decree could not be set aside as it was not fully complied with. It further held that the judgment of the Subordinate Judge was erroneous. Held, that the decree dated September 7, 1941, was not fully justified. The decree having been made absolute, the decree could have been validly passed without any application of the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. The decree did not operate as res judicata because the decree was passed in the meantime. The decree could not have been made absolute.
2933: The respondent was a firm carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of wiques, and the appellant was prosecuted for an offence under section 110(1) of the Customs Act. The Collector of Customs found that the Collector had no jurisdiction to extend the period for giving notice under section 124(a) of the Act either after the initial period of six months or extended by the extended period, but the extension of time had already expired. On appeal, the Collector held that the Collector 's order was justified and directed the Collector to make the goods seized under section 110 (1). The respondent moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the legality of the order of the Collector. The High Court held that the proviso to section 1 10(2) did not contemplate any opportunity of being heard having been given to the respondent before the expiry of the period of six month from the date of seizure. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Collector could not extend the period of four months without complying with the requirements of sub section (2) of section 110; and that the Collector acted in violation of the principles of natural justice. HELD: Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The Collector had no power to extend the time for making the search and seizure. [808 C] The Collector had also taken into consideration the fact that the Collector has made the order of extension of time. The Collector had not even considered the material on record to show that the Collector was satisfied that the Collector would have made the order. The Collector could not be said to have passed the order without hearing the parties. [810 D E] The Collector could have issued the notice under section 120 A of the Customs Rules read with section 112 of the Customs thereunder. The Collector was bound to act according to law. [811 B] The Collector was not right in holding that the Collector bad no jurisdiction to pass the order. [812 H] The Collector is not entitled to exercise his powers under section 112 of Customs Act. [813 G]
975: The appellant, a non resident assessee, filed returns for the assessment years 1957 58 and 1958 59 on the ground that he had been assessed to tax under section 34 of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer served notices under section 34 read with section 22(2) of the Act for assessment of tax in respect of those years. The appellant contended that the proceedings for assessment were commenced within the period of limitation prescribed for serving notice of assessment under section 34(1)(a). The contention was rejected by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Tribunal held that the proceedings were commenced within four years from the date of the notice issued under section 22(1), but since the notice did not comply with the requirements of cl. (a) of section 22(3) of the Indian Income Tax Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the notice issued by the appellant was invalid as the provisions of section 22 (1) applied to residents only and that an obligation to make a return of his income could be deemed to have been discharged by reason of omission or failure on the part of the assessee to make a revised return. HELD: Dismissing the appeal: (i) The proviso to section 22(6) of the Income tax Act, 1922, does not apply to a person liable to pay tax but the liability to pay tax is incurred by him. [446B] (ii) Section 22(1) of the Incometax Act, 1922 provides that if any person has taxable income to submit his return within the time specified in sub section (1) he may commence proceedings for assessment within the period prescribed by cl. (b) of section 23. The proviso requires every person who has taxable income shall furnish a return within the meaning of section 22. It is clear that the proviso applies to persons who are registered as a dealer under the Act. The proviso does not apply in the present case where the notice issued to such a dealer is served on the assessee. The fact that the notice was issued by the assessee does not make the assessee a different kind of assessment. The fact of issuing the notice does not make it a different kind than the one which is mentioned in the section. [447D E] (iii) The proviso does no more than apply

6596: The appellant, a private limited company, was assessed to the Rent Control Act, 1966. The respondent landlord filed a petition for eviction of the appellant on the ground that the said clause is discriminatory and arbitrary because it draws an artificial distinction between tenants on the basis of their income. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the clause in question did not take into account the nature of the business or other relevant factors. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1. The object of the Act is the protection of economically weaker tenants and encouragement of constructing buildings. The purpose of the Act was to provide for the protection of the rent of tenants. The object is the protection and constitutionally valid. [350D] 2.1. It is not a case where the legislature intended to treat the tenant as a class by itself. The classification has been made with reference to the tenant 's net income, whether accruing inside or outside the State, as on the date of the land lord 's application for eviction as well as on the dates of the decree for eviction. The purpose is to prevent the landlord from claiming relief in respect of the tenant 'suitable. The object being the protection of economic welfare and social welfare, the test adopted by the legislature for this purpose is with reference to tenant 's gross income, whether constitutes income. The test is to be applied to the tenant. The object to be achieved by the legislation is the protection afforded to the tenant of the building. The object must be the protection of social security and social welfare and social interests. The object should be the protection and financial interest of the tenant. [449E G] Rattan Arya & Others vs State of Tamil Nadu & Anr., ; , followed. The test of reasonable classification is based on intelligible differentia between persons or things grouped together from those who have been left out and there must be a reasonable nexus with the object to be imposed by the statute. [546C D] In the instant case, the impugned clause does not take into consideration the nature of business or other material which may reasonably be expected to be carried on. The object was to promote agitation against the tenants who are likely to get their advantage of the building, and the object being
4229: The respondent, a foreign person, was found to be carrying on an illegal business in the Indian. He was prosecuted for the assessment of the assessee under section 10(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922 for assessing him 's income and determining his tax liability. He came to the finding that out of Rs. 65,500/ incurred in the business of smuggling gold he was entitled to a deduction under section 10 (1). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order. In second appeal before the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal the assessee represented that if he was regarded as engaged in the business he would not be entitled to any deduction under section 12(2) of the Act. The High Court answered the question in the affirmative. In appeal by certificate: HELD : The High Court is right in holding that the assessee was carrying on the business of the smuggling operation. If the activity of smuggling can be regarded as a business, those who are carrying on that business must be deemed to be aware that a necessary incident involved in the business. [650 E] Badridas Daga vs Commissioner of Income tax, , followed.
932: The appellant, a private limited company, was ordered to be detained under section 15 of the , on the ground that he had been found in possession of certain properties and that he had failed to pay the tax. Held, that the notification did not infringe any fundamental rights of the appellant and it contravened article 14 of the Constitution. It was not open to the State to make an order for the exemption of the petitioner 's liability under section 15(1) of the Act. The State was entitled to recover from him the amount due as provided by the law. The State could not have made the order under section 15. The State cannot claim that the respondent was guilty of the offence charged. The State is entitled to recover only those persons who were found to be peace loving and law abiding citizens. The State has no power to pass an order for such removal. The State can make an order under section 16(2) if the person concerned has committed any act which may be deemed to be one done in his official capacity or in his capacity as a member of the public.
3105: The respondent company was a fairly prosperous concern and one of the biggest of its kind in Asia. It had two other establishments which were also recognised by the Government under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. In respect of the two establishments which were not included in the definition of "workman" in section 2(g) (a) of the Act, the workmen employed by the company were entitled to bonus as provided for in the Act. The appellant company claimed that the employees of the company represented by Bata Mazdoor Union were entitled to Bonus and therefore they were entitled to 100 per cent of the bonus payable to them. The company denied that the general bonus paid under the agreement exhibit A5 was an ad hoc or an ex gratia payment made out of charity and as a supplement to the wages and that it was not a bonus linked with production or comparable commodities. The Company contended that the general and supplementary bonus paid under these agreements could be taken into consideration only on the basis of the profits earned by the company after deducting the bonus from the profits. Held, that the claim for profit bonus is not sustainable. The company was not a party to the contract but merely a subsidiary of the contract. The company 's claim for profit was not tenable because the relevant documents produced by the company did not contain any particulars about the financial capacity of the company. The company had no capacity to pay the bonus. The company has failed to prove that the profits earned had been paid. The company could not have claimed that the general or supplementary bonus paid by it should be treated as a deduction.
931: The respondent firm which was a registered dealer under the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939 (Act IX of 1939), was assessed to sales tax on the turnover of the goods sold by him. In the assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1953 54 the Sales Tax Officer rejected the contention that the order was illegal and not supported by the authority of law. The High Court held that in view of the provisions of section 5(vi) of the Act, the liability to pay sales tax in respect of hides and skins could only be at a single point; but the rule limiting the operation of this mode of taxation to licensed dealers was ultra vires as it contravened section 5(i)(vi). In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court had wrongly decided that the rule limit ing the operation of the scheme of the Act was discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution. HELD: Dismissing the appeal: (1) The High Court was right in holding that r. 16(5) of the Madras General Sale Tax Rules, 1939, did not apply to the case of a dealer who did not take out a licence for dealing in hides and skill of his partner in hides, skins and skins. [553 C] V. Syed Mohammed & Co. vs The State of Madras, ; , followed.
1225: The appellant entered into three contracts for the construction of a dams and other works at Ranchi. The agreement was signed by one of the parties and the arbitration clause provided that the award shall be filed in Court. On the same day, the arbitrator made his award on June 4, 1948, and sent a copy thereof to the parties. The arbitrators made their award on June 3, 1948. The appellant filed an application under sections 17 and 20 of the Indian , praying for a decree in terms of the award. The respondent contended that the award was not binding on the Government but only on the basis of the agreement between the parties. Held, that the agreement was valid and the award passed in proceedings founded thereon was a nullity and could not be set aside on the ground that it was not binding upon the Government. The agreement did not comply with the requirements of section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, which was the constitutional provision in force at the relevant time. The agreement contained an arbitration clause and the award was therefore invalid.
1982: The appellant was a sugar mill. In response to the notice issued by the State Government under section 23 of the Madhya Pradesh Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Rules, 1959 made under the Act, the appellant challenged before the High Court in a writ petition filed in the High Court. The High Court held that the Act did not authorise the levy of cess on the ground that it was ultra vires the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The Act is intra vires the Act and the validity of which is challenged cannot be questioned. [526E] 2. The Act does not provide for the payment of cess or its collection. It merely provides for the payment to the Cane Development Council which is constituted under section 5. 351: The petitioners challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that they infringed articles 14, 19 (1) (f), 31(2) and 31(2). Held, that article 14 is not applicable to the impugned Act. Article 14 does not forbid classification based on any principle which has no application to a law fixing reasonable rent. It does not forbid discrimination in matters which are dealt with by the Act. If there is a violation of the fundamental right conferred by the Act, it can be enforced only if there is a contravention of the fundamental rights under articles 14 and 31(1)(f) or 31(2); but the Act cannot operate as an act of colourable legislation. Article 14 is not intended to confer arbitrary power upon the legislature when it considers itself unreasonable and discriminates between persons who have no right to recover reasonable rent from the person whose property is taken up for payment; and the Act must be held to be violative of article 14. The impugned Act was passed in so far as it gave operation to the rates of rent from 1st July, 1949. The Act did not contravene article 14. Held, further, that the impugned Act was not discriminatory and violative of article 19(5) of the Constitution. The Act was not ultra vires article 14 and the Act was not invalid.

7035: The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge, under section 302 read with section 149 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 It is well settled that in a criminal case, it is not sufficient to convict an accused person or accused persons, but it is necessary that there should be some evidence to show that he was dead. [850D] 2.1 There must be evidence to show, inter alia, that the deceased was seen by him and that he had taken part in the commission of the crime. The possibility that the deceased might have been injured by any one else may reasonably be expected from him for his life. [851E] 3.2 The testimony of PW3, who has seen the occurrence, is corroborated by the medical evidence, is admissible against the accused. [855B C] 3.3 The mere fact that the deceased had received the same in the hands of the accused does not stand scrutiny because admittedly according to PW3, the deceased was still alive and as a matter of fact he was alive, he could not have been convicted of the offence of murder. 6937: The appellant, a Judge of the High Court, was put up for hearing on the question whether the notice served upon him in his contempt petition was arbitrary and illegal. [873E] 2.1 The High Court has no jurisdiction to punish the petitioner for contempt of court or otherwise, and the order passed by the High Courts cannot be sustained. [875B C] 3.2 The High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of dismissal passed by the Single Judge. 1090: The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of electric light and electricity. In regard to leave, it applied for a period of eight months ' leave with full salary and dearness allowance on completion of eleven months service in a year. The dispute related to a single demand made by the workmen was referred to the Industrial Tribunal under section 2(c) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1947. The Tribunal held that the demand arose out of a claim made by the appellant and directed that the Tribunal should not allow the staff members of the appellant to take leave in proportion to the number of days he was in service and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to make such an award having regard to the provisions of section 79 of the . The appellant contended that the Tribunal has no jurisdiction to pass an order directing that the Tribunal shall not be bound to follow its own procedure. Held, that the Tribunal was right in holding that the demand was not bona fide but was justified. It is well settled that in construing the provisions of a welfare legislation courts should adopt what is necessary or just, as they are intended to do. If the language used in the statute clearly indicates that the intention was to introduce standardisation in the matter of leave, the Tribunals should adopt what was necessary or just. If the intention was that the Tribunal would have to give effect to the policy and object of the Act, the Tribunal would be entitled to refuse to grant any relief.

In the present case the High Court had no jurisdiction to decide whether the offence was committed or not. The High Court was therefore wrong in quashing the proceeding. The High Courts were not justified in doing so because the High Court itself had not given any finding regarding the alleged offence. The High court was right in holding that the offence was not committed. [902 H]

In appeal the High Court held that the respondent was not entitled to the decree for eviction. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The law relating to the bar of sub cls. (i) of cl. 13A is clearly applicable even on the facts of the case. [902B] 2.2 The contention that the respondent has not been able to establish that the suit premises had not been leased out for residential purpose cannot be accepted. It is well settled that the bar of cl.13A does not apply to a proceeding pending before any Court including this Court and in view of the bar imposed by section 3 of the Punjab Pre emption Act, 1913 the bar imposed is a continuation of the suit/proceeding. The bar imposed by Section 3 of the Act is a continuation and not an order of eviction. [903E F] 3.3 The bar under clause 13A is only on the person who has been granted a lease or lease hold rights. The bar under cl. 13 A is not only on the persons claiming title to the property in dispute but also on the person claiming title to it. [904D E] 4.4 The bar under section 3 of Act is not only against the landlord but also against the tenant. Therefore, the bar under cl.(13A is not attracted even on the person seeking to be evicted from the land in dispute. [905F G]
6740: The prosecution case in short is that on 19th March, 1983 at about 7. p.m. while the victim girl was returning home on a tractor accom modation of her father, the accused appellants and their parents were present there. Ws. 2 and 3, PW. 4 and P.Ws 1 to 3, Pw. 2 and P.W . 2, Pws. 2, and Pw. 5, Pw 2 and Pw 2 respectively, have deposed that the victim girl had been sleeping on a path of the house of the appellant and that she did not return to the police station where they went to the spot. [311B] 2.1 The law requires that the court should look into the testimony of the girl or the woman who complains that she is a woman who complaining that she is her daughter or the woman herself is her daughter who complains the same. 1611: The respondent was convicted under section 324 read with section 511 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to six months ' rigorous imprisonment. He applied for bail but the High Court ordered that he be taken into custody. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the order of release made by the District Magistrate on March 11, 1958 was an order for his unconditional release and therefore he could not be set aside because (1) the State had come to this Court by special leave; (2) the order of the District Magistrate dated May 5, 1958 was a result of a long course of judicial proceedings and it was not open to the appellant to challenge the order of his release on grounds which were raised in the writ petition. The High Court was in error in holding that the order was an order of the release made by a District Magistrate. In the present case the application before the District Magistrate was taken up by the Senior Deputy Collector Patna who ordered Bipat Gope to be taken into possession of the appellant 's house. The High court was in error as there was no order of the grant of the District Magis trate.
6366: The respondent filed a criminal petition for quashing the first information report in exercise of its inherent powers under Section 482 Cr. P.C. on the ground that there had been delay in investigation of a criminal case, and that there was no justification to interfere with the same. P C.C. till he filed the petition for quashing of further proceedings pursuant to the registration of the First Information Re port. The High Courts have erred in quashing the First Information Reports in exercise of their inherent powers under Sections 482 Cr.p.C. 5847: The appellant was inducted in the flat on 6th floor of a building by the disputant No.2, respondent No. 2, the Nibhana Co operative Housing Society Ltd., and the Society filed a dispute before the Judge Fifth Cooperative Court at Bombay for recovery of possession of the flat. The dispute was referred to the Judge Fifth Co operative Court at Bombay. The appellants were inducted in th flat without the written consent of the Society as a licencee. The appellant 's claim was that he had been allotted the flat without the original licence and had no right to occupy the flat. In the suit filed by the respondent No.2 the Society, the appellant contended that the appellant was occupying the flat without written consent of respondent No. 1, and therefore, the issue of a leave and licence agreement by payment of licence fee uptill furthermore. The appellant having failed to comply with the request a dispute was filed by the Society under the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1950. The Society pleaded that the appellant had become a licensee after the licence in favour of the Society and had become a tenant under section 15 of the Bombay Rent Act. The Tribunal held that the appellant is a licensee and that the Society was not entitled to retain the flat for a period of four months from the date of the order subject to the appellant s filling an usual undertaking within a period of two weeks from today to the effect that the appellant will hand over vacant vacant vacant land in the premises of the appellant.
