468: The petitioner was prosecuted for offences under section 161 Indian Penal Code and section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He was convicted by the Judicial Commissioner on March 7, 1956, but acquitted on April 4, 1956. On April 4, 1957, the Chief Secretary to the Government of Bhopal accorded sanction for prosecution of the petitioner for the offence under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5 Of the Prevention of Public Proce dure Act, 1947, and section 5(2) of the Prevention. Act provided that no sanction shall be given if the prosecution of the accused was not launched in any Court of competent jurisdiction. The petitioner filed a petition under article 32 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the order of April 4, 1955, passed by the Chief Secretary of the State of Bhopal, contending that he cannot be prosecuted and tried again for the same offences under the aforesaid order of April 1, 1956. Held, that the contention must fail. There is nothing in the provisions of the Code which makes it obligatory on the part of the Special Judge to try the accused or other offi cials mentioned therein. The provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code do not confer upon the High Court power to take cognizance of an offence without a legal sanction. It does not mean that the powers of the High Court are restricted only to cases where the offence has been committed by a special judge.
2791: The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 149 of the Indian Penal Code. They contended that they had taken a raiding party to be dacoits and as such they knew that it was a police party, they knew that the police party had come to their house and that they had arrived at the house of Gopi and Munshi and that they were keeping them in village Gunpara for committing theft. Held, that the appellants were not guilty. The prosecution case was that the appellants took the dragged into the house of the deceased and the police party was armed with arms and arms by causing simple injuries to them. The evidence showed that the appellants had taken the dragging of the dead body and the police officer had recorded the dying declaration of the deceased. The appellants could not have been convicted under section 307 read with section 34 of the Indian Evidence Act. The High Court was right in holding that the appellants did not take part in the commission of the crime. In view of this finding the appellants must be held to have committed an offence under section 302 of the Indian Indian Penal Code and he should be acquitted.
1559: The appellants were dealers in sugar and were selling sugar. They sold the sugar to the respondent company, who was a dealer under the Bihar Sales Tax Act, 1948. The sales were made by them on behalf of the State Government under the provisions of the Bihar Sales tax Act, 1948, which provided that the expression "sale ' means, with all its grammatical variations and cognate expressions, and transfer of property in goods for cash or deferred payment or other valuable consideration including a transfer of property. The Sales Tax Officer assessed the respondent company to sales tax for the assessment years 1957 58, 1958 59 and 1959 60, but the order was confirmed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the sales were not sales within the meaning of the Bihar sales tax Act, 1939, and that the sales could be said to be sales outside the purview of the Bihar Entry 48 List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. In further appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to decide whether the sales were sales covered by the definition of sale in the two Bihar Acts, at all material times, and that as the sales were in fact made in pursuance of the power conferred by the Central Legislature under the Bihar Entry 52 List II of 7th Schedule to the Constitu tion, the High Court was wrong in holding that the sales fell within the definition of the term "sale" contained in section 2(g) of the Bihar Act, 1950, and that, therefore, the sales were liable to levy tax. HELD: (i) The definition of sale connotes the word 'sale ' in the two Acts, namely, the Bihar Sales lax Act, 1948 and the Bihar Sales (Taxation on Goods Act, 1930. [312 D] (ii) The definition is wide enough to include transactions in the sense of transactions relating to the purchase or sale of goods for cash, deferred payment or otherwise payment or other document, and the definition does not give any indication of the nature of such transactions. It is only when these transactions are made out wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the Act, that is, the transaction must be regarded as a transaction which may be regarded as an inter inter inter inter sale. [313 C E] (iii
3193: The appellant and the respondents were contesting candidates for the Safidon Assembly Constituency No. 30, the Haryana Legislative Assembly held on March 11, 1972. In the election to the Haryana Legislative Council, the appellant and the four respondents were declared elected. The appellant filed an election petition in the High Court challenging the election of the first respondent on several grounds of corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(1) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the election petition was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the time the case was placed before the Deputy Registrar on April 18, 1972; (ii) the copies of the petition had been filed by the petitioner and the other defects had also been removed; (iii) the election petition having been filed after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed under section 100 of the Representation Of the People Act; and (iv) the election petitions were not maintainable as they did not contain any provision for filing the election petition. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The time the case is placed before the High Court. [278B] 2. Section 80 of the Representation. of the People Rules provides that the period of presentation of election petition shall be fixed from the date of presentation. The period of presentation has been fixed at the commencement of the institution of the election petition and the date of such presentation. The time should have been mentioned in the order of the High Court or the date of the presentation. The date of the filing of the election may be specified in the order. But the time should not be given in the order but only when the date of filing the election is mentioned in the original order. [270E F] 3. The time must be mentioned in the rule of the High Courts. The time cannot be said to be the date of submission of the election petitions. [271C D]
3421: The workmen of the appellant company in the appeal were employed by the respondent company in the factory of the appellant. Their services were terminated on the ground that they had been paid a salary for lay off and compensation. The Labour Court held that the workmen were not entitled to any lay off compensation. In an appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the workmen that (i) the workmen were entitled to the benefit of the lay off; (ii) the employer was not entitled to lay off the workmen; (iii) the employer could not be said to have refused to pay the wages; and (iv) the employer had failed to pay the same. Dismissing the Appeal, HELD: 1. The workmen are entitled to the benefits of the lay Off ed. [532C] 2. The workmen were not given their wages or compensation. They were not entitled either to lay off or retrenchment compensation. The workmen did not get any relief from the Industrial Tribunal. [533E] 3. The workmen have no locus standi to file the petition under section 10(l) of the Act. It is open to the Tribunal or the Court to award a lesser sum of Rs. 4 lakhs as damages. [535D]
2297: The appellant was a Judge of the High Court. He held that Dutta J. had no jurisdiction to act as a Judge of a High Court while he was working as a; Commis sioner of Enquiry. He submitted his report and it was accepted by the Chief Justice. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of stay granted by the Chief justice. In the appeal to this Court on behalf of the appellant it was contended that the High Court was not right in holding that Dutta j. could not act as a judge of the High court while he was functioning as a Judge. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was wrong in holding that the High Courts were not competent to act as such. [816B] (2) The High Courts are appointed under the . Commission of Enquiry Act to head Commissions for various purposes. It is remarkable that Dutta Judges ' Tribunal are appointed under a general law. Therefore, the High Courts are not authorised to act as an Additional Judge of the Court of Inquiry. [817C E] (3) The High courts are appointed under . . . . , . . . 's. Court. The High Court has power to act as the Chief Justice or other person to act as judges of the High Courts. The High Courts have been appointed under the , and they have been so doing. They have been so appointed. The High courts have been vested with powers of appointing Judges of the High High Courts. [818D] (4) The High court has power to appoint a Judge of that High Court to be appointed to the High Court of Judicial Tribunals. The High court will not exercise any jurisdiction in the matter of appointment of a Judge of High Court. [820E F] (5) The High. Court has powered itself to act as judicial tribunal. The High. Courts are appointed by the High Court and they have to function as judges of High Courts. There is nothing on this aspect of the matter which would justify the view of the High. Court. [891H 815A]
3390: The appellants, who were working as the public sectors of Delhi, were alleged to have taken a large number of telephone and non exchange lines. They had been using the same power of transmission and distribution of electricity by way of electric supply. The Chief Engineer did not apply his mind and record his own satisfaction about the existence of any emergency and as such there was a contravention of Rules 421 and 422 of the Indian Telegraphs Rules, 1951. The appellants challenged the validity of the action on the ground that no prior notice in regard to the same was given to them; and the telephones were being used for illegal forward trading and that such use was contrary to public interest in view of the existence of "economic" emergency". The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the action was bad because it was based on a 'public emergency ' declared under section 5(1) of the Indian Electricity Act, 1948. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The impugned action is arbitrary and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. [323 E] (ii) It is clear from the language of Rule 422 which has to be read together. It does not say that the impugned action must be struck down or that the action should be taken into account with the object of preventing the appellants from acting in violation of the rule. [324 C D] (iii) The appellants are entitled to proportionate refund of rent. The appellants are not entitled to the amount of damages claimed by them. [326 A B] (iv) The appellants were not entitled to any relief in respect of the period of six months before the date of the commencement of the period. The period of six month could not be treated as having elapsed since the period expired. [325 H] (v) The appellants have been rightly held to be entitled to the entire arrears of rent. [332 G]
6645: The Government of Jammu & Kashmir granted land measuring acres and 6 acres kanals and 6 mas per share in the Ziarat. In lieu of that two grants in the years 1955 and 1958 were given to Mian Lal Din but the Government did not grant any lease, and the land was sold by the Government. The defendants in their written statement resisted the suit on the grounds that the land in dispute was transferred by the Government in favour of the Ziarbari and not in favour of Narsimha Bhiya. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal the High Court set aside the judgment of the trial court holding that the two grants by the State Government were in fact made in favour of Mian Lal Parsad, that the Government had no authority to de facto grant the grant in favour of any person or his ancestor without any consideration; that the Government acted in excess of the powers conferred upon it by section 4(1)(a) of the Jammu and Kashmir (Amendment) Act, 1964 which came into force from April 1, 1964. Held, that the High Court erred in upsetting the findings of the courts below based on appreciation of evidence. The High Court has failed to do so in view of the fact that the Government took over the land in question as a whole and not in fact made the grant in the year 1955 and 1958.
2618: The first respondent joined the Baroda State Service in 1937. He was absorbed as a Sales Tax Officer, Class III in the former State of Bombay after merger. In December 1962 he was served with a charge sheet containing allegations of attempt to obtain illegal gratification from certain cloth dealers. A departmental enquiry was held and on March 15, 1964 the Enquiry Officer made certain recommendations regarding the punishment which in his opinion should be inflicted on the first respondent. On March 15, 1965 the Assistant Commissioner dismissed the respondent from service. The first respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of removal. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the failure to send a copy of the report of the Enquiry Officer containing his findings on the charges which he made in the matter of punishment constituted an offence amounted to a failure to provide reasonable opportunity of making a representation against the penalty proposed within the meaning of article 311(2) of the Constitution. The High court took the view that since the recommendations were a part of the appropriate material for the consideration of the Government in the matter, the second respondent would not be entitled to a copy of those recommendations at the time when he was called upon to show cause. Held, that the failure of the Government to make any recommendation about the punishment is not fatal to the case. The failure to give a final opportunity to the Government to consider the report of a disciplinary inquiry does not amount to denial of natural justice. The failure of the Public Service Commission to make a report under section 5(1)(c) of the Act cannot be regarded as a non compliance with the requirement of the rule.
2435: The petitioners were detained under section 3(3) of the . They filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the detention order. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that there was no valid approval by the detaining authority to the detenu. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the delay in sending the report could not have been avoided by the Commissioner and that when they were sent by him, they were sent to "detention" and that the delay was attributable to the reasons mentioned in the rule. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The delay in sending an adverse report cannot be avoided by the detaining authorities. [857D] 2. The delay is due to causes not of the making but to cause to which the activities of the Petitioners very largely contributed. It is not sufficient for the detaining authority either to make the report or even after the approval of the State Government. The delay does not mean that the authority must give its opinion. The delay may be condoned only if the decision is recorded as required by the rule. [858E F] 3. There is no provision in the Act that such an approval must be communicated to the detenu; and the authority must have been informed about the grounds of detention. [859G H]
1748: The petitioners, who were members of a joint Hindu family governed by the Dayabhaga School of Hindu Law, had been allotted certain land in the State of Bihar. In course of time, the maintenance allowance of the members of the Ruling Family was fixed arbitrarily by the Rulers of the State of West Bengal and the same was made applicable to them. The petitioners claimed that they and respondent No. 2, his widow, claiming that their right to get the said allowance was not extinguished and that the said section was ultra vires. The petitioners contended that the said Section is ultra vires the Constitution inasmuch as it contravenes article 14 of the Constitution. The petitioners further contended that the impugned section is ultra vires, because it contravenes article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution and as such, the condition precedent prescribed by it which requires the previous sanction of the Central Government before filing a suit against the Ruler of an Indian State under the provisions of the Constitution, and that the condition precedent for the application of section 86(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure does not apply to the present case. Held, that the petitioners are entitled to the protection of article 14 of tile Constitution. The impugned section is valid and the condition precedent has no application to the present petition. The petitioners are entitled only to the protection under article 32 of the Constitution of India. The petitioners have not established any infringement of article 14. The petitioners cannot claim that the impugned provision should be struck down as violative of article 14 on the ground that the impugned provisions of article 19(i)(f) are void.
3489: The respondent, a displaced person from Pakistan, applied to the Rent Controller for fixation of standard rent. The Rent Controller allowed the application and directed the respondent to pay the amount in arrears. The respondent filed an appeal before the Appellate Authority under section 7(1) of the Act. The appellant took no steps to recover the dues till December 1960 when it demanded the entire amount in arrears from May 1950 to April 1957. The respondent not having paid the appellant asked the Estate Officer to take steps to recover that amount. The respondent then filed a writ petition challenging the order against him on the ground that the time limit was not prescribed by law. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the period of limitation prescribed for a suit to recover the amount did not apply to a proceeding under the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended that since section 7 did not put a time limit for taking steps under that section and as the limitation prescribed for the suit to recover damages had expired, the Act was not applicable to a proceeding thereunder. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (i) Section 7 of the Act does not bar the remedy of a suit to recovery of arrears of rent. [869 C] (ii) The right to recover the arrears is a special procedure for the realisation of rent in arrears. It is not questioned that a creditor whose suit is barred by limitation, if he has any other legal remedy permitted him to enforce his claim, would be free to avail of it. [870 E F] (iii) The right conferred on the landlord is a right to recover arrears of rent which may have been determined by the Rent Controller. The right to receive arrears cannot be taken away unless the tenant has some other legal remedy permitting him to enforce their claim. [871 D] (iv) The right of the landlord to recover arrears cannot be enforced under the Act because the limitation prescribed is that the right to recover damages must be based upon the right of the tenant to recover the same. [872 H; 873 A] (v) The right under the Act is a special right to sue and can be availed of only by a person who is in arrears of rent or is entitled to recover the said amount. The right of a person to recover the rent is
4072: The appellants and the other successful tenderers for Rs. 14,4300/ were offered their respective offers to be accepted as their own price of jewellery and other articles specified in the First Schedule to the deed of sale. The first respondent was the managing trustee of a Hindu undivided family. The third respondent was the manager of the said trust. The first appellant made an offer on March 9, 1978 to the trustees of the trust. The second respondent made a request that the first appellant should not accept the offer. The third appellant made a further demand that the first respondent would be at the option of the trustees either to keep the said jewels or other articles mentioned in the first schedule to the deed. The third re spondent made a similar demand by the first appellant. The third proviso to section 3(c) (d) of the Act provides that where there is a concluded contract between the parties, the property of the trust shall vest in the first appellant and all such properties which are liable to be sold or dispose of by the trustees of any of the said articles. The first proviso also provided that if the whole or part of the property is held by the trustees to have been transferred to the first appellant, the second proviso would apply to the first respondent. The first appellate court dismissed the appeal holding that the second proviso did not apply to the second proviso. In the second appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the first proviso was applicable only when there was a concluded contract entered into between the parties and the second proviso was attracted; that the first Appellate Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the second proviso and that the second appellant could not take advantage of the second proviso; and that the third proviso was not applicable to the second part. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1.1 The first proviso does not apply to a case where there is an agreement between the parties. [350D] 2.1 The second proviso does not bar the applicability of the second part of the second provi sion. It is only when there is a final contract between the two parties that the first one may make a declaration that the second part will be in favour of the first respondent and the second part can be treated as a separate transaction. [360B
5027: The appellant was granted a quarry lease to M/s Pioneer Crushing Co. Ltd., a private limited company. The State of Haryana and the second respondent, the Director of Industries, on May 25, 1981 issued a writ of mandamus directing the appellant to appear before the second respondent within a week from the date of the grant of the lease. The writ petition filed by the appellant challenging the action of the Chief Minister in granting the quarry lease to the M/s. Pioneer Caves (India) Limited, was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the writ petition was not maintainable as the matter fell under article 136 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that the writ petitioner was entitled to the relief claimed. [547D] 2. The question whether a writ can be issued or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. The fact that the matter is pending before the High Court may not be called in aid unless there are good grounds for holding that the writ jurisdiction of the High Court is being invoked. A notification was issued on December 26, 1981 stating that minor mineral quarries at various places in Faridabad District would be auctioned on February 20, 1981. The appellant 's contention is that the writ petitions were not maintainable. [548C D] 3. The question of law involved in the present appeals is whether the writ petition should have been allowed or not. The question is whether the High Court will interfere with the issue of writ jurisdiction. [549E F]
1145: The appellant company was a textile mill. In respect of disputes relating to bonus for the years 1952 and 1953, the Government of Bombay issued a notification under section 114(2) of the Act directing that the award made by the Industrial Court on March 13, 1956, be enforced against the appellant. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification in the High Court. The High Court held that the order passed by the Industrial court was not enforceable as an award by the Industrial. Court. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Government of Bombay had no power to issue any such notification under section 56A of the Act. [11 C] (2) The Government could not have delegated its powers under section 114A of the , or under section 96(2) to the Industrial Court. The Government could exercise it under section 114C of the Act only after giving notice to the parties affected an opportunity of being heard. The Government did not comply with the provisions of section 114A but directed the appellant to pay the bonus payable to the respondent. [11 B C] (3) The Government has power to issue a notification under s. 114A of which the Government is empowered to make a reference to the Industrial Tribunal. The Government can also exercise its power under section 114D of the Act if it considers that it is necessary to do so in the interest of justice. [11 D E] (4) The Government cannot exercise its power to delegate its power to pass the award without issuing a notification under Section 100 of the Act and without giving the parties affected the dispute. [11 F] (5) The Government can exercise its power either under section 114E or under section 115 of the Act or under section 76A of the . [11 H] (6) The Government may, in appropriate cases, direct the award to be made by the Tribunal. The Tribunal may consider whether the award should be made by an authority competent to pass it. If the Tribunal does not consider that the award must be made by it. If it appears from the record that the decision of the Tribunal is erroneous, the Government may refuse to interfere with it. [11 H; 11 A] (7) The Government is entitled to exercise its power conferred by section 114A.
5346: The respondent landlord filed a petition under Section 10(3)(c) of the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Rent Control Act, 1957 praying for eviction of the appellant on the ground that the premises in question was not "a residential building" within the meaning of Section 2(2) of the Act. The Rent Controller upheld the contention and held that the respondent were not entitled to recover possession of non residential premises for their residential requirements and dismissed the petition for eviction. On appeal by the appellant, the Appellate Authority reversed the findings of fact rendered by the Rent Controller and held that since the ground floor constitutes a building by itself within the meaning Of section 2(2), the respondents could seek eviction only if they required additional accommodation for residential purposes or for residential purposes, and not for residential purposes. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1) That the High Court erred in interfering with the finding of fact rendered in the first appellate court without considering the evidence adduced by the parties; (2) That the Rent Controller erred in reversing the findings of the appellate authority; (3) That the order of the High Court is vitiated by an error apparent on the face of record. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has rightly interfered with the findings of facts rendered by the Appellate Authority while exercising its revisional powers under Section 25 of the Act, and as such the High Court was right in interfering with those findings. [532C] 2.1 The second appellate court has also rightly found that the respondent had taken advantage of the relevant provisions of the Act and the circumstances of the case. The High Court was in error in interfering with that finding. [533F G] 3.2 The High Court should have exercised its revisional jurisdiction under Section 25(4) of the . [534D] 435 2.2 The power conferred upon the appellate authority is discretionary and cannot be exercised sparingly or cautiously limited to circumspection of the statute and the circumstances so require. It must be exercised spelled out from the language employed in the statute and not under the general law. The power conferred on the appellate authority can be exercised spelt out from the words used therein. The power is not to be exercised
1091: The respondent company was carrying on business in shares and securities. In the return for the assessment year 1954 55, the Income tax Officer issued a notice under section 35 of the Income tax Act, 1922 read with Part B of the First Schedule to the Finance Act, 1952, read with Part C thereof as follows: "I/2 (3) income from investments in shares and stocks and stocks at rates specified in the first schedule of the Finance Act but not at rates mentioned therein or at rates which are not mentioned in the second schedule of the Act. " The respondent filed a petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notices under section 35(1)(b) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 read with Part II of the First schedule and the order of the Income 'tax Officer. The High Court held that the orders made were without jurisdiction and therefore the Income tax officer had no jurisdiction to make the order. On appeal by special leave it was contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the orders passed were without jurisdiction because they were based on a mistake apparent on the face of the record and could not be set aside merely because they were passed in a different manner and could not have been validly made. HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that there was no legal error which did not require any extraneous matter to show its incorrectness. [955 A] (ii) The High Courts have always taken into consideration the correctness of the facts and circumstances of each case and the mere fact that the High Courts have applied the correct principles of law. The High Courts should not have applied the principle of law. It is only where the High Courts can apply the correct principles. If the High Courts are satisfied that the High courts have applied the principles of law, then the question whether the High Courts do so would arise. [956 D E] (iii) The High court has to consider the correctness of all the relevant facts and circumstances before it can exercise jurisdiction under section 35. The High court must look into the relevant facts before it can come to the conclusion that the High court has acted arbitrarily or capriciously or whimsically or indirectly upon an inference which is not based on any material or substantial basis. [957 H; 9

7118: The appellant, a Medical Council of India, was appointed as Principal of the College at Jabalpur. He had been pursuing his studies in the college and had completed one year at the same college. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant is entitled to be treated as senior to Respondent No. 1. 1946: The plaintiff, who was the eider sister of the first defendant, instituted a suit in the court of the District Judge, Bangalore for a declaration that she had purchased half share in the properties described in the schedule to the plaint and for partition and separate possession of half share and for mesne profits. The trial court decreed the suit but held that the first defendant did not have any right to the suit properties and consequently he was entitled to the benefit of section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act. In appeal by the defendants, the High Court reversed this decision. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was wrong in awarding a decree against the other defendants in respect of her half share in each of the properties left by her mother, as the case fell within the purview of section 51. HELD: (1) The High Court was right in awarding a 'counter of facts '. [950B] (2) The High Courts were right in granting a decree against a defendant who has not asked for possession of the half share in a suit property. The High Court should have granted a decree against all the parties in respect of the half half share in such a suit property which is the subject matter of the suit. The High Courts are not right in granting the decree against the defendant in respect of his half share in an immovable property. [951D E] (3) The High court was right in directing the grant of a decree against defendant in respect Of her half share. [955E]
1277: The appellants, who were members of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Madras High Court, challenged the validity of the circular dated June 3, 1961 issued by the Chief Commercial Officer, Southern Railway, in the Madras Rly. Podu vs Union of India, A.I.R. , and K. C. Budhan Choudhury vs Union of Indian Railway, A. I. R. , on the question whether the provisions of article 16(4) of the Constitution apply to the appellants, the general principles of equality before the law, namely, the scope of article 16 (4), as well as the rule of natural justice, must be read together and construed in a sense that it is not possible to lay down any general or statutory rules for the grant of a right to an office which is not a temporary or temporary post but such a right cannot be enforced against a person who has been appointed to a particular post under the terms of his appointment. Held, that the impugned circular was not discriminatory and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. The impugned circular did not operate with out its application to the case of the appellants. The classification made by the impugned circular as reasonable and just, therefore, violated article 16(1)(c).
2660: The appellant firm was assessed to tax in respect of an amount of Rs. 3,99,587 received by it as profit on sale of shares. The firm paid the sum of Rs. 7,00,000 on November 4,1944 and the balance on December 6, 1944. The firm also paid a sum of Rs 1,500 on November 4.1944 and that the balance on Decem ber 4, 1944 was sold for Rs. 7.00,000. The firm claimed that it had taken over the entire share capital issued by Raymond with a view to secure its managing 'agency and had thereafter distributed the shares of Raymond and that the said transaction was a business activity which was continuous. The firm contended that the sale of shares was not for any purpose but only for the benefit of the capital employed by the firm and that the transaction being one to facilitate acquisition of a capital asset being a business activity, the profits realised by sale of shares could be characterised as a commercial loss. Held, that the mere fact that the sale took place at a profit in consideration of the capital of the assessee did not make it a capital asset within the meaning of section 2(4) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The mere fact that there was a typographical error in the second clause of the first sentence of the first proviso to section 99 of the Act does not affect the question whether the transaction is a commercial loss or a speculation.
1910: The appellant, a private limited company, was granted licence for holding the market. In 1953 54, the local board of Barpeta within whose jurisdiction the Kharma market was held issued by the Assam Government. The appellant challenged the validity of the impugned notification on the grounds that the impugned notification contravened article 14 of the Constitution and that the impugned Act violated articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution. Held, that the impugned legislation was valid and the appellant could not be held to be a tax on land within the meaning of Entry 49 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The impugned Act did not contravene article 14 of any part of the Constitution as it had been passed by the State Legislature under entry 49 of List II of the Seventh Concurrent List. The impugned legislation was therefore ultra vires article 14 and void. It was further contended that the impugned provision offended article 14 of Constitution. Held also, that the appellant was entitled to a writ petition under article 226. The impugned law was not invalid because it was not in existence at the time when the impugned Act was passed. The impugned was not in fact valid but was clearly in existence at a time when the Act was passed and the impugned Act came into force.
1487: The respondent company was carrying on the business of manufacturing sugar and sugarcane. In 1948 49, due to drought, the assessee company could not work its sugar mills and the Oppigedars did not grow or deliver the sugarcane to the respondent company. The respondent company claimed that it should ex gratia forego some of its dues, and in the year of account the said sum had been paid by it. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the expenditure was not in the nature of a capital expenditure but was an expense incurred for the purpose of earning income and deduction under section 10(3) (xi) of the Indian Incometax Act. The Tribunal also found against the respondent company 's claim that the amount of Rs. 2,87,422/ representing a loss of capital was not in fact paid by the assessee company. The High Court, however, allowed the respondent 's claim. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The expenditure was not a revenue expenditure. It was an ordinary business transaction of an advance against goods to be delivered. The assessee company had no right to sell the sugarcane to him. [981E] The High Court was wrong in holding that the expenditure is not in the character of a capital asset. [982B C]
5432: The respondent filed an application before the Rent Controller for execution of a decree. 6204: The respondents were recruited to Indian Forest Service in the year 1967 and joined service on January 7, 1973. On July 11, 1974, the Government of India issued a Notification under section 3(2)(d) of the Indian Police Service (Recruitment) Rules, 1954 providing for the appointment of officers in Class I and CI (Regulation of Seniority) Rules, 1968. In the meantime, the respondent filed an application before the Calcutta High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution praying that the said rule be declared ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the rule was not applicable to the case. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The rule is valid. [869C] 2. The rule is made operative only when the Central Government has notified the Rules or the Rules. But the rules have been framed under the Act. The Rules are not amended or repealed. [870E] 3. The rule does not make any provision for the amendment or repealing the rule. It is only prospective in operation. [871G H] 3.1 The Rule is not retrospective effect from the date of the coming into force of the Rules. The rule cannot be construed as retrospective effect from a date already known as the Central Government had notified the Rules. [872D E]
2971: The appellant company was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling textile goods. In its assessment to income tax for the relevant accounting years it claimed that the loss incurred by it in earlier years had been computed as a loss of Rs. 11,63,874/ and this was due to the loss of Rs 12,00,000/ on account of depreciation in the value of 83 shares held by the company in Elphinsto Ltd., of Bombay. The Income tax Officer disallowed an amount of Rs.11,62,874 on the ground that it related to the price paid for the shares purchased for the sake of acquiring the managing agency of the company. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the order of the Income tax Officer but the Tribunal agreed with the conclusions reached by the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner. The High Court in reference under section 66(1) of the Act held that the income derived from the sale of assets which were not assessable to income tax. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the income was liable to be taxed as the profit and gains arising out of the profits made in the previous year, and that the income must be deemed to have accrued in the previous years and therefore the dividend should be taxed. HELD: (i) The income received by the assessee in the previous assessment year cannot be taxed as income tax. [757 E] (ii) The income is taxable subject to the provisions contained in the Finance Act, 1961. Section 23A(1) provides that where the Income tax officer has satisfied that in respect of any previous year the profits and gains distributed as dividends by any company within the twelve months immediately preceding the expiry of that previous year are less than the statutory percentage of the total income of the company of that year. The Income Tax Officer could not have levied the tax on the assessee 's share in the capital gain or distribution as dividends by the company. The Income. tax Officer did not accept the contention that the income had escaped assessment because the assessee had not filed any return of income tax at all. The Income, tax Officer had no jurisdiction to assess the income tax on the basis of the assessment under section 23A(2). [759 G H; 796 A

4851: The appellant, a private limited company, was appointed as an employee of the respondent Corporation. He had been paid salary and allowances for the period from 1st April, 1957 to 31st March, 1958. In the course of his employment he received remuneration on account of the payment made by him in terms of the contract of employment with the appellant. The appellant claimed that he was entitled to the benefit of the payment of Rs. 4,000/ . The claim was rejected by the Labour Court. On appeal, the High Court held that the additional amount of commission payable to the appellant under the definition of 'wages ' meant remuneration paid or payable under the terms of the contracts of employment, express or implied, but further extended to other additional remuneration, if any, paid at intervals not exceeding two months, though outside the terms of employment. In this appeal by special leave it was contended that the additional remuneration was not paid in terms of clause (a) of section 2(1)(b) of the , because the appellant was not paid any remuneration in terms of cl. (a) Of section 2(2). Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (i) The additional remuneration sought to be included by the expression "real remuneration" occurring in clause (a), must be paid in terms thereof. [717 C] (ii) The definition of 'real remuneration ' in section 2(l)(b) is wide enough to include remuneration which though no part of the wages could be paid as part of the terms of contract of employment. [718 E] (iii) The definition includes remuneration paid to an employee in respect of any period of authorised leave, whether by way of leave or otherwise, or by way of grant or otherwise, to any person who has been employed in connection with the business of the employer, and which the employer is not a party to the contract of employments. [719 G H; 720 A] (iv) The additional amount of remuneration which was paid to the appellant in terms of a contract of employment, would be taxable under the provisions of the Act. [721 D]

1696: The Bhopal Act, which was enacted by the Bhopal State, provided for the exercise of the power to make provision for the Reclamation Officer and his subordinates and workmen. Section 7(1) of the Bhopal Act empowered the State Government to notify areas of the State as "Kans" to be used for the recanches in the areas specified therein. Section 8(2) provided that the Deputy Commissioner may, notwithstanding anything contained in any law or custom, order such officer to do so, if it appears from any record or evidence that the local authority has been authorised by him in this behalf, shall have the right to take possession of the whole or any part of the kans area and carry on eradicated or ancillary and subsidiary operations thereon. The Bhopal Act provided for the regulation of the establishment of a Sugar factory for the supply of cane to the sugar factories. The Bhopal Land Revenue Act, 1932, was passed with the object of providing for the transfer of the sugar mills to the State. In the meantime, the Bhopal Act made provisions for the collection of land revenue and other taxes payable under the Bhopal Land Revenue (Amendment) Act, 1950, which came into force on January 1, 1952, provided for recovery of the said land revenue. The Bhopal Rourksar Act, 1951, was repealed and replaced by the Madhya Pradesh Act, 1954, which came to the new Act. The Bhopal Acts were repealed and replaced with the Land Revenue (Levy) Act, 1954. The Bhopal Apt was passed on November 28, 1955, but the Bhopal Act was repealed. The Bhopal Agreements Act, 1954 was repealed and the Bhopal Act provided that the Bhopal Act would come into operation only after the enactment of the Bhopal Land Rela tion Act, 1954; and that the Bhopal Land Reforms Act, 1950 would come into force on December 31, 1955. The Bhopal and the Bhopal Land Acquisi tion Act came into force from April 1, 1956. The Bhopal came into being on June 30, 1957. The Bhopal was not competent to enact the Bhopal Act. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the Bhopal Apts Act. The High Court dismissed the same holding that the Bhopal Apea Act was validated
2165: The respondents filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of possession of the land in dispute. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the decision of the revenue court on the question of title to the suit land bars the jurisdiction of civil court; that the decision would be a bar to the maintainability of the suit in a civil court; and that the decision was not binding on the revenue court, and that the respondent could not have reagitate the same subject matter in a civil suit. HELD: (1) The question whether a civil court has jurisdiction to entertain a suit under section 71 of the Code is a question of fact which can be determined by the proper forum. [630E] (2) The question as to the jurisdiction of the civil court is a question which may arise in a civil proceeding. A civil court cannot go into the question of the correctness of the finding given by the lower courts. [631F G] (3) The question about the jurisdiction of a civil court is one of law and no other is a question relating to the jurisdiction or otherwise of the Civil Court. It is always open to the civil court to decide such questions as are decided by the revenue authorities. If the question is raised by the revenue authority, the question must necessarily be decided by the civil court. [633B C] (4) The question regarding the jurisdiction of Civil Court is a question arising out of the proceedings before the Revenue Officer under section 93(1), and the decision of such questions depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [634C D] (5) The question of jurisdiction does not arise in a criminal case where the claim is made by the parties to the proceedings before him. The question as regards the jurisdiction of an arbitrator to decide the question is a question not incidental to the main question to the jurisdiction. [635D E]
435: The appellants, who were members of a Trade Association, challenged the propriety of the award made by the Industrial Tribunal on the ground that the recommendations of the Bengal Chamber of Commerce ought to have been accepted as a valid one and not in any way affected their rights. Held, that the award was invalid as it did not deal with the question whether the recommendation of the Bengal 87 High Court or the Labour Appellate Tribunal. The decision of the Calcutta High Court was based on an expert opinion which had no application to the facts found. The report of the Bengal Metropolitan Tribunal was not binding on the parties. In the absence of any evidence to show that the recommendations were made to the Bengal Chamber for making those recommendations, the matter must be judged on its own merits. The report was not a mere recommendatory but a whole body of persons, including the employees of the appellant company. The report could not be regarded as a mere recommenda tion. The report cannot be regarded as an 'income ' as a whole body.
6500: The appellant, a private limited company, was granted a lease of the forest land to a Government. In respect of the said lands he had no subsisting right in the forest lands. He filed a suit for possession of the said land on the ground that the grant made by the erstwhile ruler was in respect of revenue yielding lands only admeasuring 263.4 bighas and not in respect of the forest lands; that the grant was in respect to a portion of the forest area of the appellant 's ancestor. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal the High Court held that the grant of the land was in respect Of a revenue yielding land only admeasures 30 acres and not 12 acres as the forest land was acquired under the Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1953. It further held that the grants were in respect of a revenue yielded lands only adme terly in favour of the Government. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the grant in question was in respect thereof only in respect of forest lands and not in part thereof. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The grant in question is in respect of land which has been acquired under the provisions of the Himachal Pradesh Estate Duty Act, 1953 and the grant in respect of trees or trees standing thereon is an existing right in the land. [817E] (2) The grant of the original grant in favour of Government of Punjab is in respect Of land which are reserved for the use of the Raja. The grant in favour being merely a grant in respect Of the forest land, the grant in favour is not in respect thereof. The grant cannot be said to have been made in respect of any other land. [718D E] (3) The grant made by virtue of the grant in his favour is in respect thereof also. The grant made in favour of any other person does not amount to a grant. The grant is in respect to the forest land. [619G] (4) The grant is not in the nature of a grant but in respect of all forest lands. The grant can be said to be in respect of an existing right. The grant could not be said to take
3897: The appellants were the tenants of a hotel. They had let out to their tenants a hotel for running a hotel. The respondents, who were the tenants in the said premises, filed a suit for eviction against them on the ground that they required the building for running a Hotel by the lessees and for this purpose the lessees were given the right to make suitable alterations in the same, but were prohibited from making any alteration which may affect the durability or damage the building. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiffs did not have proved their personal requirement of the premises and that the appellants were not entitled to eject them. In appeal the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court. In the first appeal before the Supreme Court it was contended that the finding of the High Court was not based on a discussion of evidence and circumstances of the case and the High Court has taken an erroneous view of law on the nature of the need of the appellants as also on the question of comparative advantages or disadvantages of the landlord and the tenant if a decree for eviction followed. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was wrong in holding that the appellants had not proved their personal requirements of the premises. [850D] (2) The High Courts have taken into consideration the fact that the appellants are not able to establish their personal requirement. It is well settled that where a person does not require the premises for his own use, he cannot be held to be a tenant unless he has been in possession of the premises for the purpose of earning his income. [851E F] (3) The High courts have accepted the findings of the courts below that the appellants have failed to prove their personal requirement for the premises. The burden of proof is on the appellants. The onus is always upon the party seeking relief. [855F G] (4) The appellants are not entitled to protection under section 14(1)(h) of the Jammu & Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966. [853C D] (5) The appellants have failed in proving their personal requirement in order to augment the business. The appellants have not established their personal requirement and the burden of proof lies on them. [856H; 857A
3930: The plaintiff 's father was a member of the State of Hyderabad State. He was in possession of certain lands and he had been granted a lease to the defendant No. 34 for a period of ten years. In the suit land was allotted to the plaintiff respondent No. 1, who was the proprietor of the suit property, and the plaintiff appellant was the owner of it. The plaintiff alleged that the defendants were perpetrating fraud when on 25th October 1949, the plaintiff and his brother along with his step brother and his step brother started interfering with the plaintiff 's possession and obtained possession of the land. The plaintiff 'the father of the plaintiff died on 15th November 1949. The plaintiff claimed that the defendants had no title to the lands which they belonged to him and that the defendants have not acquired any title to the land. On the question whether the plaintiff was the owner or the plaintiff as the owner of the suit lands but whether the defendants were the trespassers in the possession of the plaintiff 'could not be held to have acquired title to the suit lands. HELD : (i) The plaintiff was not the owner of a document which merely purports to confer title on the plaintiff. The document itself does not create title to the plaintiff. It is only a mortgage which is created by the terms of the document. The document merely creates a title which may arise from the terms of it. [350 H] (ii) The document merely gives a right to the plaintiff to claim the benefit of the document if it appears to be contrary to the terms of its execution. The document does not create a title which can exist against the plaintiff. [349 C] (iii) The document itself did not create title in favour of the plaintiff. There was no evidence to show that the document was either created or created an oral agreement between the parties. The document was a mere agreement to sell the land. [360 E F]
5488: The respondent filed a petition for eviction against the appellant contending that he had become liable to be evicted from the premises in question under clause (d) of sub section (1) of Section 11 of the Bihar Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant had failed to pay rent for the two months of September, 1972 even though it accepted the plea of the appellant that he had paid the rent in December, 1972. [630E] 2. The receipt under which the said advance was received does not state that the amount of Rs.140 was advanced to the appellant with an understanding that it could be set off against the rent due for the months. It is true that if the parties were in pari delicto court would not come in the representative capacity of the tenant to make payment of the amount towards arrears of rent but the receipt must be in accordance with law. 2728: The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the appellant tenant on the plea that he had committed default in paying rent. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the order of the civil court was not duly passed and that the order was not properly made. In appeal, the High Court held that the order passed by the civil court is not 'dismissed. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the decree passed by the Civil Court was not duly executed and that the respondent was entitled to remain in occupation of the accommodation in question. [327E] (2) The High Courts have taken an erroneous view of the law. The High Court has failed to take into account the fact that the respondent had been given notice under section 7(1) of the Act before the commencement of the proceedings. The High Courts were wrong in taking the view that the order did not amount to a decree passed by a civil court. [328A B] (3) The High courts have taken the correct view of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High courts are bound to follow the procedure prescribed by the Code. It is only when the legislature has used the words "that the court has jurisdiction to make such order as it thinks fit". [329D E] (4) The High court has failed to do so because the provisions of the Code have not been complied with. The High court should have proceeded on the basis that the order must be set aside. [330C D] (5) The High. courts have taken into consideration the fact that if the order was made by the Government or the District Magistrate, it would be proper to hold that the order should be quashed. [339F G] (6) The Highcourt has failed to consider the matter afresh on the ground that the order could not be challenged in the High Court. The Highcourt had failed to take note of the fact that there was no provision in the Code for giving the opportunity of being heard. [337B C] (7) The High will have to satisfy the requirements of the provisions of section 13(1)(c) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act,
2302: The petitioners challenged the vires of the Taxation Laws (Extension to Union Territories) Regulation 3, 1963. They contended that the President had no power to promulgate the Regulation under article 240 of the Constitution and that the President was not competent to enact the impugned Regulation. Held:(1) that the President has no power to pass any law in relation to the administration of Pondicherry and brought into force on January 1, 1964. Section 4(2) of the Regulation was therefore ultra vires the Central Government. The Act did not provide for the amendment of the Schedule by the Finance Act, 1964. The amended Article 240 of the Constitu tion could not be said to have been made retrospective in operation. The amended article 240 was in pari materia with section 2(3) of the Central Act, 1962. The amended articles 121 were not applicable to the Union Territory of India. The amended Art 240 was not a law providing for the acquisition or extinction of rights in respect of income tax. The amended Articles 121 were not intended to confer on Parliament an exclusive right to legislate in respect of the levy of tax. The impugned Act was passed after the passing of the Act. The impugned was therefore ultra rites as being violative of article 14 of the Constitution.
3266: The assessee, a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea, entered into certain transactions in jute. On April 17, 1958 the assessee sold to the respondent 's principal amount of Rs. 1,000/ . In the assessment year 1959 60 the assessee claimed that the loss suffered by it was not a speculative nature as contemplated in explanation to sec. 24(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer held that the transaction involving mere transfer of delivery notes and not actual delivery of the goods were of a speculative character as contemplated in Explanation 2 to section 24(1). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. The Tribunal referred two questions to the High Court which answered them against the assessee. It held that the transactions involving mere transfer did not fall within the definition of an "sale" contained in Explanation 2(b) to section 24 (1) of Income Tax Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The question whether the transaction is a speculative or characteristic as a result of which the assessee had entered into the contract with the result that the loss would be carried forward and set off against speculation profits. [301D] The assessee had entered the contracts in question in the years 1957 to 1960 and 1961. The assessee had failed to do so. The assessee could not have been allowed to deal with the same in the year 1960. The assessee has failed to discharge the obligation under section 24(2) of the Indian Income Tax Act read with section 24(i) of the Act. The assessee was entitled to claim deduction of the loss sustained by him from the speculation profits in the year 1959 60. [310B C] Raghunath Prasad Poddar vs Commissioner of Income tax, Calcutta, ; , followed.
6504: The petitioners were appointed to the Indian Army as well as in 1962 and were governed by the Defence of India Rules, 1963. They were governed by those rules which were made applicable to the Central Services. In 1964, the Central Government issued a notification under Rule 5(b) of the Defence of Defence Rules, 1965 that the said Rules would be applicable to the petitioners. By another Notification dated March 25, 1966, the President in respect of certain posts of both AMEOT and AMEOE was included in Class II of Military Land and Cantonment Service (Class I and II) Rules, 1951 for the first time in 1964. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said Notification on the ground that it contravened articles 14, 19 and 31 inasmuch as the petitioners were not being confirmed in the service of the respondent, they were entitled to be promoted to the post of a higher grade. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioners were entitled to claim seniority from the date of confirmation and that their seniority should be reckoned from the date when they came to be absorbed in the service. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The petitioners are entitled to be considered to be promoted as senior to the respondent. [667D] 2. The petitioners are not entitled to be heard before the issue of the impugned Notification. The petitioners have been rightly selected to the post in question. The petitioners cannot claim seniority from an actual date of promotion or date of confirmation. The petitioners were not entitled to seniority from the dates of initial appointment. [668C D] 3. The petitioners could not claim seniority from dates of initial recruitment or date of promotion. The petitioners had no right to claim seniority. The petitioners did not claim seniority in any particular year. The petitioners ' case is that they were entitled only to seniority from dates on which they were promoted. The petitioners therefore cannot claim seniority on the basis of the seniority assigned to them. [669B C]
4772: The first respondent secured more votes than the appellant. He was declared elected to the Assembly seat on the ground that he had not qualified for election. His election was challenged by the appellant in a petition under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the provisions of article 324 did not apply to the Election Commission and that the procedure prescribed by the Act violated article 311(2) of the Constitution and directed the Election Commission to frame rules for holding elections to the Assembly. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the procedure prescribed under the Act violated articles 324 and 327 of the Constitution, (ii) the procedure provided therein could not be said to have been followed by the procedure prescribed in the Act; and (iii) the procedure laid down in the Act violated Article 311(3). HELD: (1)(a) The procedure prescribed under section 100 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, is not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act. [969 E] (b) The procedure which has been prescribed under the Rules made under the Act is a matter of control and supervision of the preparation of electoral rolls and also for the conduct of elections to the Parliament. It does not mean that the procedure laid under the Act should be followed by the Act itself. [970 C D] (c) The procedure laid down under the Act cannot be said to be mandatory or directory. [971 F G] (dissenting to the interpretation of the Act, the procedure prescribed thereunder must be followed by a trial court. [972 A B] (c] (c), (dissolvedon, vs Tanner ([1875] 1 S.C.R. 724), referred to.

On his appointment as Chairman of a private college he had been removed from service as Principal of another board. His appeal to the State Government against his dismissal order dated 13.10.85 was dismissed by the High Court. In the Special Leave Petition filed before this Court it was contended that the termination of his services in the light of the provisions of Section 3(4) of the Haryana Act, 1969 and the Rules framed thereunder were ultra vires the powers conferred by section 3(1)(a) of the said Act and that the termination by the termination of the services of the employee in the manner provided under the heading "Tenure of Office" issued by the Governor of Haryana is arbitrary and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. The expression 'Forfeiture of office ' means the post which is filled up by promotion or by transfer or by nomination from one department for a period of two years. The word 'shall ' in the definition of 'In office means the post in which the post is filled up. [112B C] 2.1 The word 'may ' in the context of the definition of the word 'shall mean the post in the post in question. The word may be used in the context in which the word 'may" is used in the definition clause. The word "shall" in the context must receive the meaning of the words "to the contrary". The word 'should not mean the word 'on the other part of the word. The word `shall ' connotes the word 'and 'were not intended to include the word 'another part of the same word 'on '. 3992: The appellant company was incorporated under the U.P. Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1948. In 1939 the Raza Ltd., and the Buland Ltd., entered into agreements with the erstwhile State of Rampur for the supply of sugarcane to the agricultural land. Under the U. P. Agricultural Income tax Act, 1948, the parties were required to pay a fair and equitable land revenue which was to be agreed upon by the company. On 5th May, 1935, the Razeley 's Managing Director wrote to the Razdars to submit returns of their agricultural income. The Raza ltL. was also informed that the Razadar had been assessed to tax on the agricultural lands. The R.M. was also communicated to the R.M., but the R.I. was not paid. Thereupon, the R. M. filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the assessment order dated 29th June, 1962, made by the Assessing Authority against the R. I.T.O. for the assessment years 1357 F to 1359 F. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the Assessing Authority committed an error of law in assessing the two partners of the Agricultural Company, Rampur, and not assess the firm as such. Court further held that the Assessing Authorities committed an error in assessing the second partner of the Agricultural Co operative Society, and not assessing the firm as so long as it did not include the assessee in the assessment proceedings. Against this decision of the High Court, the appellant company preferred an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has rightly decided that the Assessing Officer was wrong in assessing the four partners of the Agreements. [423B] 2.1 The provisions under the United Provinces Agricultural Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1947, are mandatory and must be construed strictly. It is only when there is a provision in the statute or the rules framed thereunder that the legislature makes a provision in a statute providing for the levy of tax, the authorities while proceeding with the assessment of the tax payable by the firm or the company can proceed to determine the amount of tax payable by each member of the firm or any other person. [424
150: The petitioner was detained under section 3(1)(a) of the . On the question whether the order of remand dated the 6th March, 1951, passed by the Court of the Additional District Magistrate, Delhi, is legal. HELD : (i) It is well settled that where a person has been detained under section 344 of the Criminal Procedure Code, and if he chooses to adjourn the case pending before the Court, it cannot be said that there is no order of remand in such circumstances, and the Court should not have made any order for release on the first occasion. [902 H] (ii) In the instant case, the Court had no power to pass an order of remand as the only one day could have been fixed for the purpose of making the order of release. The order of the Court was produced before the Registrar at 5 20 p.m. and was produced before him. There was no order of detention in this case. [903 D E]
1018: The respondent was appointed to the post of Head Constable and in the time of the departmental trial he was posted as a Police Officer, in charge of police station. On November 17, 1952, the District Magistrate sent an endorsement to the Superintendent of Police that the Sub Divisional Magistrate had found substantial complaints against the integrity of the respondent. On December 17, 1952 the respondent was placed under suspension and on August 18, 1953, he was put under suspension and his dismissal from service with effect from January 1, 1954. He filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court for quashing the order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the order of the dismissal was invalid because it set aside the order of discharge and directed the respondent to be reinstated in service. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The order of dismissal passed by the High Court was not made by a police officer senior to a Superintendent; (2) the trial was vitiated by a number of serious irregularities; and (3) the specific acts constituting offences were cognizable offences and therefore the Superintendent of police had no jurisdiction to proceed with a departmental trial without complying with the provisions of sub paragraph. [413 C D] (a) The order dated February 22, 1954, dismissing the respondent was not based on any material or irrelevant consideration. The order of the High Court is not only a report but also a final report. It is only when the report is made by a competent authority or even when the report has been made by a superior authority or when the order is made by another authority or when it is made by some authority other than the lower authority. The order was made by the Chief Secretary to the State Government and the order was made after the report was made by a subordinate authority. [414 E F] (b) The order was not made in such circumstances could not have been made by the respondent in the absence of any material or relevant consideration. The respondent was not given the opportunity of being heard at the enquiry. [415 B C] (c) The order did not amount to a punishment within the meaning of Article 311(2) of the Constitution. [416 A]
2643: The appellant was a firm carrying on business in the name and style of M/s Seth Brothers. In course of its business it had two partners, one of whom was the Managing partner and another of the three partners. On the return filed by the Income tax Officer for the assessment year 1960 61, the Commissioner of Income tax, U.P., on May 29, 1962 requested for the production of certain documents and the books of account which were produced. The Income tax Officer did not include these documents at all but directed the appellant to produce those documents. The appellant 's application under section 19(1) of the Act before the Commissioner of income tax was rejected by the Income Tax Officer. The appellant then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of the Commissioner. The High Court held that the documents seized were not relevant for the purpose of any proceeding under the Act. The Commissioner appealed to this Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the documents seized was not relevant for purposes of the Act; (ii) the provisions of section 132(3) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, or under sub s.(1) of section 132 of the Act, were not applicable to the proceedings under the Act; and (iii) the provisions contained in section 132(2) were not applicable as the orders of the Commissioner were not binding on him. HELD: (i) The provisions of section 13(1)(c) of the Income tax Act are not attracted because the orders of Income tax Officer are not binding on the assessee. [601D] (ii) The provisions contained in Section 132(3), and section 132(4) are not applicable to proceedings under the Income tax Acts. The provisions of the Act do not apply to proceedings under Chapter 1A of the Act. [603E F] (iii) The provisions in section 132 (3) and section 132 (4) are only directory and not mandatory. The provisions in the section are not intended to be used in a manner different from those of the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. The provisions are not intended for the purpose for which they are enacted. The provisions have been made with reference to the provisions of sections 132 and
5431: The appellants are the legal representatives of the East Punjab Government. They were granted a requisition for the requisitioned premises under the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952. The requisition was made on July 31, 1987. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said requisition. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellants were entitled to interest at the rate of 6% per annum from March 7, 1975 to 31st July, 1987 when principal amount of compensation had been paid and or when the premises in question had been de requisitioned and handed back to the owner, on the amount awarded. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellants are entitled to interest @ 6% per cent per annum as also the period from August 87, 1985 to July 31, 1986 and for that period only at the rate Of 12% per annum; that the appellants have been paying interest @ 6 % per annum; and that the appellants being entitled to interest in place of right to retain possession of the property after the expiry of three months from the date of the judgment of the High Court, the appellants are not entitled to interest. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellants are entitled at the rate at which they are entitled to retain possession. [630E] 2.1 The right of the appellants to retain possession is an implied agreement between the parties to the contract. It is a statutory right which can be enforced against the person claiming interest. If there is any difficulty in calculating the amount, the parties will be at liberty to recover the same. [631D E] 3.2 The right of a party to claim interest cannot be taken away by the statute. The right of an interest is an implied term of the grant or grant of a contract. The right to interest is an express term of the contract. The expression "benefit" has to be understood in the context of the purpose of the statute. [632F G] 4.3 The right of interest is an important element of the right to the interest. The right must be construed strictly in its entirety. The object of the statute is to secure the protection of the statute and the legislature has always presumed that the legislature does not
927: The appellant was appointed to the Chief Secretary of the State. He was dismissed from service on March 30, 1951. On August 19, 1950 he filed a suit for declaration that his services were illegally terminated and that he had not been removed from service. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it holding that the order of compulsory retirement did not amount to removal from service within the meaning of article 311 of the Constitution and as the requirement of that Article 311(2) was not complied with it held that the termination of service effected by the order was void in law. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the order was invalid because the action was taken by way of punishment and therefore the order was bad in law. HELD : (i) The order compulsorily retiring the respondent was passed without complying with the requirements of article 311(2). The order was not vitiated by any illegality or irregularity in the manner prescribed under article 311(1)(c). [902 H] (ii) The order was passed without compliance with the provisions of article 311 and was not invalid. It was not necessary that the action was in accordance with law. [903 D E] (iii) The order of compulsory retire the respondent was not passed without complying the requirements of Article 311(3) and the order was not invalid merely because the action is taken by way Of punishment. The order was therefore illegal and could not be sustained. [904 C] (iv) The order passed by compulsory retirement was not made without complying with section 6A of the Punjab Police Act, 1947. The order of dismissal was therefore not valid. [901 F G]
3306: The appellant was convicted under section 379 read with section 34 and 664 of the Indian Penal Code. He preferred an appeal against the order of conviction and sentence to the High Court but the appeal was unsuccessful. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the provisions of section 6 were not specifically brought to the notice of the High Court and the sentence of imprisonment passed against him, and that the offence was punishable with imprisonment for life. HELD: (i) Section 4(2) of the Probation of offenders Act, 1958 is intended for the benefit of juvenile delinquents, reflecting the anxiety of the Legislature to protect them from contact or association with hardened criminals in jails and retrieve them from a life of crime and rehabilitate them as responsible and useful members of society. It is therefore clear that even though the point relating to the applicability of section 6 was not raised before the learned Presidency Magistrate or the High Court, this Court is bound to take notice of the provisions of that section and give its benefit to the appellant particularly since it is a section which is intended for benefit of juvenile delinquent on the basis of the age of the offender and the character of the appellant. [655 C D] (ii) The conditions requisite for the applicability of s 6 are, however, plainly satisfied and under section 6, Sub section (1) it is not competent to the Court to impose an order of imprisonment on the appellant unless the Court is satisfied that having regard to the circumstances of the case including the nature of the offence and the character thereof, it would not be desirable to deal with the appellant under section 3 or section 4. [656 H 657 A]
5056: The first respondent, a company registered under the . was carrying on business in the manufacture of rice. In respect of the assessment years 1950 51 to 1952 and 1955 56, the company had been assessed to sales tax for the assessment year 1957 58. The company filed a suit for a declaration that the goods were not liable to excise duty as claimed by the company. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the company was not entitled to any relief. On appeal the High Court held that the company 's claim was barred by limitation.
