3921: The appellant was a public officer in the service of the respondent. He was charge sheeted for the offences under section 5(2) read with section S(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 161 I.P.C. The trial court convicted him but the High Court confirmed it. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the sanction was not valid as required by section 6(1)(c). HELD: (i) Section 6(1) (d) is not mandatory but only directory and not mandatory. [869 C] (ii) The proviso to section 6(2) does not apply to an order under sub rule (2) of rule 11. The proviso requires that the authority specified in column 4 of Part I of the Schedule to the order must be satisfied that the offence was committed within 30 days from the date of the order. The proviso does not require that the authority should have given the sanction before the commencement of the period of the order and the authority must give the necessary sanction before the passing of the order after the expiry of the period. The proviso further provides that if the authority has made any such recommendation before the commencement, the authority may make such recommendation without giving any reasons for the same. It would be quite clear from the language of the proviso that the authority has to satisfy himself that the offence had been committed within 30 months from the date when the order was made. The proviso also contemplates that the authority must have given the necessary sanction for the same purpose. The proviso is intended to cover cases where the authority has given the necessary permission before the commencement and the authority has done so. The proviso states that the authority shall have given the requisite sanction before the coming into force of the proviso. The proviso lays down that if the authorities have given the said sanction before the close of the period mentioned therein, the authority will have no power to pass the order on the ground that the authority had acted contrary to the provisions of the proviso and that the authority could not take action under the proviso. [870 D E; 871 A B]

On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the requirement of section 5(1)(b)(ii) was mandatory and that the failure to comply with the requirements of section 5 (2) (a) (ii) was fatal. The High Court in reference held against the assessee. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of section 5 of the Act were not mandatory and that even if the requirement of s.5(2)(b)(iii) was not complied with, the requirement was not satisfied. If the requirement is satisfied, the dealer has merely issued the certificate without specifying the amount of the amount which he may be liable to pay. 5940: The petitioners, who were working as the employees of the Indian Oil Corporation, challenged the legality of the classification of employees into different grades and their seniority was fixed at Rs.50 perquisites. Dismissing the Writ Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners are entitled to the benefit of the scheme. [8D] 2.1 The scheme is not a statutory one but it is an executive function. It has been accepted by the Government and its approval is given in the scheme. The petitioners have accepted the rationalised scheme. 1187: The petitioners, who were the owners of certain properties in which they had purchased from their fathers. It was contended that the order was a nullity as the notice under section 7 of the Act on which it was based did not amount to an evacuee property and that the order could be set aside only if it was issued to the petitioners or any person claiming any interest therein. Held, that the order must be quashed. Section 8(2) of the Act does not confer upon the Custodian any title to the property vested in him. The effect of the words "any other person" in section 10 is that the property in question or any interest therein may be evacuee property. The words "any person" in the (XXXI of 1950), are wide enough to include persons who have been declared as evacuee property. In the present case, the order was passed by the Custodian under section 11(3) of the , because the property in dispute was not evacuee property.
